instruct00414.title: Star Wars X-34 Landspeeder
instruct00414.text: This was my quick and dirty Landspeeder X-34 for my sons 6th birthday party. I didn't plan on an instructable, so the photos are a mixture of construction and deconstruction. (it took up ALOT of room, I needed the garage back) It's also my first instructable, so excuse the rough edges. The first step is to find a suitable chassis. I used an "Original KettCar" that we already had. I know that they have several models and sizes. It's pedal powered, although some of the younger kids needed to get a little boost to get all of the mass moving. Once you have your chassis, you need to identify your mounting points where you can build your sub structure. this method could be used for any sort of bodywork, although it could get quite heavy the more structure you have to build. I'm not sure how much more the drivetrain could handle. I Rested two 1"x10"x6' common pine boards on my mounting rails and measured between for my cross members. Once I had them tied together, they basically rested on the frame without any hard mounting points. I boxed in the steering wheel support at the front and the seat at the back to keep the sub structure from moving fore and aft. Once that is stable I added the 90 degree supports. I attached the shelves, 1"x8"x6' common pine boards to create the horizontal surface or the deck structure. (no clear photo) Using the crossmembers, create a horizontal structure that protrudes forward to support the deck up front, that has a vertical member that approaches the ground. the vertical member will be the foundation for the bowed side skirt. For the skirts/body, I had a stack of cheap paneling that was left in the garage. it has a very 70s wood printed on the front side. as you can see it's fairly flexible. this is a deconstruction photo so the skirt has some memory in the shape. it started out quite straight. first fasten the center of the skirt to the vertical member so that from the top the entire thing looks like a large "T". Over the course of 2 or 3 days, I used ratchet straps to slowly pull in the "wings" of the skirt until I could fasten them to the shelf structures on each side. This step looked like a large crossbow as the nose radius was slowly developed. deconstruction photos Once the skirts are in place, time to deck. First fit the cockpit making sure you have enough room for the nose. Once the cockpit is trimmed flush to the pine vert pine boards directly adjacent to the seat, simply use the side skirts to trim the deck paneling. Do the same for the rear portion of the deck. created the engine pods out of wood scraps and gallon or two flower pots. I felt that it needed a little something extra in the detail area so I decided to make a bumper sticker that I think any young Luke would appreciate. make some light sabers for some epic battles. they make a good whap with a direct hit! Enjoy!!!

instruct00602.title: Dollar Patio Chair Seat Replacement
instruct00602.text: I have two wicker patio chairs that both decided to come apart around the same time. Instead of trashing the set and buying a new one, I decided to try creating a new base that I could put a pretty cushion over. I stopped at the dollar store and picked up two 1/4 inch 100 foot "cloth rope". I sort of just winged the design since I am going for more structural stability than anything. Start by finding the two ends of the rope (you may need another person to help you here) hold the two ends together and stretch the rope out until you find the middle. Wrap the middle piece over the left bar of the chair and pull the ends through to start the knot. Pull Tight and repeat on the other side.. Pull the rope over the other side of the chair and pull the rope through the middle. Pull the rope over the string furthest from you and bring the rope under the string closest to you... Bring the rope over the first row and loop under and over the bar to start the next row. Make sure to pull the loop knot in close to the bar to make it nice and tight. Pull the rope nice and tight over, under and through.... Loop over the string furthest from you, bring under and over the string closest to you. Repeat steps 5-7 until you reach the back end of the chair.. Start the cross section by looping over and under the back bar and under the first rope. push and pull the rope over and under each cross section (no need to pull the rope all the way through each section, just go along pushing and pulling the rope over and under, giving yourself enough slack each time until you reach the end. then pull the remaining rope through. Keep going making new rows and pushing and pulling through until you reach the other side of the chair. At this point I had several feet of rope left, so after tying off at the corner (shown in next few pictures) I made a X across the chair and then tied a couple knots with the last bit of rope.

```markdown
# Structured Summary of Wicker Patio Chair Repair

## System Overview
The system is designed to repair two wicker patio chairs by creating a new base using cloth rope. The process involves knotting the rope around the chair's frame to provide structural stability and a surface for a cushion.

### Inputs
- Two 1/4 inch 100 foot cloth ropes
- Two wicker patio chairs in need of repair
- An additional person to assist (optional)

### Outputs
- Repaired chairs with new rope-based seating bases

### Process Steps

START: Begin the chair repair process.

INPUT: Take the two 1/4 inch 100 foot cloth ropes.

PROCESS: Find the two ends of one rope.
  - IF another person is available to assist, request their help.
  - Stretch the rope to find the middle.

PROCESS: Begin the knotting process.
  - Wrap the middle of the rope over the left bar of the chair.
  - Pull the ends through the loop to start the knot.
  - Pull tight to secure the knot.

PROCESS: Repeat the initial knotting process on the other side of the chair.
  - Wrap the rope over the right side of the chair.
  - Pull the rope ends through to create a knot.
  - Pull tight to secure.

PROCESS: Create the first row.
  - Pull the rope over the other side of the chair.
  - Weave the rope through the middle.
  - Loop the rope over the string furthest from you.
  - Bring the rope under the string closest to you.
  - Loop the rope over the first row and under then over the bar to start the next row.
  - Pull the loop knot close to the bar for tightness.

PROCESS: Continue weaving the base.
  - Pull the rope tight, weaving over, under, and through.
  - Loop over the string furthest from you, bring under and over the string closest to you.
  - DECISION [IF]: Have you reached the back end of the chair?
    - Yes: Proceed to start the cross-section.
    - No: Repeat steps 5-7.

PROCESS: Start the cross-section.
  - Loop over and under the back bar and under the first rope.
  - Weave the rope over and under each cross-section without pulling it all the way through.
  - Provide enough slack until reaching the end, then pull the remaining rope through.

PROCESS: Complete the weaving across the chair.
  - Continue creating new rows by pushing and pulling through until reaching the other side of the chair.

PROCESS: Finish and secure the rope.
  - DECISION [IF]: Is there several feet of rope left?
    - Yes: Create an X across the chair and tie knots with the remaining rope.
    - No: Secure the end of the rope without additional patterns.

OUTPUT: The chairs now have a new rope-based seating base, ready for cushions.

END: The chair repair process is complete.
```

instruct00052.title: Arduino Solar Tracker
instruct00052.text: What is does: It searches for the brightest light source like the sun.There is a newer and better version of this project: https://www.instructables.com/id/Dual-Axis-300W-IOT-Solar-Tracker/ How it works: I'd made a sensor of 4 LDRs with sheets between them The white dots are the LDRs When the stick on top is righted to the sun or the brightest point the four LDRs get the same amount of light on them. Example1 when the light is left on top: right-top, right-down, left-down are in the shadow and left-top get the most light Example2 when the light is on top left and right down are in the shadow and top is in the light 2 x servo's Ebay link 1.5$ / piece 4 x lightdepending resistors (ldr) Cheap LDR's on Ebay 0.78$ for 20 pcs 4 x resistors 10K Resistors on Ebay 0.78$ for 50pcs free shipping1 x Arduino Arduino UNO Ebay link 3.5$ free shipping 2 x potentiometers 10k (value doesn't matter) Ebay link Just hot glue it together!!! you can download the code down this page /* this code is written by geobruce for more info check my site http://xprobe.net */ #include <Servo.h> // include Servo library Servo horizontal; // horizontal servo int servoh = 90; // stand horizontal servo Servo vertical; // vertical servo int servov = 90; // stand vertical servo // LDR pin connections // name = analogpin; int ldrlt = 0; //LDR top left int ldrrt = 1; //LDR top rigt int ldrld = 2; //LDR down left int ldrrd = 3; //ldr down rigt void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); // servo connections // name.attacht(pin); horizontal.attach(9); vertical.attach(10); } void loop() { int lt = analogRead(ldrlt); // top left int rt = analogRead(ldrrt); // top right int ld = analogRead(ldrld); // down left int rd = analogRead(ldrrd); // down rigt int dtime = analogRead(4)/20; // read potentiometers int tol = analogRead(5)/4; int avt = (lt + rt) / 2; // average value top int avd = (ld + rd) / 2; // average value down int avl = (lt + ld) / 2; // average value left int avr = (rt + rd) / 2; // average value right int dvert = avt - avd; // check the diffirence of up and down int dhoriz = avl - avr;// check the diffirence og left and rigt if (-1*tol > dvert || dvert > tol) // check if the diffirence is in the tolerance else change vertical angle { if (avt > avd) { servov = ++servov; if (servov > 180) { servov = 180; } } else if (avt < avd) { servov= --servov; if (servov < 0) { servov = 0; } } vertical.write(servov); } if (-1*tol > dhoriz || dhoriz > tol) // check if the diffirence is in the tolerance else change horizontal angle { if (avl > avr) { servoh = --servoh; if (servoh < 0) { servoh = 0; } } else if (avl < avr) { servoh = ++servoh; if (servoh > 180) { servoh = 180; } } else if (avl == avr) { // nothing } horizontal.write(servoh); } delay(dtime); }

```markdown
# Solar Tracker System Summary

## System Overview
The system is designed to track the brightest light source, typically the sun, using a sensor array made up of four Light Dependent Resistors (LDRs) and control two servo motors to position the tracker towards the light source.

## Components
- 2 x Servo motors
- 4 x Light Dependent Resistors (LDRs)
- 4 x 10K Resistors
- 1 x Arduino UNO
- 2 x 10K Potentiometers
- Hot glue for assembly

## Code Overview
- The Arduino code uses the Servo library to control the servo motors.
- It reads the light intensity from the LDRs and adjusts the servos to position the tracker towards the brightest light.

## System Operation

### Initialization
START:
- Initialize Serial communication at 9600 baud for debugging.
- Attach servo motors to the appropriate pins on the Arduino.

### Main Loop
PROCESS: Read light sensor values
- Read analog values from the four LDRs.
- Read values from two potentiometers to set delay time (`dtime`) and tolerance (`tol`).

PROCESS: Calculate average light values
- Calculate average light intensity for top, bottom, left, and right sensor pairs.

PROCESS: Determine vertical adjustment
- Calculate the difference in light intensity between the top and bottom sensors (`dvert`).
- DECISION [IF]: Is `dvert` outside of the tolerance range?
  - Yes: Adjust the vertical servo angle (`servov`) to position towards the greater light intensity.
  - No: Do not change the vertical servo angle.

PROCESS: Determine horizontal adjustment
- Calculate the difference in light intensity between the left and right sensors (`dhoriz`).
- DECISION [IF]: Is `dhoriz` outside of the tolerance range?
  - Yes: Adjust the horizontal servo angle (`servoh`) to position towards the greater light intensity.
  - No: Do not change the horizontal servo angle.

OUTPUT: Write new servo positions
- Write the new vertical angle to the vertical servo.
- Write the new horizontal angle to the horizontal servo.

PROCESS: Delay
- Wait for a period determined by the `dtime` variable before running the loop again.

END: Repeat the loop indefinitely.
```

instruct00709.title: 40mm Burst Cannon
instruct00709.text: This little cannon is powered by bursting a rubber diaphragm with a bicycle pump. I cut the diaphragms from an old bicycle inner tube. You can double them up or burst one at a time. It uses 40mm foam practice golf balls for ammo. You can also use it with just the pump but it doesn't fire with near as much force. This is not my original idea. A few years ago I saw this rocket launching toy on TV. If you make this you could use the same replacement diaphragms.UPDATE: Apparently you can use more than just a rubber diaphragm. I've also tried duct tape and aluminum foil. It works great. Plumbing parts come in all shapes and sizes. These are no different. You could make the same set up bigger or smaller. You could even modify the barrel for a smaller diameter and use it for paper rockets. What you see here cost me $14.00. You'll also need a base and a way to attach it. I'm using the base form an Estes launching pad. The support bracket came from an old portable fan. I started by drilling a pilot hole with the end cap mounted in my lathe. From there I moved it to the drill press and drilled it out with a 1/2" bit. I used sand paper to ease the edges of the hole. Having a valve stem tool is helpful but not critical. Before pulling it in place I added a little grease to ensure a proper seal. Since only one side is pressurized you only have to worry about a seal at the valve stem and at the threads to the end cap. Before threading the cap into the union coupler I applied silicone grease. For the exit side I simply threaded the adapter on hand tight. I cut a section of pipe about 3" long. I then used a razor blade to round over both the inside and outside edges. This allows the foam balls to load without getting caught up. To smooth out the finish I used sandpaper. All that's left is to push the barrel into the adapter. This part is pretty straight forward. Use a pair of scissors to cut a section of bicycle tube out. Unscrew the coupler and use the male half as a template to cut a disc out. Without a foam ball in place this cannon is "call the police" loud. Check out the video and you'll see the air burst push the camera back (see the intro video at 1:05). Out of all the discs, only one ruptured with a slit. All the others took a star shape. Sometimes I'd see pieces of inner tube in the barrel. So keep in mind more than just a foam ball could come flying out. Don't shoot your eye out. I used the bracket of an old portable fan for a mount. I hot glued it on and added a couple zip ties for support. The base is an Estes model rocket launch pad. After a little machining on an aluminum tent stake it fit right in the base (see the last picture). Finally I painted it with rubberized undercoating. The barrel has an inner diameter of 35mm while the foam golf balls are 40mm wide. This makes a snug fit which is great for launching. While I'm using an old bicycle inner tube for diaphragms you could also use these.It works without the diaphragm but it doesn't go as far. As tempting as it might be, don't shoot other people with this. Thanks for reading.

```markdown
# Comprehensive Structured Summary of DIY Cannon Blog Post

## System Overview
The system described is a DIY cannon that uses a rubber diaphragm and a bicycle pump to launch foam projectiles. The construction involves using various plumbing parts and a base from a model rocket launch pad to create a functional cannon. ## System Steps

### Phase 1: Gathering Materials
PROCESS: Collect all necessary materials and tools.

- INPUT: End cap.

  - No: Proceed without it.

PROCESS: Assemble the cannon structure.

- PROCESS: Apply silicone grease to the threads before threading the cap into the union coupler.
- PROCESS: Thread the adapter onto the exit side hand tight.
```

instruct00070.title: How to Bleach Sand Dollars
instruct00070.text: Finding Sand Dollars while at the beach is always fun to do, just like searching for sea shells or looking for neat rocks. But natural Sand Dollars will rot and give off a nasty odor if not treated. So here is my instructable on how I treat/bleach a Sand Dollar. If you want information on how to find Sand Dollars, do a quick google search and there will be hunndreds of links for you to research up on! Anything big enough to hold your Sand Dollars flat and be able to have a few inches of solution in the bottom, a bucket wil lwork perfect for this but you may also improvise wish any container. Bleach, normal is fine but It just so happens I had scented laying around which will work perfect as well. Something to dry them on: Paper towel, Cloth towel, anything will work. The sun, It shouldn't be very hard to find a nice sunny spot for a couple of Sand Dollars to sunbathe. Sand Dollars... Of course! Fill your bucket up with about 3/4 a cup of bleach, no need to measure just dump in as much as you think is necessary. Next, fill up your bucket with a little water until your Sand Dollars will be able to be completely submerged. Place the sand dollars in the solution and let the bucket of Sand Dollars and Solution sit for a full 24 hours. Either inside or outside, try to keep the bucket warm. After 24 hours your Sand Dollars should look white! They may be a little yellow (The yellow will fade in the sun more, but not completely) and possibly have a few chips out of them at this point, which is normal, you can leave them i the solution longer if you please or take them out with the bit of yellow, which in my oppinion looks more natural and better then completely white. Dump out your bucket of bleach water and Sand Dollars, careful though as the Sand Dollars are VERY FRAGILE! Rinse out the bucket and set aside, rinse off your Sand Dollars as well and place the on your towel. Bring your towel outside and set in the sun. The Sand Dollars will need to sunbathe for a couple of hours in the hot sun. Usually from noon till the sun starts to go down (around 7 or 8). Retrieve your new bleached Sand Dollars! You now have your completed Sand Dollars, that you had fun finding and bleaching! Much more rewarding to find and bleach yourself then it is to buy at a gift shop! The bleaching process will make them more fragile then they were in their naturla state, I started with two of them as seen in the pictures but my smaller one shattered in the sun when I went to retreve it this evening. At least I managed to find two in the ocean!

```markdown
# Sand Dollar Bleaching Process

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Begin the process of treating and bleaching sand dollars.

### INPUT:
- Gather materials:
  - Sand dollars
  - A container (bucket or similar)
  - Bleach (scented or regular)
  - Towel (paper or cloth)
  - Access to sunlight

### PROCESS: Prepare Bleaching Solution
- Fill the container with approximately 3/4 cup of bleach. No precise measurement is needed.
- Add water to the container until there is enough to completely submerge the sand dollars.

### PROCESS: Submerge Sand Dollars
- Place the sand dollars into the bleach solution.

### PROCESS: Let Sand Dollars Soak
- Allow the sand dollars to sit in the solution for a full 24 hours.
  - Keep the container in a warm place during this period.

### DECISION [IF]: Check Sand Dollars after 24 Hours
- IF the sand dollars look white (with possible slight yellow tint and chips), proceed to next step.
- ELSE, leave them in the solution longer if desired.

### PROCESS: Remove Sand Dollars from Solution
- Carefully dispose of the bleach water.
- Handle the sand dollars gently as they are very fragile.

### PROCESS: Rinse Sand Dollars
- Rinse the used container and set aside.
- Rinse the sand dollars thoroughly to remove any remaining bleach solution.

### PROCESS: Dry Sand Dollars
- Place the rinsed sand dollars on the towel.
- Move the towel with sand dollars outside to a sunny spot.

### PROCESS: Sunbathe Sand Dollars
- Allow the sand dollars to sunbathe for several hours, optimally from noon until sunset (around 7 or 8 PM).

### OUTPUT:
- Retrieve the bleached sand dollars, now ready for display or use.

### DECISION [IF]: Check for Fragility after Sunbathing
- IF a sand dollar shatters, note that it is a natural result of the process and some may break.
- ELSE, proceed with the intact sand dollars.

### END:
- The process of finding, treating, and bleaching sand dollars is complete.
```

instruct00759.title: Quinoa Pizza Crust
instruct00759.text: Quinoa, pronounced as "Keen-wah" is a gluten-free whole grain that provides 8 essential amino acids. Quinoa is commonly used in salads, which is another delicious way to have it, but why have salad when you can have pizza?! The quinoa pizza crust is delicious, a bit doughy and another great way to make pizza healthier! The quinoa needs to be soaked for 8 hours so I'd soak it before heading out for the day, or before bed if you want to make it for lunch. I love dairy, but dairy doesn't love me so I used Daiya vegan cheese in this recipe. It taste and melts like real cheese! You can use regular mozzarella cheese instead. Update: I've been making the crust as a 'flatbread' to eat with Indian Curry/Butter Chicken instead of naan. Instead of Italian Seasoning and Cheese, I used 1/2 teaspoon Cumin, 1/4 teaspoon chili podwer, and 1 tablespoon of oil in the batter. The recipe is really forgiving/flexible! Totally satisfies my craving for carbs! Quinoa Crust - 2 servings 3/4 cup Quinoa 1/4 cup Water 1/2 teaspoon Salt 1 Clove of Garlic, chopped 1/2 teaspoon Black Pepper 2 teaspoon Italian Seasoning 1/4 cup Daiya Mozzarella Style Shreds or Mozzarella Cheese 1 tablespoon Olive Oil Toppings - I used all veggies to keep it vegan, but use whatever you like! Pizza Sauce Daiya Cheese Tomatoes Onions Jalapeno Peppers Garlic 1. Soak the quinoa in a bowl with enough water to cover all the grains, give it a stir and cover. Let it sit for 8 hours. 2. After the quinoa has soaked for 8 hours, preheat oven to 450 degrees F. 3. Drain the quinoa with a sive. 4. Blend all the crust ingredients (soaked quinoa, water, salt, garlic, black pepper, italian seasoning, cheese), except for the olive oil in a blender or Magic Bullet until smooth and thick like pancake batter. 5. Pour the batter into your pan and spread it evenly with a rubber spatula. I like it about 0.5 cm thick. Options: a. Line a 9 inch glass pie plate with parchment paper. This makes one personal size pizza usinghalf the pizza batter. b. Grease a cake or pizza pan with olive oil, heat the pan in the oven for 5 mins prior to use. c. Grease a cast iron skillet with olive oil, heat the skillet in the oven for 5 mins prior to use. Be careful when handling the hot pans, use oven mits. Use whatever size pan/skillet you have. The size of the pizza will depend on how thick you like the crust and how big your pans are, I prefer thin crust 'cause it's pretty hearty. A thick crust gets pretty dense.Update: If you don't care for a perfect round shape, I found parchment paper and a baking sheet works just fine. Option b & c are still good if you don't have parchment paper around. Because the batter is a lot like pancake batter, you can make fun shapes! I made a heart shape by pouring the batter and finessing it with the back of a spoon. You can also use a condiment/squeeze bottle for better control. If you're not good at free hand drawing, you can use a drawing underneath the parchment paper and just trace it with the batter. Don't forget to remove the drawing before baking! Next time, I'm going to make a dinosaur pizza! 6. Bake for 15 - 20 mins, until it's a nice golden brown. 7. Remove from oven and flip the crust, return the crust to the oven and bake for another 10 mins until it's a nice golden brown. 8. Spread pizza sauce evenly over the crust, add cheese and toppings. 9. Broil the pizza in the oven for 5 mins or until the cheese has melted. Bon appetite!

```markdown
# Quinoa Pizza Crust Recipe System

## Ingredients:
- Quinoa
- Water
- Salt
- Garlic
- Black Pepper
- Italian Seasoning
- Daiya Mozzarella Style Shreds or Mozzarella Cheese
- Olive Oil
- Pizza Sauce
- Toppings (e.g., Tomatoes, Onions, Jalapeno Peppers, Garlic)

## Steps:

### Quinoa Soaking
START: Begin the quinoa pizza crust recipe.
INPUT: Measure 3/4 cup of Quinoa.
PROCESS: Soak the quinoa in a bowl with enough water to cover all the grains.
PROCESS: Stir the quinoa and cover the bowl.
PROCESS: Let the quinoa sit for 8 hours to soak.
DECISION [IF]: Has the quinoa soaked for 8 hours?
    IF YES: Proceed to preheat the oven.
    IF NO: Continue soaking until 8 hours are completed.

### Preparing for Baking
PROCESS: Preheat oven to 450 degrees F (232 degrees C) after quinoa has soaked for 8 hours.
INPUT: Drain the soaked quinoa using a sieve.

### Making the Batter
INPUT: Add the following to the blender:
    - Drained quinoa
    - 1/4 cup Water
    - 1/2 teaspoon Salt
    - 1 Clove of chopped Garlic
    - 1/2 teaspoon Black Pepper
    - 2 teaspoons Italian Seasoning
    - 1/4 cup Daiya Mozzarella Style Shreds or Mozzarella Cheese
PROCESS: Blend all the crust ingredients until smooth and thick like pancake batter.
DECISION [IF]: Is the batter smooth and thick?
    IF YES: Proceed to prepare the pan.
    IF NO: Continue blending until the desired consistency is achieved.

### Preparing the Pan
INPUT: Choose one of the following pan options:
    a. Line a 9-inch glass pie plate with parchment paper.
    b. Grease a cake or pizza pan with olive oil.
    c. Grease a cast iron skillet with olive oil.
PROCESS: If using option b or c, heat the pan in the oven for 5 minutes.
PROCESS: Add 1 tablespoon of Olive Oil to the batter if not using cheese.
DECISION [IF]: Is the pan prepared and heated (if required)?
    IF YES: Proceed to pour the batter.
    IF NO: Continue preparing the pan as per selected option.

### Baking the Crust
INPUT: Pour the batter into the prepared pan.
PROCESS: Spread the batter evenly with a rubber spatula to about 0.5 cm thick.
PROCESS: Bake for 15-20 minutes until it's a nice golden brown.
PROCESS: Remove from oven and flip the crust.
PROCESS: Return the crust to the oven and bake for another 10 minutes until golden brown.
DECISION [IF]: Is the crust golden brown after flipping and additional baking?
    IF YES: Proceed to add toppings.
    IF NO: Continue baking until golden brown.

### Adding Toppings and Final Baking
INPUT: Spread pizza sauce evenly over the crust.
INPUT: Add Daiya Cheese and other desired toppings.
PROCESS: Broil the pizza in the oven for 5 minutes or until the cheese has melted.
OUTPUT: A delicious quinoa pizza crust with toppings is ready.
END: Enjoy the quinoa pizza!
```

instruct00757.title: 12" Powerbook External Antenna Hack
instruct00757.text: Everyone knows Powerbooks have terrible wi-fi reception. Unfortunately, only 15" and 17" Powerbooks facilitate adding your own external antenna. With just a few quick cuts you can modify a 12" Powerbook to take an external antenna as well. Airport Extremes use the MC Card connector. You could use any antenna you want as long as you get the right pigtail for it (and the impedance matches, which I think is 50 ohms here). I opted for a 5.5db flat blade antenna ($15), but there are many other options over here: http://sharperconcepts.zoovy.com/category/24ghzantennas/The connector coming off the existing internal antenna is going to have to be pushed back into the notch it comes out from. You'll quickly realize it doesn't go back far enough and obstructs the little metal flap from closing back. We'll cut part of that flap off. The battery itself is another problem. You'll have to cut a notch in the flat metal that sits right above the metal Airport Express flap in order to let the cable out. Start by covering up all the little crevices and cracks with masking tape so that only the little piece of the metal flap is exposed. Take that out with a Dremel using a cutoff wheel, then blow away the filings really well with compressed air. The flap should close around the internal antenna's connector with it shoved all the way back into the notch it comes out from. Unfortunately, the flap probably won't stay put any longer because you just cut off the piece of metal that keeps it in place. But that's ok. Now you need to notch the battery to let the cable out. If you cut a notch in the Airport Extreme flap properly, you should be able to lay the battery down on top of the cable as it snakes out. You can eyeball where you'll need to cut into the battery itself, in the flat piece of metal that sticks out. Mask the battery to prevent filings from getting in anywhere, and hit it with the Dremel using a cut-off wheel Getting it all back together can be a little bit of a trick. The problem is that the original internal antenna connector juts out just a bit too much, and I feel comfortable notching neither the connector nor the part of the battery that hits it. It's so close that you can just tightly tape the connector back in it's little nook, tape the flap shut, and drop the battery down with a little bit of jiggling. Voila! You've hooked up an external antenna! Now you realize the cable is thicker than the gap under the Powerbook. You need to put new feet on the bottom that raise the whole thing up about 4mm or so. I snagged some feet from the bottom of a Sonicwall Firewall that was being rackmounted, but you can improvise with anything that suits you, and Radioshack usually has some stick-on feet that will work. Now just stick some stick-on velcro on the back of the antenna to mount it to the display. You can substitute any antenna you want, provided it's designed for wi-fi usage. However, just about anything will perform better than the stock antenna!

instruct00157.title: Tagalong Cookies Recipe
instruct00157.text: Tagalongs (or Peanut Butter Patties as I knew them in my Girl Scout days) were always my favorite. There's just something about peanut butter and chocolate that only a cookie can make better. Or ice cream. Wait, that gives me an idea. . . . What was I saying? Right! Girl Scout Cookies are awesome. But it's not always GSC season! (see what I did there?) So now you can make your own, at home, any time of year. And since it uses the same recipe base as Trefoils and Samoas, you can turn your kitchen into a cottage industry of cookie goodness! First, you'll need the basic shortbread recipe, which you can find here. Just to have it handy, here's a repeat of those ingredients: 1 cup (2 sticks) butter, room temperature 115g (1/2 cup) sugar 250g (2 cups) all purpose flour 1/4 teaspoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract 2 tablespoons milk For the topping: 1 1/2 cups creamy peanut butter (peanut allergies? try almond butter!) 1/2 cup confectioners' sugar 1/2 tsp vanilla extract 8-oz milk chocolate - you may notice my picture includes semi-sweet. Mistake! In fact, for an even more copycat type chocolate coating, use this one. Prepare the dough as according to the shortbread recipe. Use a round cutter to cut the shapes. Bake your batches of cookies one sheet at a time for 10-12 minutes, rotating the cookie sheet 180 degrees, halfway through baking. This ensures that all the cookies turn the same color instead of getting browner in the hotter parts of your oven. Using a spoon, scoop, or your thumb, make an indentation in the center of each cookie. This is your well for peanut butter filling goodness. Do it before they cool! In a microwavable bowl, sift the powdered sugar into the peanut butter and mix well. Microwave in 30 second intervals, stirring between each, until very melty. Stir in vanilla. With a spoon, piping bag, or plastic bag with the corner cut off, pile your filling onto your cookies. As you might deduce, I used a piping bag with a star tip. It was the only one I had, and it made me sad because they looked so weird. But then the peanut butter filling held its shape after being coated in chocolate, and I decided to embrace and appreciate the weirdness. Sadly, before I opened my heart to the differently-shaped tagalong toppings, I squished out their uniqueness from most of the cookies before dipping. Next time I will leave it in. The final step to these tiny masterpieces is the chocolate coating. Melt your chocolate with tiny zaps in the microwave (you know how by now, yeah? - 30 second intervals, stir frequently, etc etc). Since we'll be constantly lowering the temp of the chocolate each time we dip a cookie, you may prefer to use the double-boiler method. Otherwise, keep your bowl in another bowl with a bit of hot water in it, and be prepared to re-zap the chocolate in the microwave whenever it gets too firm to work with. Just remember - the less you heat your chocolate, the better. (that's not a technical measure or anything, just a good thing to keep in mind) Dip your cookies in the chocolate with a fork, give that fork some healthy taps on the side of the bowl to remove the excess chocolate, and place cookies on waxed paper to cool. Enjoy!

```markdown
# Homemade Tagalongs Recipe System

## Ingredients and Materials
- **START**
- INPUT: Basic Shortbread Ingredients
  - 1 cup (2 sticks) butter, room temperature
  - 115g (1/2 cup) sugar
  - 250g (2 cups) all-purpose flour
  - 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
  - 1/2 teaspoon salt
  - 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
  - 2 tablespoons milk
- INPUT: Topping Ingredients
  - 1 1/2 cups creamy peanut butter
  - 1/2 cup confectioners' sugar
  - 1/2 tsp vanilla extract
  - 8-oz milk chocolate
- INPUT: Equipment
  - Oven
  - Microwave
  - Cookie cutter
  - Mixing bowls
  - Piping bag or plastic bag
  - Fork
  - Baking sheet
  - Wax paper

## Shortbread Cookie Base
- PROCESS: Preheat oven as per shortbread recipe instructions.
- PROCESS: Prepare the shortbread dough according to the recipe.
- PROCESS: Roll out dough and use a round cutter to cut cookie shapes.
- PROCESS: Place cookies on baking sheet.
- PROCESS: Bake cookies for 10-12 minutes, rotating the sheet 180 degrees halfway through.
- OUTPUT: Baked shortbread cookies

## Peanut Butter Topping Preparation
- PROCESS: While cookies are baking, prepare the peanut butter filling.
- INPUT: Sift confectioners' sugar into the peanut butter.
- PROCESS: Mix the peanut butter and sugar until well combined.
- PROCESS: Microwave the mixture in 30-second intervals, stirring between each, until melty.
- INPUT: Stir in vanilla extract into the peanut butter mixture.
- PROCESS: With a spoon, piping bag, or plastic bag, add the filling onto each cookie.
- OUTPUT: Cookies with peanut butter topping

## Chocolate Coating
- PROCESS: Melt chocolate using microwave or double boiler, stirring frequently.
- DECISION: Is the chocolate too firm to work with?
  - IF Yes: Reheat chocolate until workable.
  - IF No: Continue to next step.
- PROCESS: Dip cookies into chocolate using a fork.
- PROCESS: Tap fork to remove excess chocolate.
- PROCESS: Place chocolate-coated cookies on wax paper to cool.
- OUTPUT: Chocolate-coated cookies with peanut butter topping
- **END**

## Final Product
- OUTPUT: Homemade Tagalong cookies ready to enjoy.
- **END**
```

instruct00443.title: How to Make a Flashing LED Paracord Bracelet
instruct00443.text: Learn how to make flashing LED paracord bracelets to make sure you can be seen! To make your LED paracord bracelet you will need the following things:ParacordTape measureScissorsLighterAn LED wrist band of some sort To make an 8" bracelet you will need approximately 8 feet of paracord. Cut a little bit longer if you want to be certain you'll have enough! When you are ready to begin weaving place your LED band over the centre of the paracord. Take the left side cord and cross it over the band and then underneath the right side cord. Then take the right side cord underneath the LED band and up through the gap you have made with the left. Then pull tight! Now you need to do the same thing but starting with the cord on the right hand side this time. Take the right cord over the LED band and under the left cord. Take the left cord behind the LED band and up through the gap. Pull tight! Now you just need to keep repeating that pattern all the way down the band. Be careful with your spacing though. Try to keep it as even as possible all way down as it can be tricking to readjust it afterwards. When you reach the end, pull the paracord tight. Snip the ends short and take your lighter to melt them slightly. Pat them down with your finger to bond them to the rest of the paracord and they won't come undone. These LED bracelets are great for wearing out in the dark whether you are walking, running or cycling to keep you safe and make sure you can be seen. And of course they are always good for a rave too! Most LED bands, like the ones I have here, have 3 lighting modes so you can make them flash slowly, fast or stay on constantly. There are tons of colour options too! Check out mine here http://ebay.eu/17USCyd

```markdown
# Flashing LED Paracord Bracelet Making System

## Inputs:
- Paracord (~8 feet for an 8" bracelet, plus extra for assurance)
- Tape measure
- Scissors
- Lighter
- An LED wrist band

## Outputs:
- A completed LED paracord bracelet with flashing capabilities for visibility in the dark

## Process:

### START:
- Begin the process of making a flashing LED paracord bracelet.

### INPUT:
- Measure and cut approximately 8 feet of paracord for an 8" bracelet, adding a bit extra to ensure there is enough material.

### PROCESS:
- Place the LED band at the center of the cut paracord.

### PROCESS:
- Cross the left side of the paracord over the LED band and then underneath the right side of the paracord.

### PROCESS:
- Take the right side of the paracord underneath the LED band and up through the gap created by the left side.

### OUTPUT:
- First knot is completed.

### PROCESS:
- Pull the knot tight.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the knot starting with the left cord tight?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Pull tighter and ensure the knot is secure before proceeding.

### PROCESS:
- Start the next knot by taking the right cord over the LED band and under the left cord.

### PROCESS:
- Take the left cord behind the LED band and up through the gap.

### OUTPUT:
- Second knot is completed.

### PROCESS:
- Pull the knot tight.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the knot starting with the right cord tight?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Pull tighter and ensure the knot is secure before proceeding.

### PROCESS [LOOP]:
- Continue repeating the pattern of alternating starting sides and knotting over the LED band until the bracelet is fully woven.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the weaving spacing even throughout the bracelet?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Adjust the knots for even spacing before proceeding.

### PROCESS:
```

instruct00695.title: Waikiki 'ahi (Tuna Steak) Sandwich
instruct00695.text: This awesome, tender tuna steak sandwich will have your friends in raptures! Simple and quick to grill, it is a winner everytime! The Hawaiian's call their tuna: 'ahi. This sandwich has been inspired by my visit to the Diamond Head Market & Grill in Waikiki, Oahu, Hawaii, in August 2007. After climbing the 232 metre volcanic crater I had worked up quite an appetite, which I sated at this roadside eatery on the walk back to my hotel. Yummy! Every time I grill this at home, it takes me back to paradise! This sandwich is very simple to create, and has always attracted rave reviews when served to family and friends. Created by Steve: SBDESIGNS Preparation Time: 10mins (Have everything ready prior to grilling) Cooking Time: 5mins Ingredients (Per Person): 100g TUNA Steak (see Note [1]) Olive/Canola/Cooking OIL (Spray cans are good) Hamburger BUN, halved Handful shredded LETTUCE 1/8 ONION, sliced, halved 1 teaspoon SOY SAUCE (SHOYU) 2 heaped teaspoon MAYONNAISE WASABI to taste (see Note [2]) Note [1]: Buy top quality Tuna steak if possible (sashimi quality is the best). It often comes in 2.5cm / 1" thick 200g steaks, so butterfly and then separate completely into individual 100g 1.25cm / 1/2" steaks. Note [2]: I buy wasabi (hot Japanese Horseradish sauce) in prepared tubes that I keep in the refrigerator. Only a 1-2cm (3/8 - 3/4") squirt is sufficient per person. Cooking Instructions: 1. Heat BBQ to HOT. 2. Combine the wasabi and mayonnaise in a small dish, set aside. 3. Split the bun and butter the insides. Ensure that all components are beside the BBQ and ready before commencing cooking, due to short cooking time. 4. Cook onions on flat plate with 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce (shoyu). When almost ready (soft), add further 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce (shoyu). 5. Whilst onions are cooking, place bun halves face down on BBQ until toasted. 6. Remove and spread bottom half of bun with wasabi mayonnaise. 7. Top with shredded lettuce. 8. Lightly coat both side of the tuna with Oil, and gently place onto the BBQ grill, and cook for around 45secs each side according to desire (see Note [3]). 9. Remove and gently place onto the bottom half of bun. 10. Top with marinated onions, cover with the top of bun. 11. Enjoy. Use toothpicks and cut in half for presentation, if desired. Simply serve on its' own for a light lunch, or for a larger meal: with a light salad, potato wedges, or both Note [3]: In cooking tuna, treat it like the 'steak of the sea' and cook to medium-rare, the heat left in the fish will continue to cook to medium whilst you are eating it. Recently I have been soaking the onions in 1 teaspoon of soy sauce for at least two hours prior to cooking. Variations: (1) THAI SWEET CHILLI SAUCE instead of wasabi in the mayonnaise. (2) Place a slice of TASTY CHEESE on tuna after the first turn. (3) Add sliced TOMATO along with the lettuce. (4) Pre-marinate tuna in GINGER-SOY or TERYAKI marinade. (5) Add a PINEAPPLE ring (grilled also, if preferred). I hope you enjoy my creation! Let me know your thoughts, Steve (SBDESIGNS). P.S.: My mate calls it the ikiki Beach Burger (Watch the movie: Spirit of 76).

```markdown
# Tuna Steak Sandwich Recipe System

## Ingredients and Preparation

### Ingredients (Per Person):
- 100g TUNA Steak
- Olive/Canola/Cooking OIL (Spray cans are good)
- Hamburger BUN, halved
- Handful shredded LETTUCE
- 1/8 ONION, sliced, halved
- 1 teaspoon SOY SAUCE (SHOYU)
- 2 heaped teaspoon MAYONNAISE
- WASABI to taste

### Notes:
- [1] Buy top quality Tuna steak (sashimi quality is the best). Butterfly and then separate into individual 100g 1.25cm / 1/2" steaks.
- [2] Use a 1-2cm (3/8 - 3/4") squirt of wasabi per person.
- [3] Cook tuna to medium-rare.

### Preparation Time:
- 10mins (Have everything ready prior to grilling)

### Cooking Time:
- 5mins

## Cooking Instructions

START: Begin Tuna Steak Sandwich preparation.

PROCESS: Preheat BBQ to HOT.

PROCESS: Combine the wasabi and mayonnaise in a small dish, set aside.

INPUT: Butter the insides of the hamburger bun.

PROCESS: Ensure all components are beside the BBQ and ready before commencing cooking.

PROCESS: Cook onions on flat plate with 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce until almost ready, then add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce.

PROCESS: While onions are cooking, toast the bun halves face down on BBQ.

OUTPUT: Toasted bun halves.

PROCESS: Spread the bottom half of the bun with wasabi mayonnaise.

PROCESS: Top the bottom half of the bun with shredded lettuce.

PROCESS: Lightly coat both sides of the tuna with oil.

PROCESS: Gently place the tuna onto the BBQ grill, cook for around 45 seconds each side.

DECISION [IF]: Is the tuna cooked to medium-rare?
- Yes: Proceed with the next step.
- No: Continue cooking until medium-rare.

PROCESS: Remove tuna from the grill and gently place onto the bottom half of the bun.

PROCESS: Top with marinated onions.

PROCESS: Cover with the top half of the bun.

OUTPUT: Tuna steak sandwich ready to be served.

PROCESS: Optionally, use toothpicks and cut the sandwich in half for presentation.

END: Enjoy your Tuna Steak Sandwich!

## Variations:

PROCESS: Consider the following variations for different flavors:
1. Use THAI SWEET CHILLI SAUCE instead of wasabi in the mayonnaise.
2. Add a slice of TASTY CHEESE on tuna after the first turn.
3. Include sliced TOMATO along with the lettuce.
4. Pre-marinate tuna in GINGER-SOY or TERIYAKI marinade.
5. Add a PINEAPPLE ring (grilled also, if preferred).

END: Variations completed.

## Serving Suggestions:

PROCESS: Serve the sandwich on its own for a light lunch, or with a light salad, potato wedges, or both for a larger meal.

END: Serving suggestions provided.
```

instruct00509.title: Ice Box Air Conditioner
instruct00509.text: This gadget will save your life in the summertime! Out of desperation, in the summer of 2002, I made this improvised "air condition" unit. 2002 was the warmest summer in years, and i almost melted! This might sound like a joke, but it truly does work. You don't need to cool down the entire room to feel comfortable. Cooling down the air in your immediate suroundings is sufficent to keep your cool. Read on to find out how to stay cool using scrap parts you probably have lying around already. Please rate it, if you like it :) To make my air conditioner, i used: 1 2-liter ice box 2 ice box lids 1 80mm PC fan 1 fan grill 1 12 Volt transformer, or any other power source from 5-12 volts. Fill the container with ice. Or ice cream, if you like that vanilla aroma in the air :) The temperature transfer happens at the surface of the ice, so the more surface, the colder the air will get. Ice cubes makes really great cold air, but melt fast. A solid block of ice doesn't get you that cool air, but can last for hours. Hope this can save your summer too! Rate it if you like it :-)

instruct00103.title: Digital Business Card With NFC
instruct00103.text: NFC is found everywhere these days from credit cards to door locks, but must importantly: your smartphone! With a few simple steps and relatively low costs you can create a digital business card that uses NFC and can be read by a smartphone to transfer contact information. This high-tech solution makes exchanging your contact information not only fast and easy, but also makes you look very cool! (this Instructable was made for the TfcD course @ TU Delft) Creating a digitalbusiness card is quite simple and doesn't have to be very expensive. Here's what you need:Some NFC tags. We got ours from nfc-nederland.nl, but you can find them on Amazon or DealExtreme as well. Be sure to check how much memory you need to put all your information on one, since NFC tags have a REALLY small storage capacity (think bytes!). A smartphone with an NFC chip (most current cell-phones have one). An App for reading and writing NFC chips. We used NFC Tools, since it allowed us to create a command that opens a link on your phone with a relatively small number of bytes. First, check to see if you're NFC chip is empty and ready for writing. Ours came with a link to the App we're using on it. Simply turn on NFC communication on your phone and hold the chip to your phone to see what's on it.If yours has some data on it as well you'll have to format it before you can use it. Now select the information you want to put on your NFC tag. Since ours couldn't contain much data we decided to simply put a link to our LinkedIn account on it. (you can print them on A4, one-sided) You can now use your card to quickly hand over your contact information and expand your network! instruct00793.text: Here's a fun little project to turn a stuffed animal in to a great hiding spot for your valuables. its cheap and super fun for kids and adults alike. Enjoy. :) Also... if you put a glow stick in the jar and then close it, it becomes a really cool night light. Take the head of carefully and cleanly and remove some stuffing. 2.A- get the jar in there with a layer of stuffing around it so the stuffed animal keeps it shape2.B- slowly hot glue the edge of the fabric to just under the threads of your jar, (push the stuffing down just a bit to make the fabric easier to glue)2.C- hold jar until glue sets you can do this with the lid attached or not. i prefer it to be on the jar so the teddy bears head is facing the correct wayglue the head on to the lid with the glue being just above the ridge of the lid to completely sink it into the head, and attach the head in the same fashion you did the body. After the head is glued on, make sure the glue held snugly and tight (you will be twisting this part on and off. after all the glue dries you will have your very own Stashimal. now your ready to hide what ever it is your little heart desires.

```markdown
# Stashimal Creation Process

## START:
- Begin the Stashimal project.

## INPUT: Gather Materials
- Stuffed animal.
- Jar with a lid that fits inside the stuffed animal.
- Hot glue gun and glue sticks.
- Scissors.
- Glow stick (optional for night light feature).

## PROCESS: Prepare the Stuffed Animal
- Carefully and cleanly remove the head of the stuffed animal.
- Take out some stuffing to make room for the jar.

## PROCESS: Insert the Jar
- Place the jar inside the stuffed animal.
- Surround the jar with a layer of stuffing to maintain the stuffed animal's shape.

- Push down the stuffing around the jar's opening.

- Hold the jar until the glue sets to ensure a strong bond.

## PROCESS: Attach the Head to the Lid
- Apply glue just above the ridge of the lid.
- Attach the head of the stuffed animal to the lid, ensuring it faces the correct way.

## PROCESS: Finalize the Stashimal
- Check that all glued parts are snug and tight.
- Allow all the glue to dry completely.

## OUTPUT: Complete Stashimal
- You now have a Stashimal ready to hide your valuables.

## DECISION [IF]: Do you want to create a night light feature?
  - Yes: Insert a glow stick into the jar and close it.
  - No: Skip this step.

## END:
- The Stashimal creation process is complete.
```

instruct00845.title: Cardboard Box Moose Head Wall Hanging
instruct00845.text: OK, so this is my first instructable, so be gentle! What to do with an old cardboard box? Easy, make a moose head with it... I'll show you how. Takes about 2-3 hours. There is a good chance you already have all the bits and pieces necessary already (making this pretty much FREE to make!). Here's a list of what you'll need: - Large cardboard box - Scissors - Pencil - Stanley knife (or box cutter) - Ruler - Cutting mat - Sellotape - Hot glue gun - Computer & projector (or an A4/A3 printer instead) - Template ZIP file (Cardboard-Moose-Head-Template.zip) attached I used my projector for this next step as it allowed me to scale up the moose to the size of the box I had, but you can use your printer if you use Poster Printing to span multiple pages (especially in Corel Draw or Illustrator in the printing preferences). - Cut up the box into flat pieces - Project the template files onto a wall and trace around them with a pencil - If printing, use masking tape to loosely stick the designs over the cardboard for cutting out the design NOTE: if printing, make sure you keep the scaling the same size so that all the pieces are the right proportionate size. If projecting, make sure 'Actual Size' is selected in your image viewer, for the same reasons. Use a new blade to carefully cut-out the pieces. This is the most time consuming part. Make sure you keep the blade at 90 degrees to the design to get a nice clean edge. For this step cut out the widths for the fitting slots according to the width of your cardboard box. The card I was using for this one was double thickness, but yours may be much narrower, so cut accordingly. The template files use conservative estimates for the fitting slots, so you will have to offer up the pieces individually to get exactly the right fit for your size cardboard. It takes a bit of trial and error, but persist because this looks great when it's finished. Next, start at the nose end and slide in the first pieces to the middle head piece (but do the nose last). As you slot in each piece use the hot glue gun on the back only to fix in place (see last two images from this step). Once you've glued all the pieces to the central main head piece, slot in the main head side pieces x2. Glue each piece with a bit of glue gun glue from the back. Once you've slotted and glued the Moose pieces together you'll need to slot it into the rear mounting shield. Same procedure as before, slot together and glue from behind. Cut out a chevron shape from some spare card, wide enough to span the width of your three main head pieces that fit into the rear shield. Wrap with a bit of sellotape to reinforce it for hanging. Cut out small pieces from the main head pieces (image 3 of this step), having marked out where they need to go with the chevron you just cut out. Hot glue gun the chevron in place and voila, one cardboard box moose! Lastly, hang on the wall and enjoy! Thanks for reading and I hope you make one for yourself :) Please post up any that you make...

```markdown
# Cardboard Moose Head Creation System

## System Overview
The system takes a user through the process of creating a moose head out of cardboard. It includes preparing the materials, cutting out the shapes, assembly, and mounting the finished product.

## Inputs
- Large cardboard box
- Scissors
- Pencil
- Stanley knife (or box cutter)
- Ruler
- Cutting mat
- Sellotape
- Hot glue gun
- Computer & projector (or A4/A3 printer)
- Template ZIP file (Cardboard-Moose-Head-Template.zip)

## Outputs
- Assembled cardboard moose head ready for wall mounting

## Process Steps

### START
- Begin the process of creating a cardboard moose head.

### PROCESS: Prepare Materials
- INPUT: Gather all necessary materials listed above.

### PROCESS: Template Setup
- DECISION [IF]: Is a projector available?
  - Yes: Proceed to use the projector.
  - No: Use an A4/A3 printer for template printing.
- PROCESS: If using a projector
  - Project the template files onto a wall.
  - Trace around them with a pencil on the cardboard.
- PROCESS: If using a printer
  - Print the template using Poster Printing to span multiple pages.
  - Use masking tape to stick the designs over the cardboard.
- STORE: Ensure scaling is consistent for all pieces.

### PROCESS: Cut Cardboard
- Cut up the box into flat pieces using a Stanley knife or box cutter.
- Maintain the blade at a 90-degree angle for clean edges.
- Adjust the widths of fitting slots based on the thickness of the cardboard.

### PROCESS: Assemble Moose Head
- Start at the nose end and slide in the first pieces to the middle head piece, excluding the nose.
- Use the hot glue gun to fix each piece in place from the back.

### PROCESS: Attach Side Pieces
- Slot in the main head side pieces x2.
- Glue each piece from the back with the hot glue gun.

### PROCESS: Attach to Rear Mounting Shield
- Slot the assembled head into the rear mounting shield.
- Glue from behind to secure.

### PROCESS: Prepare Mounting Chevron
- Cut out a chevron shape from spare cardboard for hanging.
- Wrap with Sellotape for reinforcement.

### PROCESS: Final Assembly
- Cut out small pieces from the main head pieces to fit the chevron.
- Hot glue the chevron in place.

### OUTPUT
- OUTPUT: A fully assembled cardboard moose head.

### PROCESS: Mounting
- Hang the cardboard moose head on the wall.

### END
- The cardboard moose head creation process is complete.
```

instruct00514.title: Black Pepper-Garlic Chicken
instruct00514.text: Here's one on my favorite Stir-fry recipes, inspired by Black Pepper Chicken served at Panda Express Restaurants. The savory sauce took a bit of tinkering, but I think this copycat version is really close... and it's delicious, too! Please... don't forget to start this recipe with Velveted Chicken. It's a very simple technique that'll turn any Chicken Stir-fry into a mouth-watering Asian masterpiece!Ingredients: 1 lb. Velveted Chicken (recipe link above) 2 cups thinly sliced Celery 1/2 cup thinly sliced Onion- red or yellow 1/2 cup sliced Green onions 1-2 teaspoons chopped garlic 2 Tablespoons Canola or Peanut Oil for frying Sesame Seeds for garnish- optionalSauce Ingredients: 1/4 cup Oyster sauce 2 teaspoons Soy Sauce 1 teaspoonBlack Pepper (to taste) 2-3 teaspoons mild Molasses or honey (to taste) 1 teaspoon Rice Vinegar or Rice Wine (Sake) 1/2 teaspoon Sesame OilTools: Large stainless steel skillet or wok. Teflon-coated pans are notsuitable and can be damaged by high heat. Wooden spoonPreparation: Stir all of the sauce ingredients together in a small bowl, allowing about 10-15 minutes for the flavors to mingle/mature while you slice the vegetables. Before stir-frying, taste the sauce and adjust the heat and sweetness as desired.Stir-fry: Heat 2 Tablespoons oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat until almost smoking. Add the sliced red/yellow onions to the skillet, stirring constantly for about one minute. At this point, your skillet has cooled down significantly. Crank the heat up to high if neccessary. Add the sliced celery, green onions and chopped garlic to the skillet. Stir constantly for 1-2 minutes until the celery is tender-crisp. Add the stir-fry sauce. Heat and stir until the sauce is bubbling hot. Add the velveted chicken, reduce the heat to medium and stir to coat. Let the chicken heat through, about 1-2 minutes longer.Serve overprepared Basmati or Jasmine Rice. Garnish with sesame seeds and additional sliced green onions as desired.Enjoy!

```markdown
# Stir-Fry Black Pepper Chicken System

## Ingredients Input
- INPUT: 1 lb. Velveted Chicken
- INPUT: 2 cups thinly sliced Celery
- INPUT: 1/2 cup thinly sliced Onion (red or yellow)
- INPUT: 1/2 cup sliced Green onions
- INPUT: 1-2 teaspoons chopped Garlic
- INPUT: 2 Tablespoons Canola or Peanut Oil
- INPUT: Sesame Seeds for garnish (optional)

## Sauce Ingredients Input
- INPUT: 1/4 cup Oyster Sauce
- INPUT: 2 teaspoons Soy Sauce
- INPUT: 1 teaspoon Black Pepper
- INPUT: 2-3 teaspoons Molasses or Honey
- INPUT: 1 teaspoon Rice Vinegar or Rice Wine (Sake)
- INPUT: 1/2 teaspoon Sesame Oil

## Tools Input
- INPUT: Large stainless steel skillet or wok
- INPUT: Wooden spoon

## Preparation Process
- START
- PROCESS: Mix all sauce ingredients in a small bowl
- PROCESS: Allow sauce to mingle for 10-15 minutes
- DECISION [IF]: Is the sauce flavor balanced?
  - [YES]: Proceed to stir-frying
  - [NO]: Adjust heat and sweetness of sauce
- END

## Stir-Fry Process
- PROCESS: Preheat skillet or wok with oil over medium-high heat until almost smoking
- PROCESS: Add sliced onions, stir for about one minute
- DECISION [IF]: Has the skillet cooled down significantly?
  - [YES]: Crank the heat up to high
  - [ELSE]: Continue with current heat
- PROCESS: Add sliced celery, green onions, and chopped garlic, stir for 1-2 minutes until celery is tender-crisp
- PROCESS: Pour in the stir-fry sauce, heat until bubbling
- PROCESS: Add velveted chicken, reduce heat to medium, stir to coat and heat through for 1-2 minutes
- OUTPUT: Cooked Stir-Fry Black Pepper Chicken
- END

## Serving Process
- PROCESS: Serve Stir-Fry Black Pepper Chicken over prepared Basmati or Jasmine Rice
- PROCESS: Garnish with sesame seeds and additional sliced green onions if desired
- OUTPUT: Ready-to-eat Stir-Fry Black Pepper Chicken dish
- END
```

instruct00162.title: Step-By-Step Toasting Hamburger Buns on Stove
instruct00162.text: Sometimes, when you try cooking something so simple, turns out disastrous! This is my never fail easy-to-follow toasted hamburger bun recipe. There are a number of ways to toast hamburger buns, but for me the easiest way is on the stove. 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter2 hamburger buns Put a medium sized skillet on a stove burner set to "Medium" heat. * Don't use a higher heat setting. Higher heat causes the bun to brown or burn quickly. Allow the pan to heat for approximately 30 seconds. Melt the butter. Split open the bun and brush melted butter over the cut sides of both halves.* Make sure to coat the entire cut side, including the edges, doing so helps the edges from burning. Add two buns to skillet, toasting only cut sides of buns. Toast, without moving, until both cut surfaces turn light golden brown. Check the buns after 9-11 seconds,( I count "one thousand one,one thousand two, one thousand three" then I check the toasting process). If when checking, the bun is too light, continue toasting, and toast to desired doneness.* Don't leave the stove, and keep checking to avoid buns from burning !!!!! Remove buns from the pan and use it immediately. Or toast buns 30 minutes to 1 hour ahead of time , simply cover with a warm towel (helps to keep buns from drying out) until ready to use. When toasting, burgers and sandwiches taste better because the buns do not soak up the juices of the ingredients. You can toast anything, from hamburger buns, grinder rolls, hotdog buns to assorted yeast breads and rolls!!

```markdown
## Ingredients
- 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter
- 2 hamburger buns

## Equipment
- Medium-sized skillet
- Stove

## Procedure

- Begin the toasting process.

### PROCESS: Preheat Skillet
- INPUT: Place medium-sized skillet on stove burner.

- DECISION [IF]: Are the buns light golden brown after initial check?

  - No: Continue toasting until desired doneness is achieved.
- OUTPUT: Toasted hamburger buns.

  - No: Keep checking to avoid burning.

### PROCESS: Remove and Serve

- DECISION [IF]: Will the buns be used immediately?

  - No: Continue to next step.

- End of the toasting process.
```

instruct00886.title: Hockey Equipment Drying Stand
instruct00886.text: Very quickly into my first season playing hockey, my equipment started to smell terrible. I would put my stuff back on after not playing for a week and my equipment would still be wet! My friend told me about a drying rack she'd bought on Amazon and when I looked it up, it was $70.For a little while, I persisted with my stinky and wet equipment. I would leave my bag open after practices but even then it would take several days to dry and fill my small apartment with a smell that the ventilation couldn't compete with. I then decided to try to make a drying rack for myself. I found a picture of one online and went from there. Planning ahead is not usually my strong suit, but since I didn't have a car and wouldn't be able to go to Lowes for several days I relearned the CAD skills that I'd faked learning in my engineering classes and made a model.I quickly realized that the stand would end up looking startlingly similar to a five-foot tall person, so it would need to break down easily or my roommate would kick both it and me out of the apartment. I decided to make it out of PVC so I could break it in half when it wasn't being used to dry things and it could be completely disassembled during the off-season.In all I would need 165" of PVC broken down into the following sections: 7 x 7" sections 4 x 9" sections 2 x 12" sections 2 x 18" sections 1 x 24" sectionIwould also need the following connectors:2 x 2-way connectors5 x 3-way connectors1 x 4-way connectorI ended up buying all the connectors, plus two 10-foot pipes. I got the 0.75" thick pipes which ended up just about the right size. In all, it cost about $24.Other supplies that were not included in that price, are as follows:PVC cement (I did not use this, although I think I might in the future)Some type of saw After buying the materials, I used my Dad's friend's chop saw to cut the pipe into pieces. Attached is a crop of the picture that my dad took of me cutting the materials which was highly embarrassing at the time but now I kind of appreciate (I mean, what else are dads for?).Assembly is pretty self-explanatory. I decided not to cement any of the joints together because I want to be able to break it down completely during the off-season.My helmet hangs on the middle vertical pipe. My gloves slide over the upper vertical pipes. My shoulder pads rest on the upper horizontal pipes. My elbow pads are strapped around the upper 90-degree connectors. I have suspenders on my pants so my pants hang from the upper horizontal pipes as well. My skates go upside-down on the lower vertical pipes. The straps on my shin pads are looped around the lower vertical pipes, resting on the end of the lower horizontal pipes. Enjoy the final product!Tips to make your equipment not smell bad:Clean your equipment: Wash it in the washing machine! Everything short of your skates and helmet can go into any normal washing machine. Hang it in the shower or on your brand new drying rack to dry - DO NOT PUT IN DRYER. Spray a mixture of half water half vodka on the equipment every time you take it off.Hang up your equipment to dry for at least 24 hours. If you skip the spraying down step (probably a good idea if you need your equipment the next day) still hang it up to dry.

instruct00093.title: Control Your Computer... With a LASER!
instruct00093.text: Have you ever been annoyed because you have to get close to your computer when you use it? Have you ever wished for a wireless mouse, but never quite ended up buying one? Well here's a temporary solution for you!This lets you control mouse motion (mouse clicks just added!) with an everyday $1 laser pointer from up to 20 feet away (and way, way further if you have a more powerful laser).When choosing lasers, however, use caution. If you pick a way overpowered green laser (like one that can burn things and set matches on fire), you may end up damaging the optics on your mouse. All cheapo dollar store laser pointers are perfectly safe - just use caution on any laser you need to wear "lasershades" for.You can read through the whole Instructable or just use the video below... ENJOY!Also, if you like this Instructable, please give it a (+) rating and/or comment. Thanks!NOTE: This Instructable has been updated to include mouse clicking!!! The video has also changed to incorporate this. Here's what you will need:An optical mouse (I bet your computer already uses one)A laser pointer (you can use a cheap $1 laser pointer0. Position your mouse by standing it up (leaning against the monitor). This will allow you to control the mouse from anywhere in the room! Make sure the underside of the mouse (the side with the shiny red thingy) is facing the room - not the monitor. Now for the fun part...First, identify the sensor on your mouse. It will be recessed and it will look like a tiny bubble tinted black. When you move the mouse on a mouse-pad, the mouse shines a laser below it and this sensor picks up the light and interprets it as movements. So this sensor move based on incoming light... and you have a laser which emits light.SO, by putting the two together, if you shine the laser so the dot hits the sensor on the mouse, you can control the movement of the mouse!After you first get a "lock" on the mouse, you no longer have to shine the laser directly at the sensor - just in its vicinity. If you move the laser right, the cursor moves right. It really works and it is really cool.It might not be *that* useful, but hey, it is FUN! Adding clickability is so easy!You only need these parts:LDR (about $0.50, available at any electronics store. Also called a Photo Resistor)Straw (this will be used to make the barrel for the LDR)Electrical Tape (to "insulate" the barrel from light)First, open up the mouse and find the button controlling the left mouse click. Solder two wires to the button leads.Next, go ahead and create the barrel by wrapping the straw in electrical tape. Make sure no light can pass through the side of the straw.Go ahead and solder the Photo Resistor to the two wires sticking out of the mouse (there is no polarity). When the photo resistor does not contact light, there is a lot of resistance. When it does contact light, there is very little resistance (this simulates a button click).Lastly, insert the LDR into the barrel and tape it in place.You're DONE!!!!To click,shine the laser into the barrel. It's as simple as that! If the cursor is too sensitive, it is easy to fix!Just follow these images:Also, if you want to learn more about lasers, go to the laser forumIf you want to buy the laser pointer I used, go to this laser pointer shop.Posted by Laser Community member: ghost

```markdown
# Laser-Controlled Mouse System

## System Overview
This system allows a user to control an optical mouse using a laser pointer. It includes a method for moving the cursor and simulating mouse clicks from a distance of up to 20 feet away. The system requires modifying an optical mouse with a Photo Resistor (LDR) to detect laser light for click actions.

## System Requirements
- Optical Mouse
- Laser Pointer (preferably a cheap $1 pointer for safety)
- LDR (Photo Resistor)
- Straw
- Electrical Tape
- Soldering equipment and materials

## System Steps

### START:

- INPUT: An optical mouse.
- PROCESS: Stand up the mouse against the monitor with the sensor facing the room.

### PROCESS: Identify the Mouse Sensor
- PROCESS: Locate the sensor, which looks like a tiny black-tinted bubble.

### PROCESS: Control Mouse Movement
- INPUT: A laser pointer.
- PROCESS: Shine the laser on the sensor to move the cursor in the corresponding direction.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the cursor moving correctly?
- IF Yes: Proceed to adding clickability.
- ELSE No: Adjust the laser pointer's position and try again.

### PROCESS: Add Clickability
- INPUT: LDR, straw, electrical tape, soldering equipment.
- PROCESS: Open the mouse and solder two wires to the left click button leads.
- PROCESS: Create a barrel with the straw and wrap it in electrical tape.
- PROCESS: Solder the LDR to the two wires, noting that polarity is not an issue.
- PROCESS: Insert the LDR into the barrel and secure it with tape.

### OUTPUT: Modified Optical Mouse
- The modified mouse should now be able to detect laser light for movement and clicks.

### PROCESS: Use the Laser-Controlled Mouse
- PROCESS: Shine the laser into the barrel to simulate a left mouse click.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the cursor too sensitive?
- IF Yes: Adjust mouse settings according to provided images.
- ELSE No: Continue using the mouse as desired.

### END:
- The system concludes with a fully functional laser-controlled mouse.
```

instruct00639.title: Instant Mug Mac & Cheese
instruct00639.text: Macaroni and cheese, whether out of the blue box we all know so well or made from scratch is a classic comfort food dish. Now it can be made in the microwave, in a mug. Perfect for a desired single serving or to quench a last minute Mac & Cheese craving, Instant Mug Mac & Cheese will quickly become a household favorite. Gather the following:1/3 Cup of Noodles (I used elbow noodles for the classic Mac & Cheese look)1/2 Cup of Water1/2 Cup of Shredded Cheese1/2 Teaspoon of Butter1/4 Cup of Milk1 Large Mug Spoon or Fork (for stirring and eating)For this Instructable you will also need:Microwave (mine is 1000 W)Hot Pad Pour your 1/3 cup pasta of choice into your mug. Cover with the 1/2 cup of water. Place in the microwave and heat for one minute on high. Remove the mug from the microwave and stir. Heat again for another minute on high then stir. Repeat this process two more times, so that in the end you will have heated/cooked your pasta for a total of four minutes and stirred four times. When you're done, there may still be a tiny bit of water at the bottom of your noodles. You can microwave your mug for another 30-60 seconds or you can leave it. I chose to leave it rather than potentially dry out the noodles. Stirring in these intervals allows for the water to boil and steam without overflowing down the sides of your mug. If you are still worried about water overflowing, place a plate below your mug to catch the water or place your noodles and water in a larger mug or even a bowl. NOTE: Your mug may be VERY hot. Please handle it carefully and use a hot pad to handle the mug when applicable. Once your noodles have cooked, you can add your cheese, butter and milk to your mug. Give your noodles a quick stir with all of the dairy products to evenly incorporate them. This will allow for a uniform melting and mixing of your mac and cheese. Place your mug in the microwave and heat for 30 seconds. Remove from the microwave and give your mac and cheese a final stir to make sure that every noodle is coated in cheesy creamy goodness. You're done. Be careful as your mug is most likely still very hot.Enjoy!

```markdown
# Structured Summary of Craft Stick Grabber Project

## System Overview:
The system involves creating a functional grabber from craft sticks, straws, skewers, and other designable components such as pipe cleaners and rubber bands. The process includes constructing beams, reinforcing connections, assembling the grabber, and testing its functionality through challenges.

### Inputs:
- 8 craft sticks
- 2 milkshake straws, cut into quarters
- 2 skewers
- Masking tape
- Designable components (pipe cleaners, rubber bands)
- 2 cups for testing

### Outputs:
- A completed craft stick grabber
- Tested grabber through picking up cups or other improvised challenges

## Step-by-Step Process:

START: Begin the craft stick grabber project.

PROCESS: Create four beams by inserting the craft sticks into the pieces of straws, ensuring a small gap (~1mm) between the ends of the craft sticks.

INPUT: Craft sticks, straw pieces.

PROCESS: Break off a 3-4 inch piece of skewer.

INPUT: Skewer piece.

PROCESS: Attach masking tape to the skewer piece using both hands.

INPUT: Masking tape.

PROCESS: Apply the taped skewer to the straw piece to reinforce the connection between the craft sticks.

PROCESS: Repeat the reinforcement step for all four beams.

DECISION [IF]: Are all four beams reinforced?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Repeat the reinforcement process until all beams are complete.

PROCESS: Use the pointed end of a skewer to pierce the center of a straw piece.

PROCESS: Pierce another straw piece with the same skewer, pull most of the way through, and break off, leaving a 2-3 inch piece connecting the two straw pieces.

PROCESS: Repeat the piercing and connecting process to create two 'X' shapes.

PROCESS: Connect the two 'X' shapes together as depicted, using additional craft sticks, pipe cleaners, and rubber bands to enhance the grabber's grip.

INPUT: Additional craft sticks, pipe cleaners, rubber bands.

PROCESS: Tape two cups together for testing purposes.

INPUT: Two cups.

PROCESS: Attempt to pick up the taped cups with the grabber.

OUTPUT: Confirmation of the grabber's functionality.

DECISION [IF]: Can the grabber pick up the cups easily?
- Yes: Move to improvising new challenges.
- No: Reinforce the grabber and retry.

PROCESS: If the cup challenge is too easy, improvise various other challenges to test and encourage redesign.

PROCESS: If joints are falling apart, wrap tape around the skewer pieces to prevent the straws from slipping off.

DECISION [IF]: Are all joints secure and functional after reinforcement?
- Yes: Continue to use and test the grabber.
- No: Apply additional reinforcement until secure.

PROCESS: Ensure safety by not allowing students to grab at each other or wave the skewers above shoulder height.

END: The craft stick grabber project is completed and tested for functionality.
```

instruct00186.title: The USB Powered LED CD Lamp
instruct00186.text: The USB powered LED CD lamp is a very useful gadget. It's powered by the USB port, so you don't need any external power supply. The stiff mounting wire, I used acts as a gooseneck and lets you bend the light source in different angles and directions. Here is a list of the parts you'll need to make this lamp.4 CDs or DVDs (and if you're rich, you can even use Blu-ray discs or HD DVDs)7 5mm White or warmwhite LEDs, I used warmwhite, because that I'm tired of the cold light, you get from the ordinary white LEDs. (I've posted some pictures, so that you can see the difference between the white and the warmwhite LEDs)7 Resistors for the LEDs. I calculated, that my resistors should be 68 ohms. you can find a very good resistor calculator here.Some electrical mounting wire. Should be the stiff type (the one with only one thick cupper conductor)5 AA batteries preferably Duracell, cause they're the heaviest (the batteries are just there to act as a counterweight. Without them, the lamp would just tip over and fall).A switch (optional)Some ordinary hookup wire.A USB male A connector with cord (I got mine from a broken webcam)Some wire without insulation. Drill the 7 5mm holes for the LEDs. Use a pair of compasses to mark, where you'll drill the holes. Remember, that when you drill the holes, do it on foil side. If you don't, you may rip off some of the foil. Move your mouse over the yellow boxes to view instructions. Now, mount the LEDs and resistors. Move your mouse over the yellow boxes to view instructions. Glue the second CD and the stiff wire onto the CD, where the LEDs are mounted. This is simply done by using a hot glue gun. Move your mouse over the yellow boxes to view instructions. Now, start making the base. The pictures will guide you trough this process. Move your mouse over the yellow boxes to view instructions. Now, it's time to mount the counterweights (the 4 of the 5 batteries). Simply glue them on with one of my favorite weapons: The Hot Glue Gun. In this step, I'll show you how to mount the rest of the things: the last counterweight, the switch, the USB cable and the wiring. Now hook your lamp up to the USB port and have fun. Hope you enyoyed this Instructable. Leave me a comment below.
