instruct00259.title: Customize Your Own Portable Coffee Bags
instruct00259.text: Take them camping. Throw them in your desk for emergencies. Keep a stash in your car. They are quick, tasty, and completely customizable... They're coffee bags!! In just a few quick steps you can have flavored, sweetened or just plain black coffee wherever you need it! The recipe is up to you! Materials: Iron Coffee grinder Whole bean coffee Non-Dairy creamer Sugar Tea bags (the size used for 4 cup tea pots) Grind the beans on the finest setting. The more surface area you can create in the grounds, the more flavorful your cup of coffee will be. I tried several grinds, but the finest works the best. It gives the fullest flavor. Add the coffee to a tea bag. I use three table spoons for a dark cup of coffee. My "cup" of coffee is closer to 2 c. of water. Obviously, adding sugar is optional. I have to admit, i'm not a purist when it come to coffee. I enjoy a bit of sweetness in my cup of joe. I add one teaspoon of sugar. Be sure to use non dairy creamer! They come in several flavors. I really like the Italian sweet cream and of course, French vanilla. Whatever you choice is add your desired amount. I use a half teaspoon. When the bag is filled with the desired amounts of ingredients, fold the flap over onto the bag. Leave as much "slack" as possible to allow the coffee to move around in the bag when it is steeping. (The coffee will expand when it steeps, so the more room for expansion, the better) Use your hot iron to press the flap and seal it. The heat will cause the material to stick to itself, sealing your coffee mixture securely in the bag. Heat up some water. Boiling water is preferred because the bag takes a little longer to steep than conventional coffee, and you still want your cup to be hot when its ready to drink! Be sure to press and stir the bag while it is steeping. This will ensure you get the most flavor out of the bag! You can remove the bag when your brew is at the desired potency. I leave mine in... Now, sit back and enjoy!! Mmmm.... If you make extras, which I recommend, store the bags in an air tight container to preserve the flavor.

instruct00849.title: DIY Spring Reverb
instruct00849.text: I recently spent some time at my parent's place. As I opened an old box I found one of those toy echo mics. This gave me the idea to build a small homemade spring reverb!But how does it SOUND!?!?!Glad you asked. Like this.(soundcloud link) Stuff: - echo mic toy($2) - little amp & speaker (I got mine from a 1-watt Marshall amp I had laying around) ($35 for the Marshall one I believe) (you could of course use something more DIY like a little Kemo amp for example. Make sure your speaker fits the specifications of the amp) (You might want to get an amplifier for after the piezo mic as well. I don't have it- I just use the instrument inputs on my sound card and it works fine. But in situations where you don't have gain, it might be useful.) - In the case of the Marshall MS-2, an extra 9v battery connector ($0.5) - jack socket (you might need two if you're working with a more DIY amp.) ($0.5) - a box in which it will all fit. So speaker, amp, spring, etc. will have to co-exist in this space. My box was around 18x13x7 cm. (make sure the box can close with everything in it. Mine can't fully. It's no biggie tho. ($0) - 9v battery to power amp - piezo element ($1) - 2 small paperclips/metal hooks/thingies to glue to speaker/piezo so you can attach the spring. Tools: - Soldering iron! - Glue gun! - Drill! - Saw! First you'll need to cut open the echo mic. I used a saw for this and just sawed along the side until I could get to the insides. The spring might be stuck inside, but with some force on the outsides of the mic, you should be able to get one side to detach. The other side however, is a bit tricker. I used a pen and a paperclip to kind of "fish" the other end out. FInally, you'll have a detached spring! :) So you'll either be removing the amp from something like the Marshall MS-2, or putting together your own amp. This is pretty straightforward.Test it when you've taken it out. I had to resolder the battery compartment to a more flexible one. Ignore the pot in the picture. So, we'll need something to connect the spring to. I glued (with my gluegun) SMALL paperclip-like objects to the conus of the speaker and to the contact mic. See pictures. Make sure it's sturdy and dry before you continue. Solder your piezo element to a jack output... First test if your spring will reach both sides, then glue the speaker and piezo into the box! Do a quick test if it works! Connect the spring to the hooks, Hook up something that makes sound to the amp (like a little keyboard/synth/whatever). Make sure the spring can vibrate freely, and the glue will hold. Connect the output to an input on your audio interface, preferably with instrument inputs. Go wild! Video of my prototype: When it works, you can continue. Drill holes for the pots of your amp, jack input/output, light (if your amp has one). Glue it to the inside of your box with the glue gun. I extended the wires for the battery compartment and glued it to the top. Then, you're done! Only thing you'll need now are some nice knobs for the pots. But I still have to find those for mine as well...SPRINGGGGGG! How it sounds. (Soundcloud link) -- If you like it, please have a look at my other instruments, sounds and compositions at:http://www.markijzerman.com

```markdown
# Homemade Spring Reverb System Summary

## START:
- Begin the process of creating a homemade spring reverb.

## INPUT: Gather Materials
- Echo mic toy
- Little amp & speaker
- Extra 9v battery connector (if using Marshall MS-2)
- Jack socket(s)
- Box to house the components
- 9v battery
- Piezo element
- 2 small paperclips or metal hooks
- Soldering iron
- Glue gun
- Drill
- Saw

## PROCESS: Prepare the Echo Mic
- Use the saw to cut open the echo mic along the side to access the insides.
- Apply force to detach one side of the spring from the mic.
- Use a pen and paperclip to detach the other side of the spring.
  - OUTPUT: Detached spring.

## PROCESS: Prepare the Amplifier
- DECISION [IF]: Is the amp being removed from a device like Marshall MS-2?
  - Yes: Remove the amp and resolder the battery compartment for flexibility.
  - No: Assemble your own amp.
- Test the amp to ensure functionality.
  - OUTPUT: Working amp.

## PROCESS: Connect Spring to Speaker and Piezo
- Glue small paperclip-like objects to the speaker cone and the contact mic with a glue gun.
- Ensure the connections are sturdy and dry.
- Solder the piezo element to a jack output.
  - OUTPUT: Spring connected to speaker and piezo.

## PROCESS: Assemble Components in Box
- Test if the spring reaches both the speaker and the piezo.
- Glue the speaker and piezo into the box.
- Perform a quick test to check if the setup works.
  - OUTPUT: Assembled reverb components in a box.

## PROCESS: Connect and Test the Spring Reverb
- Connect the spring to the hooks on the speaker and piezo.
- Hook up a sound source to the amp.
- Ensure the spring can vibrate freely and the glue holds.
- Connect the output to an audio interface with instrument inputs.
- Go wild with sound tests.
  - OUTPUT: Sound test completed.

## PROCESS: Finalize the Reverb Box
- Drill holes for the amp's pots, jack input/output, and light (if applicable).
- Glue the amp inside the box with the glue gun.
- Extend the wires for the battery compartment and glue it to the box's top.
- Find and attach knobs for the pots (optional).
  - OUTPUT: Completed homemade spring reverb.

## END:
- The homemade spring reverb is now ready for use.
```

instruct00487.title: Make a Simple Bipedal Humanoid Robot (Servo Walking Robot)
instruct00487.text: Bipeds are really cool because they are by far the most recognizable kind of robot. Companies have spent decades and millions to make these things. I've been wanting to make a bipedal bot for sometime now but most of them need a lot of motors and are pretty expensive to make. I managed to make a simple bipedal robot at home out of essentially four micro servo motors (which are pretty cheap), an arduino and a breadboard. The bot can walk, kick, dance, navigate slopes etc.Moreover since it's an arduino you can always add sensors or other body parts pretty easily and experiment with the bot.ALSO IF YOU LIKE THE INSTRUCTABLE PLEASE VOTE FOR IT IN THE INSTRUCTABLE CONTESTS :) 1) Micro Servo's (4 nos) : http://www.hobbyking.com/hobbyking/store/__662__HX...2) Arduino (1 nos) : I used an UNO R3 but anything works3) Mini Breadboard 4) Wires, Glue, Epoxy/Sugru/Clay/Hot-Glue-Gun.5) Bits of cardboard Yup. That's all you need to start. :) Use your epoxy/Hot-Glue/Sugru to attach two motors perpendicular to each other as shown in the pictures. Make two sets of these. Each set forms a leg. Glue the two legs together. I used a broken piece of plastic to ensure that the legs are glued flat and aren't angled with each other. Now connect the for motors on the breadboard. The last pin in each motor wire is brown signifying NEGATIVE. On the breadboard connect all the left side pins to one common negative pin. Similarly connect all the middle pins to one common POSITIVE pin. These common pins are now connected to the Gnd (for Negative) and +5V (for positive) respectively. The first pin goes into the PWM pins of the arduino. If you've used servo's with an arduino before you'll find this step awfully simple to understand. If you've never used arduino's and servo's before I recommend you view the following link to better understand how they work.http://arduino.cc/en/reference/servohttp://arduino.cc/en/Tutorial/sweephttp://playground.arduino.cc/ComponentLib/servo Now attach a piece of cardboard to the top of the legs and mount the arduino and breadboard on to it. Your robot should begin resembling a body with legs now. Wrap any excess wiring that may be present with tape into the robot. Hanging wires disrupt the robots balance while walking. Take two square pieces of card and stick them to the bottom of the legs to give the bot bigger feet and better balance. I used clay to make the join look neater. Structurally your bot is now complete! Programming is the hardest part of this bot but I have a few programs that I've already managed to get working with this bot. Load them onto the robot and watch it do wonders!Once you're done loading a program onto the bot you can use a USB-Wall pug (Like those that come with modern smartphones) to run the bot directly off the grid. Although in this configuration the power wire can occasionally disturb the bots balance making with wobble while walking. Your bot is done. Remember that this isn't the end. The above set up is very simple so you can always add to it.Two motors on the side can make arms and complete a humanoid. Moreover you can easily add sensors to the bot and make it do different stuff. For example, by adding a tiny LDR and a servo controlled pen refill I made the bot protect a car. It fired a projectile if anything came in the way. Have a look at the video.(Too see how to add an LDR to an arduino : https://www.instructables.com/id/Laser-maze-Securit... )Hope you liked the instructable. Feel free to comment below. :)Enjoy!

```markdown
# Bipedal Robot System Summary

## System Overview
A simple bipedal robot system that can walk, kick, and dance, built using inexpensive components like micro servo motors and an Arduino. The system can be enhanced with additional sensors and parts for extended functionalities.

## System Requirements
- START: Begin the bipedal robot creation process.
- INPUT: Gather the following components:
  - 4 Micro Servo Motors
  - 1 Arduino (UNO R3 recommended)
  - 1 Mini Breadboard
  - Wires, Glue, Epoxy/Sugru/Clay/Hot-Glue-Gun
  - Cardboard

## Structural Assembly
- PROCESS: Use epoxy/Hot-Glue/Sugru to attach two motors perpendicularly to form a leg.
  - OUTPUT: Two sets of these assemblies, each set acting as a leg.
- PROCESS: Glue the two legs together ensuring they are aligned flatly.
  - OUTPUT: A joined leg structure.
- PROCESS: Attach a piece of cardboard to the top of the legs to serve as a mounting platform.
- PROCESS: Mount the Arduino and breadboard onto the cardboard platform.
- PROCESS: Wrap any excess wiring with tape to avoid balance disruption.
- PROCESS: Stick two square pieces of cardboard to the bottom of the legs for bigger feet and better balance.
  - OUTPUT: The structural completion of the bipedal robot.

## Electrical Connections
- PROCESS: Connect the four motors to the breadboard.
  - PROCESS: Link all the left side pins (negative) of the motors to a common negative pin on the breadboard.
  - PROCESS: Link all the middle pins (positive) of the motors to a common positive pin on the breadboard.
  - PROCESS: Connect the common negative pin to the Gnd on the Arduino and the common positive pin to +5V on the Arduino.
  - PROCESS: Connect the first pin of each motor to a PWM pin on the Arduino.

## Programming
- PROCESS: Load pre-existing programs onto the Arduino to achieve basic robot functionalities.
  - OUTPUT: A functioning bipedal robot with programmed behaviors.
- DECISION [IF]: Is additional functionality desired?
  - Yes:
    - PROCESS: Add sensors or other body parts to the robot.
    - PROCESS: Program the Arduino to integrate new components and behaviors.

  - No:
    - OUTPUT: The basic bipedal robot ready for use.

## Powering the Robot
- PROCESS: Use a USB-Wall plug to power the robot directly from the grid.

    - Yes: 
      - PROCESS: Adjust the wire or the robot's structure to minimize interference.
    - No:

## Finalization and Testing
- PROCESS: Test the robot's functionalities like walking, kicking, and dancing.
- DECISION [IF]: Does the robot perform as expected?
  - Yes:
    - OUTPUT: The bipedal robot is successfully completed.
    - END: End of the bipedal robot creation process.
  - No:
    - PROCESS: Troubleshoot issues with structure, connections, or programming.
    - PROCESS: Re-test until the robot performs correctly.
    - GOTO: Finalization and Testing.

## Expansion and Experimentation
- PROCESS: Experiment with adding arms, sensors, or other modifications to the robot.
- PROCESS: Program new behaviors and interactions based on added components.
- PROCESS: Test and iterate on new functionalities.
- OUTPUT: A customized and possibly more advanced bipedal robot.
```

instruct00533.title: Diamond Window Cube (Modular Origami)
instruct00533.text: Follow these steps to make your very own Diamond Window Cube. I'm not sure about the origin of these types of cubes (please share if you do) or their real name. I've seen many variations of this but they all involve really weird folding to show the white side of the paper. I figured out how to do what I assume is the classic version of these and they turned out really cute. I've included pictures of each step for folding the model and also numbered them according to the text I wrote so it should be clear how to make some of these for yourself. I've also labeled the pieces for the assembly step and hopefully that helps too. Happy folding! To make a cube you will need 12 pieces of square paper. 1. Fold in half then unfold. 2. Fold the top and bottom edge in to meet the middle crease. 3. Fold the top and bottom edge in to meet the middle crease again. 4. Flip the model over. 5. Fold down the top right corner, lining up with the edge. 6. Turn the model around 180 degrees. 7. Fold down what is now the top right corner, lining it up with the edge. 8. Flip the model over. 9. This fold is a little weird but you want to fold a diagonal line from one of the folded corners to the other (see picture caption). 10. Unfold the folded corner and re-fold to line up with the diagonal fold you just made. 11. Turn the model around 180 degrees and unfold and re-fold the top right corner again. 12. Make 12 of these models. Start by holding Piece 1 in your hand and inserting Piece 2 into it as shown in the first picture. Insert Piece 3 into Piece 2, as shown. Now insert the top part of Piece 1 into the side of Piece 3 to form a triangular point. Continue connecting pieces like this until all 12 units are used and a cube is formed. If you make a lot of small ones like I did you can use a need and thread to string them and hang as decoration :)

instruct00837.title: Pasta With Onions
instruct00837.text: I love this recipe. Cooking the onions on a low heat for a long time gives them a lovely sweet flavour, rather than the usual strong taste. It is not the fastest, but it uses ingredients that I usually have on hand so there is no need to go out shopping for anything special. It is also cheap/economical and pretty healthy too. To serve 4 as a main course: 3 large, sweet onions (or 4 or 5 medium onions) 3 tablespoons of olive or sunflower oil 1 tablespoon (15ml) of tomato puree 4 fl oz or 110ml or 1/2 cup of chicken stock salt and freshly ground black pepper 1lb or 500g pasta 2 oz or 50g or 3/4 cup freshly grated parmesan cheese a knob of butter Chopped parsley - optional Peel the onions then slice them thinly. Heat the olive oil gently in a large frying pan or saucepan and cook the onion over a low heat for about 30 minutes, stirring approx. every 5 minutes until the onions are very tender and have a pale golden colour. Dissolve the tomato puree into the chicken stock and then add it to the onions and stir gently to mix. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper. Meanwhile cook the pasta in plenty of boiling salted water according to the directions on the packet, then drain it and return to the pan with a knob of butter and the sauce. Stir in the sauce and then add the cheese and toss gently to mix. Serve immediately into warmed bowls and garnish with the chopped parsley if desired. If you are of sufficient age to drink alcohol this is excellent accompanied by a glass of red wine. If like my two tasters, you are too young, you'll have to make do with soft drinks.

```markdown
# Sweet Onion Pasta Recipe System

## Ingredients:
- 3 large sweet onions (or 4-5 medium onions)
- 3 tablespoons of olive or sunflower oil
- 1 tablespoon (15ml) of tomato puree
- 4 fl oz (110ml or 1/2 cup) of chicken stock
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper
- 1lb (500g) pasta
- 2 oz (50g or 3/4 cup) freshly grated parmesan cheese
- A knob of butter
- Chopped parsley (optional)

## Equipment:
- Large frying pan or saucepan
- Large pot for boiling pasta
- Cheese grater
- Knife for chopping
- Bowls for serving

## Steps:

START:
1. INPUT: Gather all ingredients and equipment.

PROCESS: Preparing the Onions
2. Peel the onions.
3. Slice the onions thinly.
4. Heat the olive oil gently in a large frying pan or saucepan.

PROCESS: Cooking the Onions
5. Cook the onions over low heat for about 30 minutes.
6. Stir the onions approximately every 5 minutes.
7. Continue until the onions are very tender and have a pale golden color.

PROCESS: Preparing the Sauce
8. Dissolve the tomato puree into the chicken stock.
9. Add the tomato mixture to the onions.
10. Stir gently to mix.
11. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper.

PROCESS: Cooking the Pasta
12. Cook the pasta in plenty of boiling salted water according to the packet's directions.
13. Drain the pasta and return it to the pan.

PROCESS: Combining Pasta and Sauce
14. Add a knob of butter to the pasta.
15. Stir in the onion sauce.
16. Add the freshly grated parmesan cheese.
17. Toss gently to mix everything together.

OUTPUT: Final Dish
18. Serve immediately into warmed bowls.
19. DECISION [IF]: Is garnishing with chopped parsley desired?
    - Yes: Garnish with chopped parsley.
    - No: Proceed to the next step.

PROCESS: Pairing with Drinks
20. DECISION [IF]: Is the consumer of legal drinking age and prefers alcohol?
    - Yes: Accompany with a glass of red wine.
    - No: Serve with soft drinks.

END.
```

instruct00178.title: A Better Snow Shovel
instruct00178.text: Your snow shovel will perform better and you will like it moreif it's sized to suit you.See the fellow in the picture above? The top of the handle on his shovel comes just to the top of his forehead. That's just the right size. He added a piece of hardwood dowel and extended the length of his shovel, and now his back feels better and his snow gets shovelled faster.This is a very easy Instructable. If you have the right size of dowel on hand it will take only 5 - 10 minutes to complete. Once you have used the modified shovel you will wonder how you got along without it.(Note: this Instructable is especially helpful for taller people.) Start with a good shovel. This one was purchased at Canadian Tire especially for this Instructable. The blade size is about 17" x 13" - but a blade that is a couple of inches narrower will work fine and will take lighter scoops of snow. This one has a plastic blade with a bit of curve, but it's not a full snow scoop. (Scoops are for pushing snow, not shovelling.) Also required: a piece of dowel that's the right size to fit the shovel shaft a wood screw for attaching the handle Remove the D handle.Insert the dowel and fasten it with a wood screw.Reattach the D handle on the end of the dowel. Size it so top of the D handle comes to the top of your forehead - perfect size for you! Done! This is a comparison picture of the custom snow shovel mod (you can see the length of dowel that has been added), and an unmodified, stock snow shovel. You will be surprised at the performance advantage of a shovel that is properly sized for you. And what's more, with this modification the shovel shovels - and it pushes! Apologies to the Instructables community: when I first published this instructable I specified that the total length should bring the top of the handle even to the shoveller's nose. I have since found further performance advantage when the handle goes to the top of the forehead, and have amended the Instructable accordingly.

instruct00397.title: Tote Bag Made Out of Toilet Paper Rolls
instruct00397.text: Good ratio for this weaving technique is 1: 4 so I cut up toilet paper 1.5 cm (5/8 in ) wide. Make the first pinwheel by wrapping 4 links, one after another and lock the 4th link inside the first one. You build the next pinwheel by adding 3 links on the right pinwheel. Building my first row of pinwheels for until I am happy with the length of bag or basket. I added a new row the top right moving back towards the left where the first row started. Now its the perfect time to add 4 triangle corners to add height. After 4 corners are in place, we can the fill the rows moving vertically to our desired height of the bag or basket. We can finish it off by folding the flaps and run through our woven basket or bag with needle and thread for extra support (optional if you just want the bag or basket to hold light items like yarn, etc). I thought about glue, double sided duct tape or staples, but I am very happy with needle and thread so far. I have tried other materials like milk carton, plastic boxes, magazines, newspapers and brown paper bag. My favorite still toilet paper or paper towel rolls since other materials require a lot more work just to get them ready as links. Enjoy weaving!

```markdown
# Comprehensive Structured Summary of Weaving Technique

## System Overview:
The system is designed to create a woven bag or basket using paper links. The primary input is toilet paper cut into strips, which are then formed into pinwheels and assembled into the desired structure. The system allows for customization in size and offers optional reinforcement methods based on the intended use of the bag or basket.

## Process Steps:

### START:
- Begin the process of creating a woven bag or basket.

### INPUT:
- Cut toilet paper into strips 1.5 cm (5/8 in) wide, adhering to the 1:4 weaving ratio.

### PROCESS: Create First Pinwheel
- Wrap one strip of toilet paper to form the first link.
- Continue to wrap three additional links, each link following the previous one.

### DECISION [IF]: Is this the fourth link?
- IF Yes: Lock the fourth link inside the first one to create a pinwheel.
- IF No: Continue wrapping links.

### PROCESS: Build Additional Pinwheels
- Add three new links to each subsequent pinwheel, starting from the right side of the existing pinwheel.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the first row of pinwheels at the desired length?
- IF Yes: Proceed to add a new row.
- IF No: Continue adding pinwheels to the first row.

### PROCESS: Add New Row
```

instruct00490.title: Quick Release Paracord Holder
instruct00490.text: I've been doing a lot of work with paracord recently and came up with this tidy way of keeping it organised. It keeps it tidy and untangled and is really easy to unravel when needed. I would usually do it with about a meter of loose end from the main bundle but for demonstration purposes ive used red as it is more contrasting. Ive decided to call this technique "Bight Whipping" due to its similarity with other rope whipping i've seen around. Start by laying one length of cord behind the coil then fold it back so theres a loop. Then pull the end closest to you and lay it over the rest of the coil (this should be the shortest one). Now pull the loop round and over the short end. This is the start of what i call "Bight Whipping" Simply make a loop with the long loose end and pass it behind the coil and through the previous loop. As long as you do not thread it through it is pretty simple to repeat. To tighten the previous loop pull on the bottom of the loop, try and keep the loops tight as it keeps it neat and its more presentable. Using loops like this means that when you come to undo it all you tug the loose end and it will come apart almost like a zip. Keep the loops going until you're happy with it and it holds the cordsufficiently. When you're happy with it pull the loose end through the loop. Only do this once or it won't come undone properly. Keeping the loops neat will make it look pretty tidy in the end. To undo it simply pull the loose end back through the loop and tug it. If you've done it properly then it will simply fall off as each loop tugs the next. This process is great for all kinds of cord, it can be used on a coil or a bundle. For example i did this with a role of camo cord that i keep handy in my bag. It keeps it tidy and stops it catching on anything. You do the exact same thing.

```markdown
# Bight Whipping Technique for Paracord Organization

## Process Overview
This process describes a technique for organizing and storing paracord in a way that keeps it tidy, untangled, and easy to unravel. The technique is referred to as "Bight Whipping," which involves creating loops around a coil of paracord and securing it in such a way that it can be easily undone.

## Step-by-Step Summary

START: Begin organizing paracord using the Bight Whipping technique.

PROCESS: Lay one length of cord behind the coil to start.

INPUT: Fold the laid cord back to create a loop.

PROCESS: Pull the end of the cord closest to you over the rest of the coil.

PROCESS: Wrap the loop around and over the short end, beginning the Bight Whipping.

PROCESS: Create a loop with the long loose end of the cord.

PROCESS: Pass the new loop behind the coil and through the previous loop without threading it.

DECISION: Check if the previous loop is tightened.
- IF Yes: Continue to the next step.
- IF No: Tighten the previous loop by pulling on the bottom of the loop.

PROCESS: Keep the loops tight for neatness and a presentable appearance.

PROCESS: Repeat making loops and passing them through the previous loops until the cord is sufficiently secured.

PROCESS: When satisfied, pull the loose end through the last loop to secure the whipping.

DECISION: Has the loose end been pulled through more than once?
- IF Yes: Undo the last step and only pull the loose end through once.
- IF No: Proceed to the next step.

OUTPUT: The paracord is now neatly organized and secured with Bight Whipping.

PROCESS: To undo the Bight Whipping, pull the loose end back through the loop and tug it.

DECISION: Does the whipping fall off with each loop tugging the next?
- IF Yes: The process is complete.
- IF No: Check the whipping for errors and try undoing it again.

OUTPUT: The paracord is now free from the Bight Whipping and ready for use.

END: The Bight Whipping technique process is complete.
```

I used a 1.5" screen because it was a good size to attach to my glasses. * Hot glue gun & glue * Pliers (to remove the keychain from the picture frames) * Paint (to cover the glue and blend the picture frames in with the glasses better) * A computer (to download the images to the picture frames) Pop out the lenses on your glasses. This will make it easier to attach your digital picture frames. Ihad to crack the lenses with a hammer in order to remove them because they did not pop out easily. If you need to crack the lenses please be careful and wear gloves and safety glasses. Use pliers to remove the keychain clasps from your digital picture frames. There is probably a metal ring that you can unbend where it attaches to the plastic. Before you do any gluing, load your images onto your digital picture frames and test them out. They should come with a manual to tell you how to do this. Also set the slideshow time to the fastest setting to make it more 'video'-like. These particular models only have options for 5 second, 10 second, or 30 seconds. While you are at it, charge up the devices (mine came with a USB cord for loading/charging). Ihad to find a Windows machine because the brand I had was not compatible with Macs. I attached some images you can use. The animation in her video is just the words "Pop music will never be low brow". Note: Because the picture frames I used were thinner on one side, I installed one upside down so they would mirror each other (see picture). I had to upload the images for that frame upside down so they would display correctly. You can flip them in any image editing software before loading. Using a hot glue gun, attach the digital picture frames to your glasses. I worked my way around the frames a few times, layering up the glue to make a sturdy connection. Be sure to leave room between the frames to plug them in if needed (as you can see from the pictures the USB connection is right across the bridge of the glasses, that's not a lot of space to work with). If you want, use some paint to cover the hot glue and make the digital frames blend in with your glasses. And that's it. Try them out and impress your friends!

instruct00467.title: Test Tube Spice Rack
instruct00467.text: Here's a test tube spice rack that I made to hold all of my spices. I tried to improve upon previous test tube spice racks that I've seen by using a nice looking piece of bamboo plywood and by using oversized O rings to "float" the tubes in the rack and eliminate the base plate. Also, my kitchen is short on counter space, so moving the spices out of the cupboard and onto the wall was a bonus. I've got a lot of spices, so I made two of these racks, but the design would work well with just one, or as many as you might need to hold all of your spices. Sorry I can't publish this as a full step by step Instructable since this was one of the few builds I've done where I didn't take pictures along the way, but I'll do my best to explain how I made it in the text below.Materials: plywood bamboo strip approx.2" x 16" glass 25mm x 150mm test tubesfrom Drillspot size 10 cork stoppers to match test tubes from Mcmaster 22mm x 4mm rubber O-rings to match test tubes from Mcmaster assorted spices skinny measuring spoons from Lee Valley screw hook to hold measuring spoons mini L brackets hanging hardware for plaster or drywall wallsTools: saw to cut wood drill or drill press (better) to drill holes in wood and hang rack 1 1/8" Forstner bit to make clean holes that areslightly larger than test tube diameter, but smaller than O-ring.Construction: Cut appropriately sized strips of wood for your test tube rack. On a drill press, use a 1 1/8" forstner bit to create evenly spaced holes on the rack. Try to drill as straight as possible if you're using a hand drill. Slip the O-rings onto the test tubes, fill with spices, and insert cork stopper into the top.Installation: Hang test tube rack onto the wall with small steel L brackets using appropriate anchors or hardware for your specific wall type.

```markdown
# Test Tube Spice Rack System

## Summary
This system describes the process of creating a test tube spice rack using bamboo plywood, glass test tubes, cork stoppers, and rubber O-rings, designed to save counter space and organize spices on a wall. The process involves cutting and drilling the plywood, preparing the test tubes, and mounting the rack on a wall.

## Process Steps

### START: Creating a Test Tube Spice Rack

### INPUT: Gather Materials and Tools
- Materials:
  - Bamboo plywood strip (approx. 2" x 16")
  - Glass test tubes (25mm x 150mm)
  - Size 10 cork stoppers

    - No: Use appropriate hardware for the specific wall type.
```

instruct00484.title: THE BEST FRANKFURTER HOT DOG EVER!
instruct00484.text: Ingredients - 4 Italian tomatoes (make sure they are fresh and ripe) - 1 Onion - 2 cloves of garlic - Black Pepper - Green Tabasco (Jalapano) - Yellow Mustard (or Brown) - 1 cup of chopped bacon - 4 Frankfurters - 1 soap spoon of sugar - 1 tea spoon of Salt - 1 pound of Mozzarella - 1 pound of Cream Cheese - 4 Mini Baguettes (Try to find a baguette slightly smaller than your Frankfurter) - 1/2 pound of Shoestring potato NOTE: I used "Queijo Prato" instead Mozzarella and "Catupiry" instead cream cheese. ("Queijo Prato" is a Brazilian soft cheese, similar to the Danish cheese Danbo. It is one of the most popular cheeses in Brazil. And "Catupiry" is an excellent Brazilian Cream Cheese, very very taste) These are the ingredientes you will need for the sauce: 1. Bacon 2. Garlic 3. Onion 4. Tomato 5. Sugar 6. Salt 7. Green Tabasco (Jalapeno) 8. Black Pepper Chop the tomatoes (remove the seeds), onion and smash the cloves of garlic and let apart fry bacon with its own fat andadd the garlic stir with a spoon when the garlic is golden add onion Let the onions caramelize and then add the tomatoes Stir until the tomatoes begin to melt and add the Tabasco, black pepper and mustard And finally the frankfurters cook more 3 minutes and "pronto"! Grate the mozzarella Heat the cream cheese in the microwave Add in this order: Sauce, Frankfurter, cream cheese, mozzarella, potato, mustard Enjoy the best Frankfurter Hotdog EVER!

instruct00389.title: Capture 3D Models From Google Maps or Earth
instruct00389.text: Have you ever found yourself wondering through google maps and imagining how cool it would be to get access to that 3D models?? Me too! I have been thinking about this for almost 2 years now and finally decided to give it a shot. Thinking about it, this method can be applied to a lot more than google earth models... movies? In this particular case I just wanted to get the corner of a particular building in the city of New York city, but you will see how this method can to much more. In the past I remember people using programs like 3D ripper that would capture the geometry directly from openGL, I actually tried it once but without any luck. Also, I think this program only works for windows. In this Instructable I will teach you how to capture the 3d models with texture from google earth using the photogrammetry approach. Identify what you want to capture and what is irrelevant. The clear the idea here the better the chances of success. Orbit around your building, try to do it in a smooth fashion and regular speed. Having a mouse might help but not necessary. Try moving at a regular speed about the object of interest, I would say that you have about 1.5 minutes to capture all the geometry you want before you run into problems afterwards. Maybe you can push it up to 2 or even 2.5 minutes. I really haven't tried it much.A good tip here is to only capture the section of the window with no words, logs or icons, this will save you time later and increase your chances of success. This is also one of the reasons why I like using google earth better than google maps, you can turn all icons off.I am including the actual video I capture for you to get an idea of how I was moving. The free version of Autodesk Remake (formerly Memento) will only allow you to upload up to 250 frames. Now, our screen recording is about 1.5 minutes long, at 60fps, it means we have about 5400 frames. Truth to be told, most of those frames are repeated since we were moving slowly compared to the screen recording. There are probably a couple of ways to do this but the one I am most familiar is using photoshop. First import the video frames as layers, limit to every 20 frames or so (5400/20=270), let it run and then export the layers as files. This last step might take some time but that is it. This is one of the easiest steps to follow, open Remake, select Create 3D from Photos. Select the images and Create Model. The defaults work fine.You are almost done but this step actually takes a long time, hours. Go out have some nice dinner, and get back to work. Hopefully if everything went right, the moment you open remake you should be able to open your new 3D model.Oh!! What is Remake you ask? Remake, formerly called Mememnto is a super powerful tool to create 3D models from data. The data could be from a scanner or form a bunch of pictures. It is similar to 123D Make but on heavy steroids. Download it for free and give it a try!Clean the model and remove the parts you don't need. From here you can export it as an OBJ or STL, but if you do decide to go for an STL, remember to first make the mesh into a solid, since right now you will probably just have the shell. instruct00753.title: Duct Tape Rose
instruct00753.text: This instructable will teach you how to make Duct Tape roses, They are pretty good for valentines day and other events like fund raisers. *EDIT* The original idea came from the duct tape club www.ducktapeclub.com. But their Instructions are very vague and there is only four non informative pictures, after making these roses for a year or so i have my own style that I am sharing What you will need for this project is: Some time: Not a lot but at least 10 minutes Some tape: I use Duck Tape brand Duct Tape Some floral wire: found almost in any floral department Start by ripping a 2x2in strip of tape. It doesn't have to be exact, it fact i recommend making varying sizes of petals it makes it seem more real. 1. Fold the top right corner over on itself making sure you leave some adhesive on the left side 2. Fold the top left corner over on itself making a triangle with some adhesive left on the bottom. Take your newly made petal and wrap it around the top of the "Stem" Repeat steps 2 and 3 to get petals. When adding petals I have found that it works the best if you add them in the fashion in the picture below, at an angle and then wrapping them. After a good amount of petals (your choice really) You should have something that looks like this. Now you have a pretty good rose that you can use, but the wire stem is pokey and hurts when you get stabbed with it... So lets make it a little safer. Now take your stem color and rip a half strip about 1 circumference around or 1.5 depending on how long your stem is. Start at the top by the rose and wrap tightly down the stem, if you have leftover keep it for the next step. Take the excess of your stem color (or rip some more little squares) and apply them to the underside of the rose, adding another layer of protection to keeping it all together And there you go! Go crazy, use any and all the colors you want.

```markdown
# Structured Summary of Duct Tape Roses Creation

## Inputs
- Some time (at least 10 minutes)

- INPUT: Take the floral wire to use as the stem.
- PROCESS: Wrap the petal around the top of the stem.

- PROCESS: Apply the excess or new squares of tape to the underside of the rose.
- OUTPUT: An additional layer of protection, keeping the rose together.

END:
- The duct tape rose is complete and ready to use.

- A handmade duct tape rose with a safe, non-pokey stem.
- Customization options with various colors and petal sizes.
```

instruct00763.title: DIY Free Loop for Watch Strap
instruct00763.text: Recently one of my favorite wrist watches meet with an ill fate, the free loop got undone from wear and tear. This happens quite frequently and I'm tired of spending monies on replacing the whole set of straps for just one part. When it happened this time, luckily I had a light bulb moment, when I looked at the duct tape sitting on the study desk. So in this instructables I'll be showing you how to quickly fix that, in less than 10 minutes. Cut a strip of duct tape and fold it half. After the folding has been done, make sure to get rid of any air bubbles using a stiff card. At this point decide the thickness of the free loop and cut it. Now, carefully measure the length required to cover the watch band. Hey! Now you have the thin strip ready to become the loop. Wrap the thin strip around the belt on the buckle side to find out the exact length you need for the loop. One thing to keep in mind is, the loop should never be bigger than the buckle itself for obvious reason, if it is, it will fall off. Once you have it all figured out, grab a scissor and cut it to the final length. The next part will require a little dexterity with your fingers and clean hands. Flip over the watch, so the underside of the band is facing you. Grab the new loop and overlap it in position, if you want at this stage press the ends so you have a minute dent on the loop for when you fix it in place. Grab a tiny portion of duct tape, this will be used to close the loop as shown in the picture. Once you have secured the loop you can redo the securing step once more to make it firm. Vola! You have successfully completed a minor repair on your beloved watch, aren't duct tapes the most versatile tapes ever?

```markdown
# Watch Strap Free Loop Repair System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Start the process to repair the watch strap free loop.

### INPUT: Materials Needed
- Duct tape
- Stiff card
- Scissors
- Clean hands

### PROCESS: Prepare the Duct Tape
- Cut a strip of duct tape.
- Fold the duct tape strip in half lengthwise.
- Use a stiff card to remove any air bubbles from the folded duct tape.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the thickness of the loop adequate?
- IF Yes: Proceed to measure the length.
- ELSE: Adjust the thickness by cutting the tape and then proceed to measure the length.

### PROCESS: Measure and Cut the Loop
- Measure the length required to cover the watch band.
- Cut the duct tape strip to the desired width for the loop.

### PROCESS: Determine Loop Length
- Wrap the thin strip around the watch band near the buckle to find the exact length needed for the loop.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the loop bigger than the buckle?
- IF Yes: Trim the loop to ensure it is not bigger than the buckle.
- ELSE: Proceed to the next step.

### PROCESS: Finalize the Loop
- Cut the strip to the final length needed for the loop.

### PROCESS: Attach the Loop
- Flip the watch so the underside of the band is facing up.
- Place the new loop over the band and position it where the free loop should be.
- Press the ends of the loop to create a dent for reference (optional).

### PROCESS: Secure the Loop
- Cut a tiny portion of duct tape.
- Use this piece to secure the ends of the loop together.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the loop firmly secured?
- IF No: Redo the securing step with another piece of duct tape.
- ELSE: Proceed to the final step.

### OUTPUT: Completed Repair
- The watch strap free loop is repaired.

### END:
- The repair process is complete.
```

instruct00027.title: Repair Cigarette Burns on Carpet
instruct00027.text: Over the years I have forked out money to carpet cleaners to repair carpet burns. Until lately when I watched one guy do it and learned there super money making trick. Forget paying carpet cleaners or carpet repair men 45 bucks a burn. You can achieve the exact same result for free with simple tools that everyone has laying around there home!!!! Get your trusty pair of scissors out and cut the piece of ash or melted piece of carpet plastic out and plug in your glue gun Go into a closet or a part of your room thats not a heavy traffic area eg. behind bed, closets and corners of the room and find a strand of carpet thats sticking out, grab it and pull it until its about a foot in length then cut it at the base. Then cut the strands every time the ripple goes up or down and make a generous pile. Apply a SMALL amount of hot glue to the carpet and add a about half of your pile to the glue and press it down with the handles of a larger pair of scissors. Give it a minute to dry and lightly pull the excess carpet strands off Add a EXTREMLY SMALL dabb of hot glue to the surface of the burn and rub it around then add the rest of your pile again pressing it down with scissors, give it a couple minutes to cool down. Now take your trusty scissors and cut some of the final layer off to make the surface even. YOUR DONE!!!! The second image is the final product its a little shaggy in the top right corner... but its a lot better than before!!!

```markdown
# Carpet Burn Repair System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Begin the carpet burn repair process.

### INPUT:
- Gather tools: scissors, glue gun, hot glue.

### PROCESS: [Prepare the Damaged Area]
- Use scissors to cut out the ash or melted piece of carpet.

- Go to a low-traffic area of the room.
- Find a strand of carpet that is sticking out.
- Pull the strand until it is about a foot in length.

- Cut the strands every time the ripple goes up or down.
- Create a generous pile of strands.

### PROCESS: [Apply First Layer of Strands]
- Plug in the glue gun and apply a SMALL amount of hot glue to the carpet.
- Add about half of your pile of strands to the glue.
- Press it down with the handles of a larger pair of scissors.
- Wait a minute for the glue to dry.

### PROCESS: [Remove Excess Strands]
- Lightly pull the excess carpet strands off.

### PROCESS: [Apply Second Layer of Strands]
- Apply an EXTREMELY SMALL dab of hot glue to the surface of the burn.
- Rub it around to spread the glue.
- Add the rest of your pile of strands.
- Press it down with scissors.
- Wait a couple of minutes for it to cool down.

### PROCESS: [Trim and Finish]
- Use scissors to cut some of the final layer off to make the surface even.

### OUTPUT:
- The repaired area of the carpet, with a more even surface.
```

instruct00462.title: Dried Roses the Easy Way
instruct00462.text: This is an easy way to preserve a special bouquet of roses. It makes an easy, natural decoration for your wall. It's a great way to save your Mother's Day bouquet; she'll remember how much you appreciate her for years to come. Long before the flowers fade, remove them from the vase.Remove any faded leaves and blooms. Using a handy-dandy pruner, trim stems. (If I win the contest, I too, will have a handy-dandy pruner.) Gather your roses into a pleasant arrangement. Trim stems and flowers as needed to enhance your arrangement.Take a piece of sewing thread, approximately 24 inches long, and wind it tightly around the stems. Weave it in and out of the individual stems to securely fasten the entire bunch. Insert a straight pin into your wall in the desired location.Place the rose bunch upside down on the wall with the level of the thread wrap slightly above the pin. Gently lower the bunch down until the thread catches on the pin. Your roses will gradually dry, leaving you with a lasting memory of that special occasion.If you enjoyed this instructable,Please VOTE and RATE, and comment.Thanks!Special thanks again to LinuxH4x0r for the pictures.

instruct00596.title: Floating Table Top
instruct00596.text: This looks impossible, sort of a table top held in the air by string. Actually, the weight of the upper structure places tension on the center string (attached to the pencil). The other three strings prevent the top from twisting or flipping--it's really not that hard to set up.Research "tensegrity" for more information regarding this type of structure. CardboardPencilGlueTapeFishing line (or string or thread) These are the patterns for the cardboard pieces. Cut six legs. Glue three leg pieces together--twice. Cut four body pieces. Glue the four body pieces together. Glue the legs to the body. Cut six arms and poke holes in the top (to support a pencil). Glue three arm pieces together, twice. Glue the arms to the body assembly. Cut two neck pieces. Glue the center of the neck pieces (1/2 inch of neck) together as shown in the photo. Cut the head piece. Make the head as round as possible and tape the head ends together to form a cylinder. Cut a head top. Glue the head top to the head. Glue the neck piece to the bottom of the head. Glue the "wings" of the neck piece to the body. Cut two top support pieces. Glue the top support pieces together as shown. Cut a top piece. Glue the "wings" of the top support piece to the top. Cut two base pieces. Glue the base pieces together. Cut twelve brace pieces. Glue six brace pieces together twice.Glue the brace assemblies to the top support to make it more sturdy as shown in the photo. Glue the robot character to the base. Put a face on the character. First, I poked a hole in the end of the top support. Then, I used six pound fishing line (to reduce visibility) and created a loop that is about two and one half inches long. String or thread will work here--whatever you have. Cut twelve inches of fishing line (three times) and tape it to the top in the positions shown in the photo. Push the pencil through the 2 1/2" loop you made in the earlier step. Place tape (I used duct tape) on the base--at similar spots as the tape on the top. With one hand, hold the top in "floating" position while securing each of the three pieces of fishing line, one at a time. The three "strings" will have slight tension--they will not be loose. Cut off the surplus fishing line (string). This is quite stable and will even support a small load.

```markdown
# Structured Summary of Tensegrity Structure Creation

## START:
- Begin the process of creating a tensegrity structure.

## INPUT: Materials
- Cardboard
- Pencil
- Glue
- Tape
- Fishing line (or string or thread)

## PROCESS: [Preparation of Cardboard Pieces]
- Cut six leg pieces from cardboard.
- Glue together three leg pieces to form one set. Repeat for the second set.
- Cut four body pieces from cardboard.
- Glue the four body pieces together to form the body assembly.
- Glue the two sets of legs to the body assembly.
- Cut six arm pieces from cardboard and poke holes in the top of each.
- Glue together three arm pieces to form one set. Repeat for the second set.
- Glue the two sets of arms to the body assembly.
- Cut two neck pieces from cardboard.
- Glue the center (1/2 inch) of the two neck pieces together as shown in the reference photo.
- Cut one head piece from cardboard and shape it to be as round as possible.
- Tape the ends of the head piece to form a cylinder.
- Cut one head top from cardboard.
- Glue the head top to the cylindrical head piece.
- Glue the neck piece to the bottom of the head.
- Glue the "wings" of the neck piece to the body assembly.
- Cut two top support pieces from cardboard.
- Glue the two top support pieces together as shown in the reference photo.
- Cut one top piece from cardboard.
- Glue the "wings" of the top support to the top piece.
- Cut two base pieces from cardboard.
- Glue the two base pieces together.
- Cut twelve brace pieces from cardboard.
- Glue six brace pieces together to form one set. Repeat for the second set.
- Glue the brace assemblies to the top support to increase sturdiness.

## PROCESS: [Assembly of Robot Character]
- Glue the robot character (previously assembled body, arms, legs, neck, head) to the base.
- Decorate the character with a face.

## PROCESS: [Creating Support Structure]
- Poke a hole in the end of the top support.
- Create a loop with fishing line that is approximately 2 1/2 inches long.

## PROCESS: [Attaching the Support Structure]
- Cut three 12-inch lengths of fishing line.
- Tape the three lengths of fishing line to the top piece at the positions shown in the reference photo.
- Push a pencil through the 2 1/2" loop created earlier.

## PROCESS: [Finalizing the Structure]
- Apply tape to the base at locations corresponding to the tape on the top piece.
- Hold the top piece in a "floating" position.
- Secure each of the three pieces of fishing line to the base, one at a time, ensuring slight tension.

## OUTPUT:
- Excess fishing line is trimmed off.
- A stable tensegrity structure that can support a small load is completed.

## END:
- The creation process of the tensegrity structure is concluded.
```

instruct00085.title: Halloween Brimstone Bread
instruct00085.text: I love making brimstone bread. Between the dark crunchy topping and the soft inner core, it's perfect for everything from sandwiches, to burgers, to just slathering with butter and eating warm from the oven.Rumor has it, when demons in Hell make this bread, they roll the dough in the deep pits of sulfur and soul dust and cook them in the hot brimstone vents. Unfortunately, as you are mortal and have neither access to soul dust or brimstone vents, I've had to make a few adjustments to the recipe for you.While these rolls aren't actually "Hell Authentic," they're close enough to get the job done. To make your own brimstone bread you will need:1 box instant bread mix2 Tablespoons active dry yeast1 cup warm water (between 105/115F)2 Tablespoons sugar2 Tablespoons vegetable oil1/2 teaspoon salt1 1/2 Cups rice flourBlack food coloring or activated charcoal*Red food coloring*Activated charcoal can present problems for anyone who is on certain medications. While the activated charcoal does turn food a fantastically dark black color, it's better to be safe than sorry. For more information on charcoal and how it interacts with medication, check out this link. When in doubt, use a black liquid or gel food coloring. Start by first making your boxed bread mix according to the directions. Add enough red food coloring to the dough to bring it to a deep dark blood red.Divide your dough into 12 small balls. Place the balls onto a cookie sheet and cover with a damp towel.Allow to rise for as long as the directions on your box mix indicate. While your bread balls are rising, it's time to make the topping. In your mixer, combine the yeast, sugar, oil, salt and rice flour. Mix your black food coloring in with your water and add that to the mix. You want your topping to be as black as you can make it, so feel free to be liberal with the food coloring. You can also augment the blackness with activated charcoal if you have that, but I wouldn't add more than three capsules as that can change the flavor of the bread later on (please see the disclaimer in step 1 if you plan on using charcoal and are on any medications).The topping should be thick and sticky, but still fluid enough to slowly ooze and drip off the end of your whisk.Cover and allow to sit for 15 minutes.Take a big old wad of your black topping and smear it all over the top and sides of your red dough balls. Don't worry about it being too thick, you're better off erring on the side of too much than not enough. If the topping is too thin, it won't crackle the way you want it to. You could do this with a knife or a spoon, but trust me when I say it's so much easier to just use your (clean, washed and dried) hands.Let stand, uncovered, for another 15 minutes. This allows the topping to really adhere to your dough balls. Cook your bread according to the directions on your box mix, making sure that the pan is on the center rack of your oven.As it cooks, your topping will crisp up and shrink back, creating the deep cracks and fissures that make brimstone bread so distinctive.Once they're done cooking, allow to cool until they are comfortable to handle. Once you can touch them without burning yourself, crack one open, slab on a fat slice of butter, and enjoy your brimstone bread!If you want even more creepy recipes like this for Halloween, swing by my main Instructables page or check out my horror themed food blog, The Necro Nom-nom-nomicon.Bone appetite!

```markdown
# Brimstone Bread Recipe System

## Ingredients and Tools
- 1 box instant bread mix
- 2 Tablespoons active dry yeast
- 1 cup warm water (between 105/115°F)
- 2 Tablespoons sugar
- 2 Tablespoons vegetable oil
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1 1/2 Cups rice flour
- Black food coloring or activated charcoal
- Red food coloring
- Mixer
- Whisk
- Cookie sheet
- Damp towel
- Oven

## Procedure

### START:
- Begin the brimstone bread-making process.

### PROCESS: Prepare Bread Dough
- INPUT: 1 box instant bread mix.
- OUTPUT: Prepared bread dough.
- PROCESS: Follow the instructions on the bread mix box.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the bread dough prepared?
  - Yes: Proceed to color the dough.
  - No: END (Unable to proceed without prepared dough).

### PROCESS: Color the Dough
- INPUT: Red food coloring.
- OUTPUT: Blood red colored dough.
- PROCESS: Add enough red food coloring to the dough to achieve a deep dark blood red color.
- STORE: Colored dough for shaping.

### PROCESS: Shape the Dough
- INPUT: Colored dough.
- OUTPUT: 12 small dough balls.
- PROCESS: Divide the dough into 12 small balls.
- STORE: Dough balls on a cookie sheet.

### PROCESS: First Rise
- INPUT: Damp towel.
- OUTPUT: Risen dough balls.
- PROCESS: Cover the dough balls with a damp towel.
- PROCESS: Allow dough balls to rise as per bread mix box instructions.
- DECISION [IF]: Have dough balls risen?
  - Yes: Proceed to make the topping.
  - No: END (Unable to proceed without risen dough balls).

### PROCESS: Make Topping
- INPUT: Active dry yeast, sugar, oil, salt, rice flour, black food coloring, warm water.
- OUTPUT: Black topping mixture.
- PROCESS: In a mixer, combine the yeast, sugar, oil, salt, and rice flour.
- PROCESS: Mix black food coloring with warm water and add to the mixture.
- DECISION [IF]: Is topping black and thick?
  - Yes: Proceed to cover and let sit.
  - No: END (Topping must be black and thick to continue).

### PROCESS: Rest Topping
- OUTPUT: Ready topping.
- PROCESS: Cover the topping mixture and allow to sit for 15 minutes.
- STORE: Rested topping mixture.

### PROCESS: Apply Topping
- INPUT: Risen dough balls, black topping mixture.
- OUTPUT: Dough balls with black topping.
- PROCESS: Smear the black topping over the top and sides of the red dough balls using hands.
- DECISION [IF]: Is topping applied generously?
  - Yes: Proceed to let stand.
  - No: END (Topping must be applied generously to continue).

### PROCESS: Second Rise (Topping Adherence)
- OUTPUT: Dough balls ready for baking.
- PROCESS: Let the dough balls stand uncovered for another 15 minutes to adhere the topping.

### PROCESS: Bake Bread
- INPUT: Prepared dough balls, oven.
- OUTPUT: Baked brimstone bread.
- PROCESS: Cook the bread according to the box mix directions on the center rack of the oven.
- DECISION [IF]: Is bread cooked and cracked?
  - Yes: Proceed to cooling.
  - No: END (Bread must be cooked and cracked to continue).

### PROCESS: Cool Bread
- OUTPUT: Cooled brimstone bread.
- PROCESS: Allow bread to cool until comfortable to handle.

### OUTPUT: Finished Brimstone Bread
- Enjoy the brimstone bread with a slice of butter.

### END:
- The brimstone bread-making process is complete.
```

4.Q: During a Halloween bake sale at her school, Emily decided to make the brimstone bread from a recipe she found. instruct00062.title: How to Remove a Tick From a Dog
instruct00062.text: In this instructable I will demonstrate how to easily remove a tick from your dog without pulling it out. The tick will crawl out on it's own and you won't have to deal with 'did I get it all out?'. This sounds like a magic trick and you might even think it is, I did. My sister inlaw had been telling me how to do it for quite a while and I just never tried it, because I didn't think it would work. One day when I was at the vet getting my dogs their yearly shots, my vet found a tick and removed it using this method and I was sold. I easily remove about 20 ticks a year from my two dogs. When I used the old way, which was get your tweezers as close to the head of the tick and pull straight out, it would often leave parts of the tick behind. Ticks seem to like areas near the eyes and ears, which would leave marks and scars that wouldn't ever go away.So how do you do it? Rub the tick in a circular motion and pretend you're trying to make the tick dizzy. I generally stick with one direction, clockwise. It usually takes less than a minute, so if it's not working, make sure the body of the tick is moving around. Remember you can't get dizzy unless you're actually moving in a circle, quickly. I doubt the tick actually gets dizzy, but they sure don't like something about the movement and they crawl out on their own.This was too difficult to document with photos, so here's the video. The only troubles I have had with this technique, is when you catch the tick early in it's attaching process. It makes it harder to actually get the body of the tick to move around and you feel like you're just rubbing the tick. If it won't come off, I will usually wait another day instead of risking leaving part of the tick behind in my dog.This method should work on people as well, but I haven't had the chance to try it out. I don't think it will work as well, because you generally catch the tick early on and there's no body to move around. It's also easier to get parts of the tick out as you can use tweezers and then just like removing a splinter, get the rest out. Once you have the tick out, wrap the tick in a piece of tape to kill it. If you're taking it off yourself or another person, you probably want to put it in a jar of rubbing alcohol and get it tested for Lyme disease.

instruct00118.title: Devil's Kite (Super Easy Paper Kite That Really Flies!)
instruct00118.text: What I will show you is a traditional Turkish kite called "Seytan Ucurtmasi", which means "Devil's Kite". It's so easy, that a 5 year old can make and fly it. You'll need a few easy to find household items: - Square paper of any kind and size. Something light is better. (Even though I'm gonna use origami paper here, newspaper works great) - String - Scrap plastic bag for the tail (if you can't find a plastic bag around, you can use another piece of paper) - A piece of sticky tape to strenghten the briddle points (optional) - Small piece of cardboard for the string winder (optional) Fold the square in half along the center diagonal line. Fold so that the blank side of the paper is inside, and the color side is visible. Now take one edge and make a fold to the centerline as you may see in picture. Turn the paper and repeat the step for the other side. Fold the small corner to the center line. Repeat it for the other side as well. Use some tape to strenghten the sides you see at the pictures. After that, use a paper punch or scissors to make holes at the points. Cut two 20 cm (8 inch) strings. You'll tie these to the two holes at the parts, which are looking like wings. Now, let's make the tail! Fold the bag a few times and cut 2 pieces of it. Open up the pieces and you'll get 4 longer bag parts. Stick them together with a piece of tape to make it even longer and finally attach it to the back of the kite (where you punched a hole before) Making a winder is not a big deal. Just wrap the string around some piece of cardboard or even a pen and attach the end of it to the briddle of your kite. Congratulations, you now have a "Devil's Kite". Go and fly it, it doesn't need lots of wind.

```markdown
- Go fly the "Devil's Kite".
```

instruct00064.title: 44 Orange Liqueur Recipe
instruct00064.text: While researching orange liqueurs, I came across a basic recipe for one called "44 Orange" and had to try it. It is a traditional european apertif made using an orange, coffee beans, sugar, and grain alcohol (vodka can also be used in a pinch). Some recipes call for cloves, cinnamon, and honey, but I will probably wait for my next batch to use some of these. Ingredients:1 Large Orange6 Tbsp Sugar44 Coffee Beans4 Cups Grain Alcohol/ Vodka (highest proof you can find)You Will Need:A mason jar, or other airtight containerKnifeVeggie Wash (Optional) I recommend buying organic produce because it yields the best flavor but any kind of orange will do. Remember to wash it thoroughly, preferably with a fruit/veggie wash. This is important because the entire orange will be submerged in alcohol and whatever is on the orange peel will end up IN your final product. Poke 44 holes in the orange and insert a coffee bean in each opening. This was more fun that I originally imagined. Then put the orange inside of the jar. Fill the jar with 4 cups of grain alcohol/vodka. If you are using a regular-sized mason jar, this should take you pretty close to the tap.. Now add your sugar over the top of the alcohol. The original recipe called for 44 sugar cubes but I substituted 6 tablespoons of sugar. Because sugar cubes come in so many sizes, the amount of sugar can too easily get out of hand, so proceed with caution. I found 6 tbsps to be a good starting amount and more can be added later to taste. It is a good idea to put a tag on the jar somewhere so that you remember the date you created this concoction. You will need to store it for 44 days in a dark, cool place before removing the orange/coffeebeans. Be sure to shake it up every once in awhile to ensure the sugar dissolves. After the 44 days are up, remove the orange and coffee beans, and strain the rest. If you used Everclear (grain alcohol), it will be much too strong to enjoy straight, so add at least one cup of water. Some may prefer a bit more water to tone it down. If you used vodka it should not be too powerful but it is really up to taste. Put it in a new bottle and enjoy it chilled!

```markdown
## Ingredients and Tools:

- STORE: A mason jar or other airtight container
- STORE: Knife
- STORE: Veggie Wash (Optional)

## Steps:

START: Begin the process of creating 44 Orange Liqueur.

PROCESS: Purchase organic produce for the best flavor.
DECISION [IF]: Is the orange organic?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Consider buying organic for better flavor.

PROCESS: Wash the orange thoroughly.
- IF using veggie wash, apply it according to instructions.
- ELSE, rinse under running water.
- OUTPUT: Clean orange ready for use.

PROCESS: Using a knife, poke 44 holes in the orange.
- OUTPUT: Orange prepped with holes.

PROCESS: Insert a coffee bean into each hole in the orange.
- OUTPUT: Orange studded with coffee beans.

PROCESS: Place the studded orange into the mason jar.

PROCESS: Fill the jar with 4 cups of grain alcohol or vodka.
- OUTPUT: Orange submerged in alcohol.

PROCESS: Add 6 tablespoons of sugar over the top of the alcohol.
- OUTPUT: Sugar added to the mixture.

PROCESS: Label the jar with the date of creation.
- OUTPUT: Labeled jar for tracking duration.

PROCESS: Store the jar in a dark, cool place for 44 days.
- OUTPUT: Infusion process initiated.

PROCESS: Shake the jar occasionally to ensure the sugar dissolves.
- OUTPUT: Well-mixed infusion.

DECISION [IF]: Have 44 days passed?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: Continue to store and wait until 44 days are up.

PROCESS: After 44 days, remove the orange and coffee beans.
- OUTPUT: Orange and coffee beans removed.

PROCESS: Strain the liqueur to remove any remaining solids.
- OUTPUT: Refined liqueur.

- Yes: Dilute with at least one cup of water.
- No: Proceed to the next step.

DECISION [IF]: Is the vodka-based liqueur too strong?
- Yes: Dilute with water to taste.
- No: Proceed to the next step.

PROCESS: Transfer the liqueur to a new bottle for storage.
- OUTPUT: Liqueur ready for consumption.

PROCESS: Chill the liqueur before enjoying.
- OUTPUT: Chilled 44 Orange Liqueur ready to be served.

END: The process of making 44 Orange Liqueur is complete.
```

instruct00876.title: Bucket Sifter for Beach Cleanups
instruct00876.text: We run at least one beach cleanup per month in NYC and we thinking about how we can make the cleanup process a bit more efficient.This instructable will show you how to make a sifter from a bucket to bring with you to your next beach cleanup. We found all of the materials in the free section of our local craigslist listings. You can also purchase all of the materials (minus the tools) at your local hardware store for less than $15.Full disclosure we know there are still a lot of microplastic pieces falling through the cracks, but we are working on something to tackle that soon. Be sure to follow us to get notified when we post that instructable! A 5-gallon bucketA gutter guardA drill8 sheet metal screwsA pair of snips (or Dremel) Gather the materials listed above and let's get to work!Place the gutter guard across the bottom of the bucket and make 4 marks 1" toward the center from the outside of the guard. Then connect the lines and draw a curved line 1" from the edge to connect the 2 straight lines.Then take your rotary tool and cut along the lines.Note: We make the markings 1" from the edge of the guard so when we screw it in from the inside it has something to grab onto. If this step seems confusing, look at the next step to see the guard over the hole. Place your guard across the hole you just cut, and mark the curve of the bucket with a permanent marker. Then take either your rotary tool or snips (snips work better in my opinion) and cut along the lines.Look how the guard in the first photo has about an inch border, this is what I was referencing in the previous step when marking it. This step is optional (but helpful).Drill holes along the guard's edge to line up from the inside when attaching the screws later. You can also drill from the inside but I found this to be much easier. Align the holes you just predrilled and attach the screws through the guard and to the bottom of the bucket from the inside. I placed 8 screws per bucket to make sure the guard laid flat on the inside. Optional step depending on the length of screw you purchased. We had some laying around that were just a little too long, so we decided to cut them down.Note: if you are cutting them down, leave about 1/8" (3mm) exposed to ensure the bucket has something to grab onto just incase the screws loosen over time. Find a spot with some trash laying around, and put a couple of good scoops in there. Note: Don't put too much all at once or else you will slow the sifting process. One or two scoops of sand is a good amount for quick sifting. Go on, start sifting! Begin splitting up the pieces of debris you've collected document them then dispose of them appropriately. Your local counties will have information on what can and cannot be recycled.Feel free to document your findings through the attached excel spreadsheet and submit them to <EMAIL>. We keep diligent records of all trash and recycling collected, and would love to hear about the results from any cleanups you organize!I hope you have found this instructable interesting and useful! Let's all make waves and remove waste together!

```markdown
# Beach Cleanup Bucket Sifter System

## Summary
This system is designed to create a sifter from a 5-gallon bucket using a gutter guard, a drill, sheet metal screws, and a pair of snips or a Dremel tool. The sifter is used to separate debris from sand during beach cleanups. The process involves cutting a hole in the bucket, attaching the gutter guard, and then using the sifter to filter out trash. The system also includes documenting and disposing of the collected debris.

## Steps

### Preparation
START:
- PROCESS: Gather the necessary materials and tools.
  - INPUT: 5-gallon bucket, gutter guard, drill, 8 sheet metal screws, snips or Dremel tool.

### Creating the Sifter
- PROCESS: Place the gutter guard across the bottom of the bucket.
  - INPUT: Gutter guard, bucket.
- PROCESS: Mark four points on the gutter guard 1" inward from its edge.
  - OUTPUT: Marked points on the gutter guard.
- PROCESS: Connect the marks and draw a curved line to form the cutting guide.
  - OUTPUT: Curved cutting guide on the gutter guard.
- PROCESS: Use a rotary tool to cut along the guide lines.
  - OUTPUT: Cut gutter guard to fit the bucket bottom.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the gutter guard cut correctly?
  - Yes: Proceed to the next step.
  - No: END: Adjust cutting as necessary and retry.

### Attaching the Guard
- PROCESS: Align the cut gutter guard over the bucket and mark the curve of the bucket on it.
  - INPUT: Permanent marker.
  - OUTPUT: Curve marking on the gutter guard.
- PROCESS: Cut along the marked lines with snips or a rotary tool.
  - OUTPUT: Gutter guard shaped to match the bucket's curve.
- PROCESS: Optionally pre-drill holes along the edge of the guard.
  - OUTPUT: Pre-drilled holes for easier screw attachment.
- PROCESS: Align the holes and attach the screws from inside the bucket to secure the guard.
  - INPUT: Screws, drill.
  - OUTPUT: Gutter guard securely attached to the bucket.
- DECISION [IF]: Are the screws too long?
  - Yes: Cut down the excess length of the screws.
  - No: Proceed to the next step.

### Using the Sifter
- PROCESS: Find a spot with trash and add a couple of scoops of sand to the sifter.
  - OUTPUT: Sand and debris in the bucket sifter.
- PROCESS: Sift the sand to separate debris.
  - OUTPUT: Separated debris and clean sand.
```

instruct00278.title: Easy No-Mess Chocolate Chunks From Chocolate Bars
instruct00278.text: How to make easy to clean up no-mess chocolate chunks from bars of chocolate. This is for all those chocolate chunk recipes, people who have allergies and can only find chocolate bars (cannot find chocolate chips) and those people who would like to make chocolate chunk cookies out of their favorite chocolate bars. Also is great for melting chocolate in a double boiler, the smaller the chunks the faster the chocolate melts. I have "kid" tested this with a 4 year old and they could break the bar a few times but I ended up doing most of the work. Thus kids please have an adult help with this activity. Figure out how many chocolate bars are needed for the recipe. Most chocolate bars I have used are about 3-3.5 oz and recipes will call for 12-16 oz of chocolate chips. So to replace chips one for one to chunks you will need to break up 4-6 bars. I have found one to two bars broken up works find in the recipes I make. (I like them on the lighter side of chocolate.) I normally add chunks until the batter looks "full" or it looks like I will get 4+ small chunks per small spoon dropped cookie. Materials needed: Chocolate bars* Plastic bags (gallon freezer bags are less likely to break and will keep this "no-mess") Large metal spoon** *Calculated from previous step. **Plastic will not work well due to the plastic absorbing the force. The chocolate bars need to be frozen (over night). The bars will not break well into little pieces if not frozen through. Unwrap the chocolate bar and put into a freezer bag large enough to hold the whole bar. (Picture shows half a bar so the bag would fit in the pictures) Do not decide to save the bag and go on to the next step with the chocolate in the silver wrapping. The silver wrapping will break apart and throw chocolate chunks all over and the size of the chunks will be very inconsistent due to no viability through the wrapping. Start smacking the bars with the back of the spoon. The chocolate bar will start to break into smaller and smaller pieces. Try to smack the bar in the middle of the area that needs breaking. If the bar starts to dent or mush then refreeze. I like my chunks smaller then chocolate chips so I break the pieces more then if some liked large chocolate chunks. The smaller chunks melt better in recipes, like double boilers. Once the chunks are the desired size add to recipe.

```markdown
# No-Mess Chocolate Chunks from Chocolate Bars System

## Summary:
This process describes how to create chocolate chunks from bars of chocolate for use in recipes, especially when chocolate chips are unavailable or when a specific type of chocolate bar is preferred. The method ensures a no-mess preparation and is suitable for melting chocolate in a double boiler as well. It's recommended that children have adult assistance when following these steps.

## Steps:

START:
- Begin the no-mess chocolate chunk preparation process.

PROCESS: Determine chocolate quantity
- INPUT: Identify the number of chocolate bars needed based on the recipe requirement.
- OUTPUT: Quantity of chocolate bars to be used.

PROCESS: Prepare materials
- INPUT: Gather chocolate bars and plastic bags (preferably gallon freezer bags).
- OUTPUT: Prepared materials ready for use.

PROCESS: Freeze chocolate bars
- INPUT: Unwrap the chocolate bars and place them in the freezer bag.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the chocolate bar fully wrapped in the freezer bag?
  - Yes: Proceed to the next step.
  - No: Ensure the chocolate bar is fully enclosed in the freezer bag to avoid mess.

PROCESS: Freeze the chocolate bars overnight
- INPUT: Place the wrapped chocolate bars in the freezer.
- OUTPUT: Frozen chocolate bars ready for breaking.

PROCESS: Break the chocolate bars into chunks
- INPUT: Remove the frozen chocolate bars from the freezer.
- INPUT: Use a large metal spoon for breaking the chocolate.
- PROCESS: Smack the bars with the back of the spoon to break into smaller pieces.
- DECISION [IF]: Are the chocolate bars breaking into desired chunk sizes?
  - Yes: Continue to the next step.
  - No: Refreeze the bars if they start to dent or mush, then resume breaking.

PROCESS: Achieve desired chunk size
- DECISION [IF]: Are the chunks smaller than chocolate chips as desired?
  - Yes: Proceed to add them to the recipe.
  - No: Continue breaking the pieces until the desired size is achieved.

OUTPUT: Chocolate chunks ready for recipe use
- INPUT: Desired size chocolate chunks.
- OUTPUT: Chocolate chunks ready to be added to the recipe.

END:
- The no-mess chocolate chunk preparation process is complete.
```
