```markdown
# Chocolate Chip Cookie Recipe System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Begin chocolate chip cookie recipe process.

### INPUT:
- Gather the following ingredients:
  - 9 ounces of unsalted butter (room temperature)
  - 6 ounces of light brown sugar
  - 6 ounces of granulated sugar
  - 2 eggs
  - 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  - 13 ounces bread flour
  - 1 teaspoon salt
  - 1 teaspoon baking soda
  - 12 ounces of semisweet chocolate chips
- Optional: Chopped walnuts (if desired)
- Equipment needed:
  - Hand or stand mixer (dough hooks optional)
  - Large mixing bowl
  - Cutting board
  - Sifter
  - Wooden spoon
  - Sheet pans
  - Parchment paper
  - Knife
  - Spatula
  - Cooling rack
  - Tape measure (for measuring dough)

### PROCESS:
- Preheat oven to 375 degrees Fahrenheit.

### PROCESS:
- Using a mixer, beat together the butter, brown sugar, and granulated sugar at medium speed until well combined.

### INPUT:
- Add the eggs and vanilla extract to the mixture.

### PROCESS:
- Sift the bread flour, baking soda, and salt together.

### PROCESS:
- Gradually mix the sifted dry ingredients into the batter until well incorporated.

### DECISION [IF]: Are you adding walnuts?
  - Yes: Stir in the chocolate chips and chopped walnuts into the batter.
  - No: Stir in only the chocolate chips into the batter.

### OUTPUT:
- The dough should come together and form a ball.

### PROCESS:
- Divide the dough into 3 equal pieces, each weighing approximately 1 pound.

### PROCESS:
- Roll each piece into a rope 16 inches long.

### PROCESS:
- Use a tape measure to mark the rope at one-inch intervals.

### PROCESS:
- Cut each rope into 16 equal pieces.

### PROCESS:
- Line sheet pans with parchment paper.

### PROCESS:
- Place the pieces, cut side up, on the prepared sheet pans, staggering them to avoid baking together.

### DECISION [IF]: Are cookies spaced properly?
  - Yes: Proceed to baking.
  - No: Re-space cookies properly then proceed to baking.

### PROCESS:
- Bake cookies in the preheated oven for approximately 10 minutes.

### DECISION [IF]: Are cookies just done with slightly brown edges?
  - Yes: Proceed to cooling.
  - No: Continue baking for a short while, then check again.

### PROCESS:
- Remove cookies from oven when done and allow to cool for a few minutes on the sheet pans.

### PROCESS:
- Transfer cookies to a cooling rack to cool completely.

### OUTPUT:
- Perfect chocolate chip cookies, slightly underbaked, soft and chewy inside, lightly crispy outside.

### PROCESS:
- Store cookies in an airtight container.

### END:
- Enjoy your delicious homemade chocolate chip cookies!

## Notes:
- This recipe yields approximately 48 cookies.
- The cookies should be 2 1/2 - 3 inches in diameter.
- The actual baking time may vary depending on individual oven characteristics.
- Always use best judgment when cooking with raw ingredients and adjust as necessary.
```

instruct00717.title: How to Make Your Own Greeting Cards
instruct00717.text: This instructable is a guide in making a simple handmade greeting card. It can be used to make Birthday party invites or other handmade invitations as well! - some coloured paper according to the theme- white card paper (card stock)- craft glue- glue stick- 2 skewers- scissors- paper hole punch- pencil- flat nose plier (optional) Fold the card paper in half, and smooth the edge with your fingernail.I used the flat nose plier to crimp the edge to give it some texture. Take your coloured paper and cut out small boxes to your preferred shapes. You can use chalk to colour over some of the boxes, to give it some texture. Just take your different coloured papers and punch away! Collect the circle shaped confetti from the paper puncher and stick it on your gift boxes the way you like. Draw a straight line as reference on the bottom of the card. Then use this guide to paste your gift boxes on the card, using your glue stick. Cut thin strips of coloured paper, hold it in one hand with your fingers. Then using one side of the scissor blade scrape the paper strip to curl it. Stick these onto your gift boxes using the craft glue. Just cut out oval shapes with small stems from the coloured papers in different sizes, and use these as your balloons. You can decorate it with some of your confetti or chalk. Now you can attach using the craft glue two skewers to the sides of the of the gift boxes as an added embellishment. Glue the balloons to the top of the skewers on both sides and add more ribbons and other thin strips of contrasting colour paper to the gift boxes to give an added effect.

```markdown
# Handmade Greeting Card System

## Summary Representation

### START:
- Begin the process of making a handmade greeting card.

### INPUT:
- Gather materials:
  - Coloured paper (theme-based)
  - White card paper (card stock)
  - Craft glue
  - Glue stick
  - 2 skewers
  - Scissors
  - Paper hole punch
  - Pencil
  - Flat nose plier (optional)

### PROCESS: Fold and Texture Card Stock
- Fold the white card paper in half to create a card base.
- Smooth the edge with a fingernail to firmly crease the fold.
- [IF] Flat nose plier is available:
  - Use the flat nose plier to crimp the edge for added texture.
  - [ELSE]:
    - Proceed without crimping the edge.

### PROCESS: Create and Texture Gift Boxes
- Cut out small boxes from coloured paper to preferred shapes.
- [IF] Texture is desired on boxes:
  - Use chalk to colour over some of the boxes for texture.

### PROCESS: Make Confetti
- Use the paper hole punch to punch out circle-shaped confetti from different coloured papers.
- Collect the confetti.

### OUTPUT:
- Prepared card base, textured gift boxes, and confetti.

### PROCESS: Arrange Gift Boxes on Card
- Draw a straight reference line on the bottom of the card.
- Use the glue stick to paste the gift boxes along the reference line on the card.

### PROCESS: Create and Attach Ribbons
- Cut thin strips of coloured paper for ribbons.
- Curl the strips by scraping them with one side of the scissor blade.
- Stick the curled ribbons onto the gift boxes using craft glue.

### PROCESS: Create and Decorate Balloons
- Cut out oval shapes with small stems from coloured papers for balloons.
- [IF] Additional decoration is desired:
  - Decorate the balloons with confetti or chalk.

### PROCESS: Attach Skewers and Balloons
- Use craft glue to attach two skewers to the sides of the gift boxes as embellishments.
- Glue the balloons to the top of the skewers, positioning them on both sides.

### PROCESS: Final Embellishments
- Add more ribbons and other thin strips of contrasting colour paper to the gift boxes for an added effect.

### OUTPUT:
- Completed handmade greeting card with gift boxes, balloons, and embellishments.

### END:
- The process of creating the handmade greeting card is complete.
```

```markdown
### START:
- Begin the process of creating a 3D Solar System model.

### INPUT: Materials Required
- Foam balls of different sizes for the Sun and all the planets.
- Black foam board.
- Acrylic paint.
- Hot glue.
- Foam sheet.
- White chalk.

## Construction

### PROCESS: Painting the Sun
- Choose the largest foam ball to represent the Sun.

- For texture, apply tissue paper to the painted surface.

### PROCESS: Painting the Planets
- Hand paint each foam ball to represent the planets.

### DECISION: Does Saturn need a ring?
  - IF Yes:

- Cut the foam board into the following pieces:

  - Two pieces measuring 3x11 inches.
  - Two pieces measuring 3x20 inches.
- Assemble the pieces into a box shape using hot glue.

### PROCESS: Painting the Base
- Paint the assembled foam board box with acrylic paint using tissue paper to create texture.

### PROCESS: Adding Stars
- Dip a toothbrush into white paint.
- Flick the bristles with your finger to create a starry effect on the black foam board.

### PROCESS: Drawing Orbits
- Use white chalk to draw the orbital paths of the planets on the base.

### PROCESS: Attaching Planets and Sun
- Use hot glue to attach the painted foam balls representing the Sun and the planets onto the base, following their respective orbits.

## Completion

### OUTPUT:
- The completed 3D Solar System model.

### END:
- The process of creating the 3D Solar System model is completed.
```

instruct00838.title: PVC Recorder
instruct00838.text: Always wanted to make your own recorder? me too. check out this tasty musical instrument. steps 1-7 = photo instructablestep 8 = video instructable +The PVC Recorder uses 3/4" diameter, 1/16" wall PVC. Pipe length is variable. A foot length is a good place to start. + about an inch of 7/8" or 15/16" dowel rod. + a saw, a drill, a file, tinsnips. cut a small length of pvc, about 1" long. Then use the snips and cut once along the length of pipe. cut a pice of dowel rod the same length as the pvc-jaws (piece 1) with the longer piece of pvc, snip out a ~ .25" x 1.25" rectangle out of and end of the pipe. The length of the cut should be the length of the wood stopper + ~.25". flatten out any hanging edges with a file. put the woodstopper inside the end of the long pvc tube, on the side with the gap. put the pvc-jaws over the end of the pvc with the woodstopper. Push the woodstopper and pvc-jaws around so that a proper gap is in place. Blow into the recorder. It should sound like a recorder. The recorder might not work on the first toot. If so, mess with the placement of the wood-stopper and pvc jaw on the long pipe - The air hole size is crucial for a working wind instrument. tinker and test! Also, use a file to smooth (don't "round") the edges of the wood stopper and pvc. Smoother surfaces make for better air flow over the surfaces. If the woodstopper is moving around too much inside the pvc tube, stick some duct tape on the stopper to widen the stopper. in my experience, tinkering just to get sound shouldn't take more than a few minutes. drill some holes in the long pvc pipe to add notes to the pvc recorder. You can do alot of reading and measuring and get western notes, or you can drill haphazardly and get cool stuff.
instruct00838.summary:
```markdown
# PVC Recorder Making Process

## START:
- Begin the process of creating a PVC Recorder.

## INPUT: Gather Materials
- 3/4" diameter, 1/16" wall PVC Pipe (length variable, start with a foot)
- About an inch of 7/8" or 15/16" dowel rod
- A saw
- A drill
- A file
- Tinsnips

## PROCESS: Prepare PVC Jaws (Mouthpiece)
1. Cut a small length of PVC, about 1" long.
2. Use the snips to cut once along the length of the pipe. This piece is referred to as PVC-jaws.

## PROCESS: Prepare Dowel Rod Stopper
1. Cut a piece of dowel rod to the same length as the PVC-jaws.

## PROCESS: Create Air Gap on Long PVC Pipe
1. With the longer piece of PVC, snip out a rectangle approximately 0.25" x 1.25" from one end of the pipe.
2. Ensure that the length of the cut is the length of the wood stopper plus about 0.25".
3. Use a file to flatten out any hanging edges.

## PROCESS: Assemble Mouthpiece
1. Insert the wood stopper inside the end of the long PVC tube, on the side with the gap.
2. Place the PVC-jaws over the end of the PVC with the wood stopper.
3. Adjust the wood stopper and PVC-jaws to create a proper gap.

## DECISION [IF]: Does the Recorder Produce Sound?
- Blow into the recorder to test if it sounds like a recorder.
  - [YES]: Proceed to the next step.
  - [NO]: Tinker with the placement of the wood stopper and PVC-jaws.

## PROCESS: Tinker for Sound
1. Use a file to smooth the edges of the wood stopper and PVC-jaws.
2. If the wood stopper moves too much, use duct tape to secure it.

## OUTPUT:
- A functioning recorder mouthpiece that produces sound.

## DECISION [IF]: Is the Mouthpiece Stable?
- Check if the wood stopper is stable within the PVC-jaws.
  - [YES]: Proceed to drill holes.
  - [NO]: Apply duct tape to the stopper to widen and stabilize it.

## PROCESS: Drill Holes for Notes
1. Drill holes in the long PVC pipe to add notes to the recorder.
2. Decide between precise measurements for western notes or drill haphazardly for unique sounds.

## OUTPUT:
- A completed PVC Recorder with holes for playing notes.

## END:
- The process of creating a PVC Recorder is complete.
```

instruct00220.title: Swan Carved From an Apple
instruct00220.text: My friend's mom made this once as the centerpiece for a fruit tray and I took a crack at it. So now I am here to show all of you do it as well! :) You will need: a good sized apple a sharp paring knife and a cutting board Cut off one side of the apple (as shown). This will be the head and neck. Cut a wedge about the size of a quarter of the apple about 1/2 an inch from the center. Cut a smaller wedge out of the one you just cut leaving about a quarter of an inch of the first wedge. Cut a smaller wedge from the wedge you just cut so you have sizes resembling the picture. Repeat steps 3-5 for the other side making sure to leave some uncut apple (3/4-1 inch is good). Assemble your wedges as seen in the picture and place them on the body. Cut the head out of the side of the apple you have left as in the pictures. Make sure you cut off the skin of the side. Cut a small hole for the head in the body and stick the neck in there. You now have an apple swan! (you may want to sprinkle it with lemon juice to preserve it)

```markdown
# Apple Swan Creation Process

## Inputs
- A good-sized apple
- A sharp paring knife
- A cutting board
- Lemon juice (optional, for preservation)

## Outputs
- An apple swan centerpiece

## Process Steps

START:
- Place the apple on the cutting board.

PROCESS: Cut off one side of the apple
- Use the paring knife to cut off one side of the apple. This piece will serve as the head and neck of the swan.

PROCESS: Cut the first wedge
- Cut a wedge about the size of a quarter of the apple, approximately 1/2 an inch from the center of the apple.

PROCESS: Cut the second wedge
- From the first wedge, cut a smaller wedge, leaving about a quarter of an inch of the first wedge.

PROCESS: Cut the third wedge
- Cut a smaller wedge from the second wedge to create three decreasing sizes of wedges.

DECISION [IF]: Is the other side of the apple intact?
- Yes: Proceed to the next step.
- No: END (The apple cannot be used to create the swan).

PROCESS: Repeat the cutting process for the other side
- Repeat steps of cutting the first, second, and third wedges on the other side of the apple, ensuring a portion of the apple remains uncut (3/4-1 inch is good).

PROCESS: Assemble the apple swan
- Arrange the cut wedges on the body of the apple as seen in the reference picture.

PROCESS: Cut the head of the swan
- From the remaining side of the apple, cut out the head of the swan as shown in the pictures. Ensure to remove the skin from the side that will serve as the head.

PROCESS: Attach the head to the body
- Cut a small hole in the body of the apple where the head will be attached.
- Insert the neck into the hole to attach the head to the body.

DECISION [IF]: Will lemon juice be used for preservation?
- Yes: Sprinkle the apple swan with lemon juice.
- No: Proceed without lemon juice.

OUTPUT: An apple swan centerpiece

END: The apple swan is now complete and ready to be displayed.
```

instruct00852.title: Recycled Milk Jug Bird House
instruct00852.text: As Earth Day is around the corner, and birds are starting to build nests, I decided to make a recycled bird house. This bird box is designed for chickadees. Chickadees happen to be my favorite bird since I have built houses for two generations of these birds. Chickadees prefer houses about 6 or 7 inches square, with a hole about 1" in diameter.And so a milk jug is about perfect for Chickadees. On to the parts list!!!! Parts!! -A milk jug -duct tape -scissors -a sharpie -a long bolt or pencil Take your Sharpie and draw a straight line around the whole thing. Start your line about a centimeter underneath the handle. Next, take the part that you just cut off and locate the little line that goes around the bottom of the jug. Cut on that line. If you put the bottom and top of your jug together you will basically have shortened version of the original milk jug. Tape or glue the two pieces together. Try to keep it as watertight as possible!!! We don't want to accidentally drown a couple of baby birds. I decided to make my house look as ugly as possible and slather the thing in duct tape. You can do whatever you want to do with it. Use you handy dandy scissors and cut off very top of the jug, right where the threads are. Then poke a small hole right underneath the entrance and put a bolt or pencil into it. Try your very best to tape or glue it in place so that it doesn't wobble. Finally, poke a hole in the back of the house and hang it up on a nail. (Chickadees prefer there houses to be about five feet from the ground.) You are done!!!!! I hope that you will enjoy your baby birds as much as I have, and remember RECYCLE!!!!!!!!!!

```markdown
# Recycled Bird House Creation System

## Summary
This system guides the user through creating a birdhouse from a recycled milk jug, designed specifically for chickadees. The process includes cutting and reassembling the jug, making an entrance, and adding a perch. The final product is a recycled birdhouse ready to be mounted outdoors.

## Process Steps

### START:
- Begin the birdhouse creation process.

### PROCESS: Prepare the Milk Jug
- INPUT: A milk jug.
- Use a sharpie to draw a straight line around the milk jug, starting about a centimeter below the handle.

### PROCESS: Cut the Jug
- INPUT: Scissors.
- Cut along the marked line to separate the jug into two pieces.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the cut line even?
  - Yes: Proceed to the next step.
  - No: Adjust the cut to make it even.

### PROCESS: Cut the Bottom Line
- Locate the little line that goes around the bottom of the jug.
- Cut along this line to create two separate jug pieces.

### PROCESS: Assemble the Jug
- Combine the bottom and the top of the jug to form a shortened version of the original milk jug.

### PROCESS: Seal the Jug
- INPUT: Duct tape or glue.
- OUTPUT: A sealed, watertight birdhouse.
- Seal the two pieces together, ensuring it is watertight to prevent water from entering.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the birdhouse watertight?
  - Yes: Continue to the next step.
  - No: Apply additional sealing materials until watertight.

### PROCESS: Decorate the House
- INPUT: Decorative materials (optional).
- OUTPUT: Aesthetically customized birdhouse.
- Decorate the birdhouse as desired, or cover it with duct tape for a simple finish.

### PROCESS: Create the Entrance
- Cut off the very top of the jug, right where the threads are, to create an entrance hole about 1" in diameter.

### PROCESS: Add the Perch
- INPUT: A long bolt or pencil.
- OUTPUT: A birdhouse with a perch.
- Poke a small hole underneath the entrance and insert the bolt or pencil to serve as a perch.
- Secure the perch in place with tape or glue to prevent it from wobbling.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the perch stable?
  - Yes: Move on to the mounting step.
  - No: Reinforce the perch until it is stable.

### PROCESS: Mount the Birdhouse
- INPUT: A nail or mounting hardware.
- OUTPUT: A mounted birdhouse.
- Poke a hole in the back of the house for mounting.
- Hang the birdhouse on a nail, preferably about five feet from the ground.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the birdhouse securely mounted?
  - Yes: The process is complete.
  - No: Secure the birdhouse properly before proceeding.

### OUTPUT:
- A complete, recycled birdhouse ready for chickadees.

### END:
- The birdhouse creation system is concluded.
```

instruct00568.title: Portable Fire Pit With Built in Log Storage Rack.
instruct00568.text: If you ever wanted a fire pit without spending $80+ dollars, this if for you. The total cost of this project was under $15.00. Depending on materials on hand, you should be able to put one of these together for about the same amount of money. You start with a search for a suitable shopping cart which has to be one with a chrome finish. I found mine close to the loading dock area of a local grocery store and there it was next to a trash compactor. I went in the store and asked the manager if I could purchase it and was told I could have it for free. The generosity stemmed from the fact that current shopping carts have a powder coat finish so the old style chrome carts are no longer used. I would suggest staying away from the powder coat carts as the heat generated by burning wood in the basket will destroy the finish. The chrome finish will continue to look good after several burns. MATERIALS Chrome shopping Cart 27" x 8' steel lath galvanized steel drip edge flashing galvanized steel corner bead 3 cookie sheets hinges handle 1 pr galvanized steel hurricane ties nuts and bolts The first step after obtaining your cart is to remove all things rubber and plastic. There is no reason to leave those attached to the cart and the heat will make quite a mess of them. I left the handle in place and after a few test burns found that the heat from the fire did not affect the handle in any way. With the rubber and plastic parts removed, you are ready to start your project. Build a frame that will fit snugly in the bottom of the basket. For this I used a section of galvanized steel drip edge flashing which I found at the Habitat for Humanity ReStore location. A plug for ReStore a great source of materials donated by contractors, big business and individuals. Use caution when cutting and bending the flashing as, I can tell you from personal experience, the edges are sharp. The purpose of the frame is to keep any embers from rolling out of the basket. When your wife is not looking, grab her cookie sheets and cut the sides off with a jig saw. Measure and cut so they fit inside the frame. On this step you can substitute with materials on hand e.g. a piece of sheetmetal, car hood. The gap between the bars on the shopping cart are probably not close enough for keeping embers from flying out so, to play it safe, I lined all four sides with steel lath which I found at the local builders supply store for under $9.00. The sheets are 27" x 8' which is enough for all 4 sides and a piece left over that you can use for a spark screen cover. Steel lath is miserable stuff to work with so keep bandages on hand. With large washers you can bolt the four sides of lath to the shopping cart. Cut the remaining piece of steel lath to the same dimensions as the opening of the basket and then frame the lath with the galvanized corner bead. Use nuts and bolts on all four sides to keep everything in place. I used two of the sides that were cut off the cookie sheet and bolted them to the bottom pan. This will create a small gap between the burning wood and the pan to give you a better burn. The hurricane ties are bolted to the shopping cart and will support the hinges that connect the spark screen to the shopping cart.

```markdown
# Fire Pit Creation from a Shopping Cart - Process Summary

## START:
- Begin the process of creating a fire pit from a shopping cart.

## INPUT: List of Materials
- Chrome shopping cart
- 27" x 8' steel lath
- Galvanized steel drip edge flashing
- Galvanized steel corner bead
- 3 cookie sheets
- Hinges
- Handle
- 1 pair of galvanized steel hurricane ties
- Nuts and bolts

## PROCESS: Obtain a Shopping Cart
- Search for a suitable chrome-finished shopping cart.
- Locate a cart near a local grocery store's loading dock area.

## DECISION [IF]: Is the shopping cart available for free?
- IF YES: Proceed with the project.
- ELSE: Negotiate or purchase the cart.

## PROCESS: Prepare the Shopping Cart
- Remove all rubber and plastic parts from the cart.
- Leave the handle in place if it is not affected by heat.

## PROCESS: Build a Frame for the Basket
- Obtain galvanized steel drip edge flashing from a ReStore location or other source.
- Cut and bend the flashing to fit snugly in the bottom of the cart's basket.

## PROCESS: Modify Cookie Sheets
- When unnoticed, take 3 cookie sheets.
- Cut the sides off the cookie sheets to fit inside the frame made from flashing.

## DECISION [IF]: Do you have alternative materials?
- IF YES: Use materials like sheet metal or a car hood instead of cookie sheets.
- ELSE: Use the cookie sheets as planned.

## PROCESS: Line the Cart with Steel Lath
- Purchase steel lath from a builder's supply store.
- Measure and cut the lath to line all four sides of the cart.
- Bolt the lath to the cart with large washers.

## PROCESS: Create a Spark Screen
- Cut a remaining piece of steel lath to the dimensions of the cart's opening.
- Frame the lath with galvanized steel corner bead.
- Secure the framed lath with nuts and bolts.

## PROCESS: Enhance Burning Efficiency
- Use the sides cut from the cookie sheets.
- Bolt them to the bottom pan of the cart to create a gap for better burning.

## PROCESS: Install Hinges and Support
- Attach galvanized steel hurricane ties to the cart.
- Bolt the hinges to the ties to connect the spark screen.

## OUTPUT:
- A fully assembled, cost-effective fire pit made from a repurposed shopping cart.

## END:
- The fire pit creation process is complete.
```

instruct00324.text: My name is Evan Pickett. I graduated as a dual major in both mechanical and manufacturing engineering. I see a use for contractors, beach goers, race pit crews, and so many other areas. My wheelbarrow will go up hills, through mud, gravel, sand, bark dust, over small obstacles on the ground, all with little effort from the user. With the prize money I will purchase enough parts to build 50 wheelbarrows as a first edition build. With these 50 units, I will have enough product to get my wheelbarrows UL certified and bring them to market. I will use the rest of the money to define my business brand with the help of a marketing team. I am also working on a website that the wheelbarrows will eventually be sold from. www.deadnutsdesignco.com

instruct00252.title: How to Make Clay
instruct00252.text: Have you ever wanted to make your own clay and not buy the expensive clay at the hobby store?Well, heres the instructable, How to make clay!This instructable will be explaining how to make a type of clay is made from not rocky stuff, but food. The clay is easy to make and you can easily get the ingredients from most food stores. You can keep this type of clay for a very long time if stored in a air-tight container in a cool dark place. It also has another advantage, instead of most types of clay that needs to be baked to solidify, it can be air-dried to solidified, so that clay is a bit 'green' too, you don't have to waste electric or gas just to solidify clay models.And one more thing... This type of clay is great for all ages! It is time to go shopping or dig into your cupboard to get the ingredients! Get the things as listed...3 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour1/2 cup of salt1 tablespoon of cream of tarter2 1/2 tablespoons of oil2 cups of water,Of course, you can divide or add more ingredients.And the tools...Anything that can boil waterLarge mixing bowlWooden spoonCookie sheetAll of this stuff are optional, used to decorate your work pieces...food coloringPaintCarving toolsCookie cutterLarge needleOr what ever you think it is the best! Okay, you got all of the stuff you need (hopefully) and lets start making clay!Add water into anything that can boil water, preferably a pot. Start boiling the water and if you are going to make colored clay, add a few drops of food coloring now. (Note to kids: you will need your parents supervision to boil water.) While you are waiting for the water to boil, put all the dry ingredients into the large mixing bowl and mix it all up! After the water is boiling, remove it from heat and then add in the oil and mix it together. Slowly pour the hot oiled water into the large bowl with the dry ingredients and mix it together thoroughly using the wooden spoon. After you have mixed it thoroughly, let the mixture sit somewhere cool to cool down the warm mixture.If you like, you can add a little vanilla extract to the mixture to make aromatic clay! After the mixture in the bowl cooled, take it all out of the bowl and put it down on the cookie sheet and begin kneading the mixture until it becomes pliable consistency like that of store-bought clay. Done!You now made the clay that is cheap to make compared to the expensive store-bought clay!Now you can hand it over to your little kids to play with. And after they have done playing with it, store the clay in an air-tight containers to retain its moisture so it can be used again!Or...Make models out of clay and let it dry out in air (never bake this type of clay, it will ruin it) and then paint it!Or...Make pottery out of that clay, carve it with your carving tools or something like that, then air-dry it, and paint it!I hope you enjoyed this instructable!If you have any questions, or need help, or found an error, or anything, make a comment! I like comments!

```markdown
# How to Make Clay from Food-Based Ingredients

## Summary Representation

START: Begin the process of making homemade clay.

INPUT: Gather all ingredients and tools.
- 3 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup of salt
- 1 tablespoon of cream of tartar
- 2 1/2 tablespoons of oil
- 2 cups of water
- Optional: food coloring, vanilla extract
- Tools: pot for boiling water, large mixing bowl, wooden spoon, cookie sheet, additional tools for decoration (paint, carving tools, cookie cutters, large needle)

PROCESS: Boil water in a pot.
- DECISION [IF]: Is colored clay desired?
  - Yes: Add a few drops of food coloring to the boiling water.
  - No: Proceed without adding food coloring.

PROCESS: Mix all dry ingredients in a large mixing bowl.
- 3 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup of salt
- 1 tablespoon of cream of tartar

PROCESS: Once water is boiling, remove from heat.
- Add 2 1/2 tablespoons of oil to the hot water and mix.

PROCESS: Slowly pour the hot oiled water into the bowl with dry ingredients.
- Mix thoroughly with a wooden spoon.

PROCESS: Allow the mixture to cool in a cool area.

DECISION [IF]: Is aromatic clay desired?
  - Yes: Add a little vanilla extract to the mixture.
  - No: Proceed without adding vanilla extract.

PROCESS: After cooling, knead the mixture on a cookie sheet.
- Continue kneading until it reaches a pliable consistency similar to store-bought clay.

OUTPUT: The homemade clay is now ready for use.
```

instruct00202.title: Movable Record Player Greeting Card From a Floppy Disk
instruct00202.text: The actual disk part of an old 3.5" floppy disk looks suspiciously like a record, doesn't it? It only takes a few minutes to turn one into this personalized turntable greeting card. The best part is that the card is assembled with brads so the record spins and the player arm moves, too. Perfect for audiophiles and geeks alike. For this project you'll need:- an old 3.5" floppy disk- a flathead screwdriver- scissors- hole punches- blank greeting cards or cardstock to make your own- small brads- cardstock or corrugated paper for the record player arm- embellishment items: stamps, collage paper, glue stick, etc.If you don't have 3.5" floppy disks of your own, try a local second-hand store. In the Portland, OR, area both SCRAP and Free Geek usually have them for 25 cents or less apiece. Start by busting into the floppy disk. Pull off the protective flap and slide the screwdriver between the plastic sides and twist to pop the disk case open. Try to avoid marring the disk inside with the screwdriver. At this point I always remember past teachers' admonishments to never! touch! the disk! Ha! I'm touching the disk!After you've broken it open, you'll be left with several parts of the floppy disk case that are not used in this Instructable. All you need right now is the round, magnetic disk. You can use the other bits to make something else. Lay the disk on the card and mark spots in the middle of the disk and where the arm of the record player will be located. Punch small holes where you made the marks in the last step. You can use a narrow punch like this one, a darning needle, or whatever else you have handy. Attach the disk to the card with a brad. I like to punch a larger circle of paper to go between them, but it's not required. Cut a thin strip of corrugated paper or cardstock to be the arm of the turntable. Punch a small hole in one end and attach it with the second brad. Now decorate the card however you like. I tend to favor silly music-themed puns cut from old magazines, but maybe that's just me. You're done! Now go give the card to someone. Oh, and if you come up with other cool uses for the leftover disk parts, please mention them in the comments here or on my blog.

```markdown
# Turntable Greeting Card System

## Inputs
- Old 3.5" floppy disk
- Flathead screwdriver
- Scissors
- Hole punches
- Blank greeting cards or cardstock
- Small brads
- Cardstock or corrugated paper for the record player arm
- Embellishment items (stamps, collage paper, glue stick, etc.)

## Outputs
- Personalized turntable greeting card with a spinning record and movable player arm

## Process

### START:
- Begin the process of creating a turntable greeting card.

### PROCESS: Acquire Materials
- INPUT: Check for an old 3.5" floppy disk.
  - DECISION [IF]: Is a floppy disk available?
    - Yes: Continue to the next step.
    - No: Visit a local second-hand store to purchase one. Then continue.

### PROCESS: Disassemble Floppy Disk
- Use a flathead screwdriver to remove the protective flap of the floppy disk.
- Slide the screwdriver between the plastic sides and twist to open the case without damaging the disk inside.

### PROCESS: Prepare Greeting Card
- INPUT: Select a blank greeting card or cardstock.
- Lay the magnetic disk on the card.
- Mark the center of the disk and the location for the record player arm on the card.

### PROCESS: Punch Holes
- Punch small holes at the marked spots using a hole punch or a darning needle.

### PROCESS: Attach Disk
- Attach the disk to the card with a brad.
  - DECISION [IF]: Do you want to add a larger circle of paper between the disk and the card?
    - Yes: Punch and place a larger circle of paper before attaching.
    - No: Attach the disk directly with a brad.

### PROCESS: Create Turntable Arm
- Cut a thin strip of corrugated paper or cardstock for the arm.
- Punch a small hole in one end of the arm strip.

### PROCESS: Attach Arm
- Attach the arm to the card with the second brad, ensuring it can move.

### PROCESS: Decorate Card
- Decorate the card with music-themed embellishments using stamps, collage paper, glue stick, and other items.

### OUTPUT:
- The personalized turntable greeting card is complete and ready to be given away.

### END:
- The process of creating the turntable greeting card is finished.

## Additional Notes:
- Store the remaining parts of the floppy disk for future projects.
- Encourage sharing of ideas for using leftover disk parts in the comments section.
```

```markdown
# Super Mario Ornaments Creation Process

## Inputs
- Two different sizes of styrofoam balls
- Paint (red, green, white, or original colors)
- Mod podge or spackle
- Glue
- Small gauge wire or pre-formed ornament hook
- Wire cutters
- X-acto knife
- Sandpaper
- Paintbrush and cups for water
- Masking tape or contact paper

## Outputs
- Finished Super Mario-themed Christmas ornaments

## Process

START:
1. Gather all materials needed for the project.

PROCESS: Carve the Styrofoam Balls
2. Mark both styrofoam balls with cutting lines to create an even circle guide.
3. Cut each of the pieces flat along the marked lines.
4. On the larger ball's flat side, mark a circle approximately the size of the smaller ball's circumference.
5. Hollow out the inside of the larger ball using the circle as a guide.
6. Check if the stem piece fits inside the larger ball and make adjustments if necessary.
7. Sand the flat sides of each ball to ensure an even, smooth edge.

PROCESS: Create the Ornament Hook
8. [IF] Do you already have ornament hooks?
   - [YES] Proceed to Mod Podge or spackle application (Step 13).
   - [NO] Continue to Step 9.
9. Cut a small length of wire with wire cutters.
10. Form a small spiral around the handle of the X-acto knife or a pencil.
11. Pierce through the inside of the mushroom cap with the wire, flattening the spiral to prevent slipping.
12. Form the wire into a hook shape and trim as necessary.

PROCESS: Apply Mod Podge or Spackle
13. Paint a thin layer of Mod Podge or spackle over the outer surface of the mushroom pieces.
14. Let the Mod Podge or spackle dry thoroughly.
15. Sand the surface lightly.
16. Repeat the Mod Podge or spackle application and sanding if necessary for a smooth finish.

PROCESS: Paint the Ornaments
17. Create a mask for the mushroom cap by tracing and cutting out circles from masking tape or contact paper.
18. Place masking circles around the mushroom cap, pressing down all edges.
19. Paint the main color over the masked mushroom caps.
20. Paint the stems white and let them dry.
21. Remove masking circles from the mushroom caps.
22. Paint white circles on the caps, using the edges of the masking as a guide.

PROCESS: Assemble the Ornaments
23. Glue the mushroom stem into the cap.

PROCESS: Final Touches
24. Using paint or a marker, draw on the eyes.

OUTPUT:
25. Hang the completed Super Mario ornaments on your Christmas tree.

END
```

instruct00346.title: Unicorn Barf
instruct00346.text: Ever since I found out that you can buy cereal marshmallowsin bulkon the internet, I have been dreaming about making cereal marshmallow marshmallow treats. Similar to rice cereal treats, but with only the best part of any cereal- the cereal marshmallows! They have affectionately become known as "unicorn barf" around these parts, for obvious reasons, but what is a bad day for a unicorn is a delicious day for everyone else! They are super simple to make and look really pretty! For this recipe I used:2 cups of marshmallows2 1/2 cups of cereal marshmallows1/4 cup butter for the treats, plus extra for greasing everythingYou will also need a sharp knife, a sauce pan, a spatula and a baking tray or glass tray.This recipe made 15 small pieces of unicorn barf but of course you can make more or less depending on how much you want, just keep the ingredients proportional. Before you do anything else, butter up everything you are going to use for this recipe. This will keep it from getting as sticky from the melted marshmallows. Butter up your baking sheet or glass tray beforehand. Don't skimp on the butter. Butter your hands if you want to use them for mixing. Trust me, you'll thank me later! Melt the 1/4 cup of butter in the sauce pan over low heat, and add the two cups of regular marshmallows and stir constantly until the marshmallows are completely melted. I found this goes faster if you chop up your marshmallows before you add them to the butter. Keep stirring until the marshmallows are completely dissolved and combined with the butter and have a smooth consistency. This step you have to move fast.When your plain marshmallows and butter are combined and have a smooth texture, take them off the heat and add your cereal marshmallows. Stir them together quickly with your spatula until the cereal marshmallows are evenly coated, but not too much that the melted marshmallows start to dissolve your cereal marshmallows! It's an art. When the cereal marshmallows are thoroughly coated, spread the mixture onto your buttered baking tray or glass tray in a roughly rectangular shape about an inch thick. It will probably stick together fairly well. The shape doesn't matter too much since you are going to cut it up later, but it's helpful if it has relatively even thickness. This is the hardest part. Put it in the fridge and wait for about 20 minutes. This is the perfect time to wash out the pan before the marshmallow starts to solidify in it. I found that using very hot water is the best way to get the sticky marshmallow goo out of the pan. I cut this batch into a rectangle because the cute sides look really pretty with all the different colors of cereal marshmallows. I cut the rectangle into 15 pieces that were about 1.5 inches square. These things are so sweet, that's probably going to be all you want!
instruct00346.summary:
```markdown
# Unicorn Barf (Cereal Marshmallow Treats) Recipe System

## Ingredients and Tools
- INPUT: 2 cups of regular marshmallows
- INPUT: 2 1/2 cups of cereal marshmallows
- INPUT: 1/4 cup butter (for the treats)
- INPUT: Extra butter (for greasing)
- INPUT: Sharp knife
- INPUT: Saucepan
- INPUT: Spatula
- INPUT: Baking tray or glass tray

## Instructions

### Preparation
- START
- PROCESS: Grease the baking tray or glass tray with extra butter.
- PROCESS: Optionally, butter your hands for easier mixing later.

### Melting Marshmallows
- PROCESS: Melt 1/4 cup of butter in the saucepan over low heat.
- DECISION: Are the marshmallows chopped? [IF YES] [ELSE NO]
    - IF YES: Add the chopped marshmallows to the melted butter.
    - ELSE NO: Chop the marshmallows before adding to the melted butter.
- PROCESS: Stir the marshmallows constantly until completely melted and smooth.

### Combining with Cereal Marshmallows
- PROCESS: Remove the saucepan from the heat once marshmallows are smooth.
- PROCESS: Quickly add the cereal marshmallows to the melted marshmallow mixture.
- PROCESS: Stir with the spatula until the cereal marshmallows are evenly coated.

### Shaping and Cooling
- PROCESS: Spread the mixture onto the greased tray into a rectangular shape, about an inch thick.
- PROCESS: Place the tray in the fridge to set for about 20 minutes.

### Cleaning
- PROCESS: Clean the saucepan immediately using very hot water to remove marshmallow residue.

### Cutting the Treats
- PROCESS: Remove the set mixture from the fridge after 20 minutes.
- PROCESS: Cut the mixture into a rectangle and then into 15 pieces, each about 1.5 inches square.
- OUTPUT: 15 small pieces of Unicorn Barf (Cereal Marshmallow Treats).

### Serving
- END: Serve and enjoy the Unicorn Barf treats.
```

instruct00105.title: Modular Water Jug Storage Bins
instruct00105.text: Around here I have more odds and ends than I know what to do with. I used to keep it in piles strewn about our tiny apartment until my fed up girlfriend came up with a solution to make the room a little more organized.It basically involved drinking a lot of bottled water and using the jugs the water came in to store stuff. Using her method, not only do you get a $2 rugged modular plastic storage bin, but you also get 2 gallons worth of drinkable water for free. I highly advocate such a storage system. Especially if you are overrun by small parts. Before you can even consider starting to store stuff in the plastic water jugs, you have to drink the water they're holding. It's recommended that you drink 8 full glasses of water a day. However, drinking a little more than that will not hurt you and may, in fact, be beneficial. If there are two people drinking water from the container, you should be able to go through one in about two to three days. When you are done drinking, cut open the jug. You should do this by slicing away the label on the front side of container. You don't want to make too large of a hole or the container will lose it's structure. You also don't want to make too small of a hole or it will be hard to put things inside. Make the hole just right (see below). There may be a little water left inside. You can shake this water out in the sink and then let it air dry for a day or two before putting things inside. If you're really in a rush and don't care about moisture, wipe out the inside with a dry rag. Once you have completed four water jugs, you want to start bundling them together so that you can begin stacking them without worrying about the whole thing collapsing. The 2 gallon jugs fortunately have two grooves that can be used to tie them together. I used some basic white string that I got at the hardware store. I wrapped the string completely around the outside of the front groove on all of the four containers. On one end of the string I tied a loop using a figure-8 knot (although, any old knot should do). With the other end, I cut the line a little long and pulled the extra string through the loop I just made. I made sure the string was in the grooves all the way around the four containers. Then I folded the string all the way back and tied it onto the taught part of the string using a slipknot. I pulled this knot to make sure the bundle was very tight. To begin with, I would then glue the slipknot in place using hot glue, but I later realized that this wasn't necessary. I then repeated this process for the other groove until there were 2 taught bands wrapped around the whole bundle. Finally! The time has come to start organizing and putting your stuff away into your new cubbies. The nice thing about this is that you can expand cheaply and efficiently to your heart's content.A tip:Once your shelving is of a considerable height and width (say 10 wide by 4 high), you are going to want to tie the whole thing together with two long strings. See the image below to see what in the heck I'm talking about. Did you find this useful, fun, or entertaining? Follow @madeineuphoria to see my latest projects.

instruct00847.title: Make a Homemade Trumpet/Bugle
instruct00847.text: Here's how to make a trumpet out of household items. It sounds just like the real thing, except for the fact that it has no valves. Ya need... O Small length of garden hose O Medium sized funnel O Trumpet mouthpiece (found at any music store) OR use the metalconnector at the end O Duck Tape Make the hose into a circle (Picture 1). Cut both it's metal head off, and you're ready! Now, tape it as shown in picture 4. If you don't have a mouthpiece, only cut one part off. Stick the funnel in one end and if necessary, tape it. Do the same with the mouthpiece. Play it just like you would a trumpet or bugle, if you know how. If you don't, here are snippets from http://www.howtodothings.com/hobbies/a3743-how-to-play-the-trumpet.html. Begin by wetting your lips and press your lips lightly together as if you are about to say "m." Your teeth should be slightly apart. Hold the mouthpiece to the center of your lips, and blow until your lips vibrate. Your lips should be flat and not pursed as in blowing a kiss. Keeping your lips in the same position, move your tongue as if you are about to pronounce the letter "t" (press the tip of your tongue slightly between your teeth without allowing it to stick out of it). Next, slightly withdraw your tongue and simultaneously blow, again creating a vibration. You should just as quickly return your tongue to the "t" position and repeat the steps several times. This movement of the tongue is known as tonguing. Tonguing is important in order to distinctly start and stop between the notes in the music you will be playing. To increase the pitch, you will also need to press your lips more tightly together.Have fun with your new trumpet/bugle.Original idea from a book called: "101 Great Science Experiments" can be found at: http://us.dk.com/nf/Book/BookDisplay/0,,9780756619183,00.html?strSrchSql=101+great+science/101_Great_Science_Experiments_Neil_ArdleyAttached is a demonstration of the three major notes it can play.

```markdown
# Homemade Trumpet System Summary

## START:
- The process to create a trumpet from household items begins.

## INPUT:
- Gather the following materials:
  - A small length of garden hose
  - A medium-sized funnel
  - A trumpet mouthpiece (can be purchased at a music store) or use a metal connector as a substitute
  - Duck Tape

## PROCESS: [Prepare the Hose]
- Shape the garden hose into a circle.

## PROCESS: [Modify the Hose]
- Cut off both metal heads of the garden hose.

## DECISION: [IF] Do you have a trumpet mouthpiece?
  - Yes: Proceed to taping the hose.
  - No: Cut off only one metal end of the hose.

## PROCESS: [Tape the Hose]
- Secure the hose with Duck Tape as shown in the provided picture 4.

## PROCESS: [Attach the Funnel]
- Insert the funnel into one end of the hose.
- IF necessary, secure the funnel with Duck Tape.

## DECISION: [IF] Is the trumpet mouthpiece available?
  - Yes: Attach the mouthpiece to the other end of the hose.
  - No: Use the metal connector as a substitute for the mouthpiece.

## PROCESS: [Secure the Mouthpiece]
- IF using a mouthpiece, insert it into the other end of the hose and tape if necessary.
- ELSE, secure the metal connector with Duck Tape as a substitute mouthpiece.

## OUTPUT:
- The homemade trumpet is now assembled and ready to play.

## PROCESS: [Play the Trumpet]
- Wet your lips and press them lightly together, as if saying "m".
- Keep teeth slightly apart.
- Hold the mouthpiece to the center of your lips.
- Blow until your lips vibrate, keeping lips flat, not pursed.
- Move your tongue as if pronouncing "t", with the tip slightly between your teeth.
- Withdraw your tongue, blow to create vibration, and quickly return to "t" position.
- Repeat the steps several times for tonguing, which starts and stops notes distinctly.
- To increase pitch, press lips more tightly together.

## OUTPUT:
- You can now play notes with the homemade trumpet.

## END:
- The process of creating and playing a homemade trumpet from household items is complete.
```

instruct00172.title: Paracord Watchband/bracelet With a Side Release Buckle
instruct00172.text: This tutorial will show how to make a paracord watchband with a side release buckle using the alternate half-hitch. It can also be made without a watch for use as a paracord bracelet, or on a larger scale as a dog or cat collar. More projects, links, knot references can be seen on my blog page, Stormdrane's Blog. Supplies needed: 10 feet of paracord, scissors, torch lighter, tape measure, a watch with the watchand pins, and a 5/8 inch side release buckle. The 5/8 inch curved buckles can be found at Creative Designworks or ITW Nexus brand ones on ebay, either will work fine. I use paracord with the 7 inner strands from the Supply Captain, but other similar types/diameter of cord will work as well. Measure your wrist size by taking the end of the length of paracord and wrapping it around your wrist. Take note of where the end meets the other part of the paracord and lay it out along a tape measure to find your wrist measurement. Attach the paracord to one end of the side release buckle by finding the center of the length of core and putting that end thru the buckle and run the free ends of the cord thru the loop. Because this 5/8 inch buckle is wide, you need tor run the free ends around the buckle one more time and back thru the loop again so you have four loops showing inside the buckle. Attach the watch by sliding the two free ends of cord over the pins, under the watch, and back out over the other pins. Slide the watch to about what will be the halfway point between the two parts of the buckle once the other buckle is attached. Loop onto the other part of the side release buckle, and loop it a second time so there are four loops filling the gap in the buckle. At this point you make sure the length is your wrist size and no more than a 1/2 inch more than your measured wrist size. The length tends to stretch out as you tie the half-hitches, so before you trim and melt the ends, try it on. You may have to untie it and reset the length making it longer or shorter depending on if it's too loose or tight. Now you'll start tying the alternate half-hitches by taking the working ends of the paracord, start with the left piece. Take the left cord under the two center cords and then back thru the loop of the left cord and tighten. Now take the right side cord going under the two center cords and back thru the right loop and tighten. Again with the left, under the two center cords and back thru the left loop, etc.. continuing alternating the left and right cords. When you get about halfway, run the working ends of cord along side the center cords under the watch and slide the watch tight up against the finished portion before you continue the half-hitches on the other side of the watch. Keep tying until you reach the other buckle, then you can trim off the excess cord with scissors. Take your torch lighter and melt the ends and press them so they attach to the surrounding cord. *Be careful not to burn yourself on the molten cord, you may use superglue instead of a lighter if you prefer. You can make the alternate half-hitch without the watch for use as a paracord bracelet, and on a larger scale as a dog or cat collar. You may also use two colors of paracord. If using two colors, instead of one 10 foot piece of paracord, use 5 feet of each color and melt or sew the two ends together and go from there.

```markdown
# Paracord Watchband/Band Bracelet System

## System Inputs:
- 10 feet of paracord (or 5 feet each if using two colors)
- Scissors
- Torch lighter (or superglue)
- Tape measure
- A watch with watchband pins (optional)
- 5/8 inch side release buckle

## System Outputs:
- A completed paracord watchband or bracelet

## Process Steps:

### START:
- Begin the process to create a paracord watchband or bracelet.

### INPUT:
- Gather all necessary supplies.

### PROCESS: Measure wrist size
- Wrap the end of the paracord around your wrist.
- Mark where the end meets the paracord.
- Lay the paracord against a tape measure to find the wrist measurement.

### PROCESS: Attach paracord to the buckle
- Find the center of the paracord length.
- Put the center through one end of the side release buckle.
- Run the free ends of the cord through the loop created.
- Run the free ends around the buckle again and back through the loop for a total of four loops inside the buckle.

### DECISION [IF]: Is a watch being attached?
- YES: Proceed to attach the watch.
- NO: Skip to attaching the second part of the buckle.

### PROCESS: Attach the watch (conditional)
- Slide the two free ends of cord over the pins, under the watch, and back out over the other pins.
- Position the watch at the approximate halfway point between the two buckle parts.

### PROCESS: Attach the second part of the buckle
- Loop onto the other part of the side release buckle.
- Loop it a second time to have four loops filling the gap in the buckle.

### PROCESS: Adjust length to wrist size
- Ensure the length is the wrist size plus no more than a 1/2 inch extra.

### DECISION [IF]: Is the band fitting correctly?
- YES: Proceed to tying half-hitches.
- NO: Adjust the length accordingly.

### PROCESS: Tying alternate half-hitches
- Start with the left piece of paracord.
- Take the left cord under the two center cords and back through the left loop, then tighten.
- Take the right cord under the two center cords and back through the right loop, then tighten.
- Continue alternating left and right cords.

### PROCESS: Position the watch (conditional)
- If a watch is attached, run the working ends of the cord alongside the center cords under the watch.
- Slide the watch tight against the finished portion before continuing.

### PROCESS: Continue tying until the end
- Keep tying alternate half-hitches until reaching the other buckle.

### PROCESS: Trim and melt the ends
- Trim off the excess cord with scissors.
- Melt the ends with a torch lighter and press them to attach to the surrounding cord.

### DECISION [IF]: Is using a torch lighter unsafe or undesirable?
- YES: Use superglue instead.
- NO: Continue with the torch lighter.

### OUTPUT:
- The completed paracord watchband or bracelet is ready for use.

### END:
- The process of creating the paracord watchband or bracelet is complete.
```

instruct00861.title: Easy Chilaquiles
instruct00861.text: What are easy chilaquiles? Check it out: fried tortillas, eggs, cheese, spicy tomato sauce!! Combine those powers together and you get an awesome breakfast. I guess you could use (cringe) tortilla chips to make this even faster....just don't tell me you did. 6 corn tortillas oil for frying 5 eggs whisked 1 can of El Pato sauce shredded cheese (whatever you have in the cool box). Heat the oil in your pan (use canola or vegetable oil) on medium high heat. Stack your tortillas on top of one another, get your trusty knife and cut into triangles. Once your oil is hot, add your tortillas in 2 shifts. Don't crowd your pan because you want the tortillas to get a little crispy. Add tortilla shift one back in the pan with tortilla shift two and add your eggs. Stir the eggs around to cook, season with a little salt, lower the heat to medium low. Add your can of El Pato sauce and stir, coating all the eggs and tortillas. Turn the stove off. Add as much shredded cheese as you like and stir until the cheese melts. Plate it up, grab a fork, say your thanks and dig in! Happy Eating!

```markdown
# Easy Chilaquiles Recipe System

## Ingredients and Tools
- INPUT: 6 corn tortillas
- INPUT: Oil for frying (canola or vegetable oil preferred)
- INPUT: 5 eggs, whisked
- INPUT: 1 can of El Pato sauce (or similar spicy tomato sauce)
- INPUT: Shredded cheese (quantity as desired)
- INPUT: Salt, to taste
- TOOL: Pan
- TOOL: Knife
- TOOL: Stove

## Instructions

### START: Prepare Ingredients
- PROCESS: Stack the 6 corn tortillas.
- PROCESS: Use a knife to cut the stacked tortillas into triangles.

### Heating Oil
- PROCESS: Heat oil in a pan on medium-high heat.

### Frying Tortillas
- DECISION [IF]: Is the oil hot?
  - Yes: Proceed to add tortillas.
  - No: Continue heating oil.
- PROCESS: Add half of the tortilla triangles to the pan (Shift One).
- DECISION [IF]: Are tortillas lightly crispy?
  - Yes: Proceed to next step.
  - No: Continue frying until lightly crispy.

### Adding Remaining Tortillas and Eggs
- PROCESS: Add the remaining tortilla triangles (Shift Two) to the pan with Shift One.
- PROCESS: Add whisked eggs to the pan.
- PROCESS: Stir the eggs and tortillas to cook together.
- PROCESS: Season with salt.
- PROCESS: Lower the heat to medium-low.

### Adding Sauce and Cheese
- PROCESS: Add the can of El Pato sauce to the pan.
- PROCESS: Stir to coat all eggs and tortillas with sauce.
- PROCESS: Turn the stove off.
- PROCESS: Add shredded cheese to the pan.
- DECISION [IF]: Has the cheese melted?
  - Yes: Proceed to plating.
  - No: Continue stirring until cheese melts.

### OUTPUT: Plating and Serving
- PROCESS: Plate the chilaquiles.
- PROCESS: Grab a fork and say thanks before eating.

### END: Enjoy the Meal
- OUTPUT: Serve the prepared easy chilaquiles for a delicious breakfast.
```

instruct00788.title: Cemetery Archway Entrance
instruct00788.text: Just like my Faux Fireplace, I also saw something out at a store like this, and this time it was very well crafted, but way more money than I was wanting to spend, so I figured I would make my own. Please keep in mind that this is made out of cardboard, so I would not suggest having it outside if it is raining. Ok, So again, using the same technique that I made my Faux Fireplace with, I used my leftover priority shipping boxes. This time since the boxes were bigger and a bit heavier, I had to put a couple of screws/bolts between each one to keep them together better. Using spray foam insulation, spray between the boxes. Let this dry, then scrape down the excess foam. For the first coat, I used just plain gray spray paint. For the second coat, I used the fleckstone spray paint to cover the whole thing. This makes it look like real brick. I went to Hobby Lobby and bought a long flexible piece of wood, and some foam letters. I hot glued the letters to the wood, and then bent the wood into an arch. I used tape from one end of the wood to the other to temporarily hold it into an arch. To keep the letters together at the bottoms, I used toothpicks to join them (This is why foam letters work best!) Then you spray the entire thing black. I added spider webs to the entire thing, and bought black birds and 2 stone gargoyles from the dollar store to make it look better. Then just add to your Halloween Scene, and enjoy!!

instruct00720.title: How to Freeze Fresh Yeast
instruct00720.text: I find that fresh yeast works so very much better than the dried stuff. The problem is that it has a very short shelf life. It keeps in the fridge only a matter of days before it starts to go brown and die. Given that recipes call for only a small amount, and I bake bread only once or twice a week, it becomes very wasteful. So now I freeze the yeast in loaf-sized portions and just take it out as I need it. Here's how. First weigh your yeast. My bread machine needs about 11 or 12g (a scant half-ounce) per loaf, so I have enough here for ten loaves. Crumble the yeast into a bowl and add about twice as much flour. It's not critical how much flour, but it helps to make it up to a convenient multiple of loaves. In this case I've made it up to 350g, so each one will be about 35g. Rub the yeast into the flour as if you were making pastry. You should have a fine homogenous mixture with no lumps.The idea is to coat all the particles of yeast with flour so they they don't stick together and will thaw very quickly. Put a piece of cling film onto your scales and weigh out 35g of your mixture. Twist into a ball the size of a golf-ball. Keep it nice and loose so that it crumbles easily when you come to use it. Put all the balls into a ziploc bag and freeze. To use, take a ball out of the freezer and crumble it onto a plate. It will defrost almost immediately, so by the time you have weighed out your other ingredients for the loaf it will be ready. Just add it to the pan after everything else, sprinkling it over the top. You can set the machine going straight away. Tadaaaa! Perfect results every time!

instruct00205.title: How to Make a Clay Bust of Someone You Know. (bronze Finish)
instruct00205.text: What do you buy the man who has everything? Well,I decided to make something he couldn't or wouldn't buy for himself. A clay likeness of himself. At first my plan was to make a clay model then cast itin silicon then concrete for his driveway but I got to such a detail level that I wasn't certain the cast would take so I have given it a bronze like finish. When I have the time I will make one each for my mum and dad in concrete to put at the end of the driveway! This is my first instructable so if you have any questions/critisims then let me know. Find a front facing picture and a profile shot if possible. The green lines are the features that need to be just right and the red lines are all the bumps that make my dads faceHIS face. :-) I built a really simple frame then padded it with plastic bags and as little tape as possible. I then started to mould clay onto the bags witha halfinch thick layer of clay. Once you've got a bulk of clay on in a vaguely human shape, start pressing in detail. Continue adding detail. Remember the shapes you picked out from the photo. My dad was in a seious accident in his yoof which led to quite a bit of scarring. This led to it being easier for me to pick out features. However i had to get them in exactly the right place. I stopped referring to the photo onceI had everything in the right place then changed a coupla details based on memory.Ultimately, its what YOU see in that person that represents them rather than a photo. It sorta helps that I look like him too! Once the bust was dry (this took about a week) I painted it with cheap acrylic paint. I used cheap stuff because its quite plasticy which makes it dry quicker and not soak into the clay. Do not used a water based paint for this. Stick the brush into every nook and cranny. Then I used a couple of Plasti-Kote products to add the bronze. I used what I had simply because I am lazy and a little bit poor. I used liquid enamel in brass with a soft brush to stipple all over the bust till it looked how i wanted it. The trick is to have a higher shine on protruding bits and leave black in the deeper creases. This is the effect of an old polished statue. I thought it looked too brassy so I used a spray on Antique Gold to darken it a bit. I sprayed it on then quickly polished it in with a sponge. When dry, polish lightly with a soft cloth. Done!

instruct00117.title: Magnus Glider
instruct00117.text: Use curveball physics to make this glider fly! This is one of the 48 projects for our Instructables: Made In Your Mind (IMIYM) exhibition at the Children's Museum of Houston showing from May 26, 2012 - November 4, 2012. Produced in partnership with Instructables, IMIYM is an exhibit where families work together to build different fun, toy-like projects that help construct knowledge and skills related to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics while instilling a "do-it-yourself" attitude in kids so they feel empowered to explore, tinker, and try to make things themselves. To learn more, check out the article here. For this project, we were inspired by the$0.05 Toy Hovercraft/HelicopterInstructable created by Hoopajoo, but there may be others on Instructables that are also similar. Often, the materials and process for building our projects are designed for use with a large number of visitors (we see over 800,000 annually) and the need to ensure safety in a mostly non-facilitated environment. So, yes, many of these projects have room for improvement in both materials and methodology, which is PRECISELY what we want to encourage the kids to do. So please do share your ideas for improvement and modifications! We are selective in our materials for cost, ease of use, and safety due to our high traffic (800,000 visitors annually). So, for our purposes, this design worked best. But you may have other ideas - please share! 2 12 oz. Styrofoam cups 4 Rubber bands, #19 Masking Tape We offer optional video segments of each step for this project in the actual exhibit. Here is a compilation of all the steps. Tape the bottoms of the cups together so that the open mouths face away from each other. Make sure the cup bottoms line up evenly with each other. Use several wraps of tape. Take two rubber bands and loop one around the edge of a second, then back through itself. Pull to make the knot tight. Repeat to connect the other bands to the chain. Use your thumb to hold one end of the chain in the center of the cups. Stretching the rubber bands, but not so tight they damage the cups, wrap the chain around the taped part of the cups while holding onto the end of the chain. Once almost completely wrapped, hook the other end of the chain over your other thumb so that the chain is coming out under the cups. The video may be helpful. To launch, hold the hand with the cups behind the other hand. Make sure the rubber band chain is coming out under the cups. Aim your forward hand up in the air, pull the cups back (unwind a little if needed) and let go of the cups. It won't fly high, but rather glide gently to the ground. It is especially cool if you do it at the top of the stairs or off a balcony! The way we explain this in the Museum is that this glider uses the Magnus Effect to give it the slow, gentle glide you see. As the cups spin through the air, they create a sort of "whirlpool" of air around them. This "whirlpool" of air exerts an upward force on the cups. Baseball pitchers rely on this same effect to throw a mean curveball! The next step would be to try to build their own version. What if: They used more cups? They used different sized cups? They used different size rubber band? They used longer or shorter rubber band chains? They used different kind of cups (plastic, paper, etc.)? Only one way to find out! Please post your results in our comments!

```markdown
# Curveball Physics Glider System

## System Overview
The system describes the process of constructing a simple glider using household materials that operates on the principle of the Magnus Effect. The system inputs include common materials and the output is a functional glider that can glide through the air when launched. The system is intended for educational purposes to teach children about physics and the DIY approach.

## Materials (Inputs)
- INPUT: 2 x 12 oz. Styrofoam cups
- INPUT: 4 x Rubber bands, #19
- INPUT: Masking Tape

## Process Steps

### Step 1: Prepare the Cups
- START
- PROCESS: Align the bottoms of the two Styrofoam cups evenly with each other.
- PROCESS: Tape the bottoms of the cups together using several wraps of masking tape, ensuring the open mouths face away from each other.

### Step 2: Create Rubber Band Chain
- PROCESS: Loop one rubber band around the edge of a second rubber band, then back through itself.
- PROCESS: Pull to tighten the knot, forming a link in the chain.
- PROCESS: Repeat the linking process to connect the remaining rubber bands into a chain.

### Step 3: Attach Rubber Band Chain to Cups
- PROCESS: Hold one end of the rubber band chain with your thumb at the center of the cup's bottoms.
- PROCESS: While maintaining tension but not so tight as to damage the cups, wrap the chain around the taped part of the cups.
- DECISION: Is the rubber band chain almost completely wrapped around the cups?
  - IF YES: Proceed to the next step.
  - IF NO: Continue wrapping.

### Step 4: Secure Rubber Band Chain
- PROCESS: Once the chain is nearly fully wrapped, hook the other end of the chain over your other thumb, ensuring the chain is coming out under the cups.

### Step 5: Launching the Glider
- PROCESS: Hold the hand with the cups behind the other hand.
- PROCESS: Ensure the rubber band chain is coming out from under the cups.
- PROCESS: Aim your forward hand up in the air.
- PROCESS: Pull the cups back to create tension in the rubber band chain (unwind a little if needed).
- OUTPUT: Release the cups to launch the glider, which will glide gently to the ground.

### Step 6: Observe the Magnus Effect
- PROCESS: Observe the glider as it spins through the air, creating a "whirlpool" of air around it.
- OUTPUT: The "whirlpool" of air exerts an upward force on the cups, demonstrating the Magnus Effect.

### Step 7: Experimentation and Modification
- DECISION: Do you want to modify the design?
  - IF YES: Proceed to experimentation.
  - IF NO: END.

### Step 8: Experiment with Variables
- PROCESS: Experiment with different variables such as the number of cups, size of cups, rubber band sizes, length of the rubber band chain, and types of cups.
- OUTPUT: Observe how changes affect the flight and glide of the glider.

### Step 9: Share Results
- PROCESS: Encourage sharing of results and modifications to improve the design.
- END: Encourage a DIY attitude in kids and instill a sense of exploration and innovation.

## End of System
```

instruct00728.title: Gyro Flyer
instruct00728.text: Make a cylindrical paper airplane! This is one of the 48 projects for our Instructables: Made In Your Mind (IMIYM) exhibition at the Children's Museum of Houston showing from May 26, 2012 - November 4, 2012. Produced in partnership with Instructables, IMIYM is an exhibit where families work together to build different fun, toy-like projects that help construct knowledge and skills related to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics while instilling a "do-it-yourself" attitude in kids so they feel empowered to explore, tinker, and try to make things themselves. To learn more, check out the article here. For this project, we've taken an Instructable created by someone else and modified it for use in the Museum. This specific project is based on theFlyingGyroscope Out of a Single Pieceof Paperproject by mspark400, but there may be others on Instructables that are also similar. Often, the materials and process for building our projects are designed for use with a large number of visitors (we see over 800,000 annually) and the need to ensure safety in a mostly non-facilitated environment. So, yes, many of these projects have room for improvement in both materials and methodology, which is PRECISELY what we want to encourage the kids to do. So please do share your ideas for improvement and modifications! We are selective in our materials for cost, ease of use, and safety due to our high traffic (800,000 visitors annually). So, for our purposes, this design worked best. But you may have other ideas - please share! 1 - 8" x 11" sheet of paper Masking Tape We offer optional video segments of each step for this project in the actual exhibit. Here is a compilation of all the steps. Lay the piece of paper landscape (horizontal) on a flat surface. Fold the top edge of the paper to the bottom edge and unfold to create a crease. Fold the top edge of the paper to the crease. Fold along the crease. Fold the current top edge to the bottom of the folded part of the paper (basically, fold the folded part in half). Roll the paper, sliding the edge of the left side of the ring into the slot on the inside of the right side of the ring. Tape it shut along the seam. To throw it: hold it in your hand with the thicker edge forward and toss it like a football, using your fingers to give the paper a spin as you throw it. The video shows it a little better. The Gyro Flyer isa simplified (and much cheaper) version of theX-Zylo toy. Inboth cases, they useboth aerodynamics and gyroscopic motion to fly. Much like a plane's wing, the front of the Gyro Flyer is thicker than the back end. This causes the air as it flows over and throughthe Gyro Flyer to provide lift, or push it slightly up. The gyroscopic motion is created by the spinning of the tube. Much like a spinning top doesn't fall over, the spinning of the tube keeps the front end aimed forward and prevents gravity from flipping it or losing its angle of attack through the air as fast as a normal paper airplane, which is why it can fly so well.

```markdown
# Cylindrical Paper Airplane System

## Inputs
- 1 sheet of 8" x 11" paper
- Masking tape

## Outputs
- A cylindrical paper airplane (Gyro Flyer)

## Process Steps

START:
- Place the 8" x 11" sheet of paper in a landscape orientation on a flat surface.

PROCESS: Fold Creation
- INPUT: Top edge of the paper.
- Fold the top edge of the paper to the bottom edge.
- OUTPUT: A horizontal crease across the middle of the paper.
- Unfold the paper to reveal the crease.

PROCESS: First Fold
- INPUT: Top edge of the paper.
- Fold the top edge of the paper to the newly created crease.
- OUTPUT: A fold along the crease.

PROCESS: Second Fold
- INPUT: Current top edge of the paper.
- Fold the current top edge to the bottom of the folded part of the paper, effectively folding it in half.
- OUTPUT: A narrower strip of folded paper.

PROCESS: Rolling into Cylindrical Shape
- Begin rolling the paper to form a cylindrical shape.
- INPUT: Left edge of the paper.
- Slide the left edge into the slot created on the inside of the right edge.
- OUTPUT: Cylindrical form of paper.

PROCESS: Securing with Tape
- INPUT: Masking tape.
- Tape the cylindrical form along the seam to secure it.
- OUTPUT: Completed cylindrical paper airplane (Gyro Flyer).

PROCESS: How to Use the Gyro Flyer
- Hold the Gyro Flyer with the thicker edge forward.
- DECISION [IF]: Is the thrower familiar with throwing a football?
    - Yes: Use a similar motion to throw the Gyro Flyer, adding a spin with fingers.
    - No: Learn to toss it gently to give it a spin.
- OUTPUT: Gyro Flyer in flight demonstrating aerodynamics and gyroscopic motion.

END: The cylindrical paper airplane (Gyro Flyer) is now ready for use and can be thrown to observe its flight capabilities.
```

instruct00330.title: How to Tie a Tie (windsor Knot)
instruct00330.text: Wearing a tie can help you make a good impression. This is a step by step tutorial on how to get it tied right. Place tie over your shoulders with the wide end hanging over your left shoulder. Make sure your collar is up. Adjust the tie so that you only have about a foot hanging on your right side. Cross the left end over the right end about 4-6 inches past the tip of the short end. Pinch the cross-over and pull the wide end up behind the cross-over to make a loop. After you have pulled the wide end out of the loop, make sure that it hangs to the left side of the knot. Take the wide end at your left and pull it around the back. Pull tight. Pull the wide end over the front of the knot and through the hole. Tighten to the left. Pull the wide end around the front and back again and up through the hole. Pull the wide end through the knot behind the front layer of the tie which you just wrapped around the knot in Step 6. Pull the wide end down to tighten up the knot. Make sure it looks good as you tighten it. Pull on the thinner end and push up on the knot to pull the knot up to your collar. Fix your collar and you're done!

```markdown
# How to Tie a Tie: Step-by-Step Process

## Start
START: Begin with a tie and a collared shirt.

## Preparing the Tie and Collar
PROCESS: Place the tie over your shoulders with the wide end on your left side and the narrow end on your right side.
INPUT: Adjust the tie so that the narrow end is about a foot long hanging on your right side.
PROCESS: Make sure your shirt collar is up to accommodate the tie.

## Creating the Knot
PROCESS: Cross the wide end over the narrow end about 4-6 inches past the tip of the narrow end.
PROCESS: Pinch the crossover point to create a reference for the knot.
PROCESS: Pull the wide end up behind the crossover to form a loop.
DECISION: Did you manage to pull the wide end out of the loop?
    IF Yes: Continue to the next step.
    ELSE No: Repeat the process of pulling the wide end up behind the crossover to form a loop.

## Shaping the Knot
PROCESS: Ensure the wide end is now hanging to the left side of the knot.
PROCESS: Take the wide end and wrap it around the back of the knot and pull tight.
PROCESS: Bring the wide end over the front of the knot and pass it through the loop.
PROCESS: Tighten the knot by pulling the wide end to the left.
PROCESS: Wrap the wide end around the front and back again, then up through the loop.

## Finalizing the Knot
PROCESS: Pull the wide end through the knot behind the front layer of the tie.
PROCESS: Pull the wide end down to tighten and shape the knot.
DECISION: Does the knot look symmetrical and neat?
    IF Yes: Proceed to finish the tie process.
    ELSE No: Adjust the knot by tightening or loosening it until it looks good.

## Finishing Touches
PROCESS: Pull on the narrow end while pushing the knot upwards to position it snugly against the collar.
PROCESS: Fix your collar down over the tie.
OUTPUT: A properly tied tie.
END: The tie is now tied, and the process is complete.
```
